s: 1.1 Arguing is something you already do
x: You have argued your whole life. You talked a teacher into an extension, convinced a friend to see the movie you wanted, or explained to a parent why the car needed new tires. Each time you had something you wanted another person to believe or do, and you gave them reasons. This book is about doing that on purpose. Argumentation is the practice of giving reasons to convince someone that an idea or action is right or wrong. Debate is a structured contest in which two sides argue over the same question in front of someone who decides between them. The skills overlap almost completely, which is why a debate class is useful far beyond debate: in a job interview, a city council meeting, or a disagreement at home, you are still building reasons, answering objections and deciding what matters most. Start with what happens whenever one person tries to reach another.

Every debate is an act of communication, so it helps to have a map of how communication works. The communication model breaks any act of communication into eight elements. It was built to describe communication in general, from a phone call to a television ad, but it maps cleanly onto a debate. To see how, follow one speaker through it. Maya, a community college student, has four minutes to convince a judge that her college should give every student a free transit pass. (This example is hypothetical.) Figure 1.1 The communication model in a debate The eight elements of the communication model laid out as one debate: the debater sends arguments through a timed speech to the judge, feedback returns to the debater, and noise interferes with the channel. The sender is the person or source trying to communicate. In a debate, the sender is the debater who has the floor: right now, Maya. The model starts with the sender because communication starts with someone who wants something. Maya wants the judge's ballot, and every other element in the model either helps her get it or gets in her way. Encoding is turning thoughts into a message: deciding what to say and how to say it. Maya knows more about transit than she can fit in four minutes, so encoding is where she chooses. She leads with students who miss class because the bus costs too much. She cuts the history of the transit district. She explains what "fare-free" means instead of assuming the judge knows. Most of what you will learn in this course, from building arguments to choosing which ones to extend, is a lesson in encoding. It helps to think of encoding as curation. A museum curator has far more artifacts than the gallery floor can hold, so every exhibit is a set of choices: which pieces go on display, which stay in storage, what order visitors meet them in, and what the placards say. Each choice serves a goal, whether that is teaching visitors something or giving them a particular experience. A debater faces the same problem. You will almost always know more than your speech time can hold, so encoding means curating: picking the arguments and evidence that best serve your goal with this judge, arranging them so the judge meets the most important ones first, and leaving the rest in storage. When Maya cuts the history of the transit district, she is not hiding it. She is deciding it does not earn floor space in this speech. The message is the information being communicated. In a debate, the message is the arguments, not the speech as a whole. That difference matters. A speech can be long and polished and still carry a thin message, and the judge votes on the message. The channel is the medium the message travels through. A debate's channel is a spoken speech in a timed format, and that channel shapes everything else. How much the judge can go back and check depends on the format. In an extemporaneous format such as parliamentary debate, the judge's only record of the round is their flow, the notes they write while you speak. A sentence they miss is gone, so a spoken argument has to be clearer and more repetitive than a written one. In an evidence-based format such as Lincoln-Douglas or policy debate, the judge may also have a speech document: a file of the formatted, cited evidence the debaters read from. The judge can reread a piece of evidence, but the document holds the evidence, not your explanation of why it matters, so what you say aloud still decides how the judge understands it. The clock means that every sentence Maya spends on one argument is a sentence she cannot spend on another. The receiver is the audience that takes in the message. In a debate, the receiver is the judge. The opponent and anyone watching also hear the speech, but only the judge decides. Maya is not trying to persuade her opponent, who was assigned the other side and is not going to change their mind. Still, persuading the judge is not her only obligation. Her opponent is also a receiver: they have to understand her arguments to answer them, and the debate is only fair if they can. An ethical speaker makes reasonable accommodations for the other side, such as slowing down when asked, explaining jargon, and sharing evidence when the format calls for it. Winning because your opponent could not follow you is not the same as winning the argument. Decoding is how the receiver interprets the message. A judge decodes by listening, writing the argument down and deciding what it means. Decoding is where good encoding pays off or falls apart, and it is where communication most often breaks down, because every receiver interprets a message through their own context. Picture a text from your partner or a close friend that says only "K." If things between you are fine, it reads as a quick, efficient yes. If you argued that morning, the same letter can read as "I am furious with you." The message did not change; the context you brought to it did. Judges decode the same way, through what they already know, believe and expect. If Maya says "transit access improves retention" and the judge does not know that retention means students staying enrolled, the judge decodes a weaker argument than the one Maya meant. Encoding and decoding mirror each other: the sender's job is to make the receiver's job easy. Feedback is the receiver's response, which tells the sender how the message landed. In conversation, feedback is constant: a nod, a puzzled look, a question. A debate gives you three kinds. The judge's reactions during your speech, such as writing, stopping or frowning, arrive immediately. Your opponent's answers in the next speech show what the other side thinks is weakest. The decision and the judge's comments come last. Strong debaters use all three. If the judge stops writing, slow down. If your opponent spends half a speech on one of your arguments, it probably mattered. Noise is anything that interferes with the message getting through. It deserves a closer look, because most of what goes wrong in a debate is noise, and it comes in three kinds. Physical noise comes from the room: a hallway conversation, a buzzing projector. Psychological noise comes from inside the people communicating: a debater's anxiety, or a judge who is tired or has already made up their mind. Semantic noise happens when the words themselves get in the way, such as jargon the judge does not know or a term the two sides define differently. Maya's "retention" problem was semantic noise. You cannot remove all noise, but you can reduce it, and Chapter 5 shows how. Each use of the model happens inside a communication situation, a single, bounded event where communication takes place. For our purposes, a communication situation is one debate. That is why the same speech can win one round and lose the next: the judge, the room and the opponent are different each time. Of the eight elements, the one that matters most in this class is the receiver. You do not win a debate by being right in the abstract. You win by convincing a specific judge. Every choice you make when encoding, from which arguments to read to how fast to talk, should start from the question "what does this judge need to hear?" At a glance Element Definition In a debate Sender The person or source trying to communicate The debater Encoding Turning thoughts into a message: choosing what to say and how to say it Curating: choosing which arguments to make, in what order, and how to phrase them Message The information being communicated The arguments Channel The medium the message travels through A timed spoken speech; in evidence formats, also a speech document Receiver The audience that takes in the message The judge Decoding How the receiver interprets the message How the judge understands and records each argument Feedback The receiver's response, which tells the sender how the message landed The judge's reactions, the opponent's answers, and the decision Noise Anything that interferes with the message getting through Nerves, a fast or unclear delivery, a loud room, an unfamiliar term

More than two thousand years ago, Aristotle described three ways a speaker persuades an audience. They are still the most useful starting point. Ethos is an appeal to credibility: the audience believes you because of who you are or who you cite. "As an emergency room nurse, I have seen what this policy does." Pathos is an appeal to emotion: the audience is moved by what the argument makes them feel. "Imagine telling a child there is no room for her at the shelter tonight." Logos is an appeal to reason: the audience is persuaded by evidence and logic. "Three studies across ten years find the same result." Good arguments usually use all three. In academic debate, logos carries the most weight, because judges are trained to decide on reasons and evidence. Ethos shows up every time you cite a qualified source, and pathos shows up when you make an impact feel real instead of abstract. A statistic about poverty is logos; describing what poverty does to one family is pathos; citing the Census Bureau for the statistic is ethos.

s: 1.4 From an argument to a debate
x: An argument is one message inside a communication situation. A debate is the communication situation itself. Here is a working definition: Debate is a regulated and timed discussion of a proposition between two or more matched sides, decided by an audience, in which one side affirms and the other negates. Each part of that definition names something every debate has: The resolution. The proposition being debated, also called the topic. "This college should replace letter grades with pass/no pass in general education courses." The sides. The affirmative argues that the resolution should be accepted. The negative argues that it should not. Other formats call them government and opposition, or pro and con. The judge. The person or panel who decides who won, and who often enforces the rules, such as speech times. Constructives and rebuttals. Speeches come in two kinds. In constructive speeches, debaters may make new arguments. In rebuttal speeches, they may not, except to answer something new from the speech just before. That rule keeps the debate fair: nobody gets to introduce an argument the other side never has a chance to answer. Three other features appear in most debates without being part of the definition. A criterion is the standard the judge uses to decide the round; you will learn the criterion for each kind of resolution in Chapter 3. Flowing is the note-taking system debaters and judges use to track every argument; Chapter 4 teaches it. Cross-examination is a period where debaters question each other directly; it gets its own chapter, Chapter 11.

The goal of every debate is simple to state: convince the judge to vote for you. Everything else in this book serves that goal. That has a useful consequence. If you lose, the most productive thing to believe is that you did not convince that judge, not that the judge was wrong. Maybe your best argument was never explained clearly. Maybe you answered the arguments you expected instead of the ones your opponent made. Treating the decision as feedback, the seventh element of the model, tells you what to change next time. Blaming the judge tells you nothing. Debating in a class with a judge in the room is practice for any situation where someone else makes the decision: a hiring manager, a jury, a voter, a landlord. In each case, the person deciding is the receiver, and your job is to give them what they need to decide in your favor.

Most speeches open by telling the judge where they are going. Here are frames you can use from your first practice debate: "I am on the affirmative today, and I am arguing that ___." "The resolution asks whether ___. I will give you two reasons to say yes." "My opponent's case rests on one claim: ___. Here is why that claim is wrong." "When you decide this debate, the question to ask is ___." A short opening that uses all three modes of persuasion might sound like this: "As a student who works thirty hours a week, I know what a single failed exam costs. The resolution asks whether this college should grade general education courses pass/no pass. I will give you two reasons to say yes: it lowers the stress that drives students to drop out, and it lets them take the courses they are curious about instead of the ones that protect their GPA."

Situation: A friend is deciding whether to start at a community college or a university, and you think the community college is the better choice. Element Applied Sender and encoding You decide to lead with cost, because you know your friend worries about money, and to keep it short. Message Two years at a community college cost far less in tuition, and the credits transfer. Channel A conversation over lunch, not a group chat, so you can see how they react. Receiver and decoding Your friend hears "cheaper" and worries you mean "worse." Noise Psychological: their parents expect a university, and that expectation filters everything you say. Feedback They push back on prestige, which tells you the next argument has to be about outcomes, not cost. Notice that the most important information came from feedback. Your first message was not wrong; it answered a question your friend was not asking.

Resolution: The United States federal government should establish a universal basic income. In a classroom debate on this resolution, the affirmative is the sender and the judge is the receiver. The affirmative encodes the case as two advantages, about poverty and about health. The channel is a timed constructive speech. Noise comes from the affirmative's nerves, from a negative who uses a term like "labor force participation" without explaining it, and from a judge who arrived with doubts about government spending. Feedback arrives in the negative's answers and, finally, in the decision. A debater who thinks about every one of those elements before the round has already done half the work.

A judge cannot weigh an argument they never understood. Before any of the weighing you will learn later, your argument has to survive decoding: the judge has to hear it, understand it and write it down. Judges reward debaters who make that easy by announcing structure, defining terms and speaking clearly. They also notice the modes of persuasion. An argument with a credible source and a real-world consequence carries more weight than a bare assertion, even when the logic is the same.

Arguing to the opponent instead of the judge. Your opponent is not going to concede. Every sentence is for the person with the ballot. Treating noise as someone else's problem. Speed, jargon and nerves are all noise you can reduce. Ignoring feedback. A judge who stops writing or looks confused is telling you something. Slow down, explain, or move on. Relying on one mode of persuasion. Pure emotion feels manipulative, and pure statistics can feel abstract. Combine them. New arguments in a rebuttal. Unless you are answering something new from the previous speech, a judge will ignore it.

Drill: three audiences (15 minutes, groups of three). Each group picks one scenario: convincing someone not to drop out of high school, asking a boss for a raise, or asking a professor for an extension. Write a 30-second appeal. Then rewrite it twice: once for a receiver who trusts you completely, once for a receiver who is skeptical of you. Mark which mode of persuasion each version leans on, and present the three versions to the class. Writing exercise. Describe a real argument you had in the last month, in 200 to 300 words, using all eight elements of the communication model. Identify the main source of noise and one thing you could have changed in your encoding.

By the end of this chapter you should be able to: Name the four qualities every good argument has. Break an argument into the six parts of Toulmin's model. Find the unstated warrant in an everyday argument. Explain how the narrative paradigm judges arguments differently from Toulmin's model. Recognize the two structures debaters use most: the Contention Model and the Uniqueness Model.

In everyday speech, "argument" means a fight. In this class it means something narrower: an argument is a reason or set of reasons given to persuade others that an action or idea is right or wrong. That definition rules out a lot. "Pineapple on pizza is gross" is an opinion, not an argument, because it gives no reason. "Pineapple on pizza is gross because sweet fruit clashes with salty cheese" is an argument, even if it is a weak one. Every good argument has four qualities: A claim: the statement you want the audience to accept. A warrant: the reasoning or evidence that supports the claim. An implication: why the claim matters, the "so what." It is true. An argument can be well built and still fail because its claim or evidence is false. Students often skip the implication. "Zoos shorten animals' lives" has a claim and could have a warrant, but until you say why a shorter life matters to the decision being made, the judge has nothing to do with it. Chapter 6 turns these four qualities into the structure you will use in your first debate.

The philosopher Stephen Toulmin noticed that real arguments, the kind people make in courtrooms and newspapers, do not look like the syllogisms in a logic textbook. In The Uses of Argument (1958), he proposed a model with six parts. Three are present in nearly every argument, and three more appear when an argument is more careful. Toulmin's model also splits the "warrant" from Section 2.1 in two. There, warrant meant all the support for a claim. Toulmin separates the evidence itself (the grounds) from the reasoning that connects it to the claim (the warrant), because arguments usually break at that connection. To see all six parts, we will build one argument a piece at a time. You are in your backyard at night and you hear barking and howling somewhere down the street. Figure 2.1 Toulmin's model The six parts of Toulmin's model and how they connect: grounds lead to a claim, the warrant and its backing hold up that step, the qualifier sets how strong the claim is, and the rebuttal names the exceptions. The claim is the conclusion you want your audience to accept. Here, the claim is "there are dogs nearby." The claim is the part of an argument people notice first, and the part beginning debaters most often mistake for the whole argument. On its own, a claim is only an assertion: it tells the judge what to think without giving a reason to think it. In a debate, the claim usually appears as the tag that introduces an argument. The grounds are the evidence or facts offered in support of the claim. Toulmin called them "data." Your grounds are what you heard: barking and howling. Grounds answer the question "what have you got?" In a debate, grounds are often a piece of evidence, such as a statistic, a study or an expert's statement, but they can also be an example, a fact both sides accept, or something your opponent said. Arguments are rarely won or lost on grounds, because it is hard to deny that a study says what it says. The warrant is the connection that explains why the grounds support the claim. Your warrant is "dogs bark and howl." Warrants answer the question "how do you get from there to here?" They are the most important part of the model, for two reasons. First, they are usually unstated: people say "I hear barking, so there are dogs" and leave the listener to supply the bridge. Second, because they are unstated, they are where arguments are weakest. Opponents rarely attack your grounds. They attack your warrant: "the study is about adults, and this resolution is about teenagers." When you build an argument, say your warrant out loud. When you answer one, look for the warrant your opponent skipped. Backing is support for the warrant itself, for when the audience doubts the connection. Someone might point out that plenty of animals make noise at night. Your backing is "few other animals in a suburban neighborhood bark and howl like that." Backing is a second layer of proof, and not every argument needs it. You need it when the warrant is what the debate is about. If your opponent says the study about adults does not apply to teenagers, your backing is the reason it does. A qualifier is a word or phrase that marks how strong the claim is, such as "probably," "in most cases" or "almost certainly." Your honest qualifier is "probably," since you have not actually seen a dog. Qualifiers can feel like weakness, but in a debate they are armor. A debater who claims something "always" happens can be beaten with a single counterexample. A debater who claims it "usually" happens can only be beaten with evidence that it usually does not, which is much harder to find. The rebuttal is the set of conditions under which the claim would not hold. Some textbooks call it the reservation. Your rebuttal is "unless someone is playing a recording, or there are coyotes in the hills." Do not confuse this with a rebuttal speech, which Chapter 1 introduced and Chapter 12 teaches. Toulmin's rebuttal is an exception built into your own argument. Naming the exceptions yourself does two things: it shows the judge you have thought the argument through, and it lets you deal with the exception on your terms before your opponent raises it. Put the six parts together and the full argument reads: "I hear barking and howling, and since dogs make those sounds and few other animals around here do, there are probably dogs nearby, unless someone is playing a recording or there are coyotes in the hills." Nobody talks like that. But in a debate, the more of those parts you can supply when an argument is challenged, the harder that argument is to beat. At a glance Part What it does Example Claim States the conclusion There are dogs nearby. Grounds Offers the evidence You hear barking and howling in the distance. Warrant Connects the evidence to the claim Dogs are animals that bark and howl. Backing Supports the warrant Few other animals in a suburban neighborhood make that sound. Qualifier Sets how strong the claim is Probably. Rebuttal Names the exceptions Unless someone is playing a recording, or there are coyotes in the hills.

Most real arguments leave something out. Aristotle called an argument with an unstated premise an enthymeme. "The Earth revolves around the Sun. I'm an astronomer, I would know" has a claim and grounds, but the warrant is never said: astronomers are experts in astronomy, so their statements about astronomy should be believed. Leaving the warrant unstated is efficient when the audience already accepts it. It is risky when they do not. Many arguments that sound convincing fall apart once you say the hidden warrant out loud. "My opponent failed algebra, so don't trust his tuition plan" depends on the unstated warrant that anyone who failed algebra cannot design a tuition plan. Stated plainly, the warrant is obviously false. That pattern, an argument that relies on a bad hidden warrant, is behind most of the fallacies in Chapter 7. A good habit: when you hear an argument you think is wrong, ask what the speaker must be assuming for it to work. That assumption is usually where to aim your answer.

s: 2.4 A different test: the narrative paradigm
x: Toulmin's model assumes people are persuaded by evidence and reasoning laid out step by step. The communication scholar Walter Fisher argued that this leaves something out. In 1984 he proposed the narrative paradigm: people understand the world through stories, and they judge arguments by how good a story they tell. Fisher offered two tests for a story: Narrative coherence: does the story hang together? Are the characters consistent, and does each event follow from the last? Narrative fidelity: does the story ring true with the audience's own experience and values? The narrative paradigm explains why some arguments win without the best evidence. A judge who hears a clear, consistent story about what happens after the plan passes, and finds it matches what they know about the world, will often prefer it to a pile of statistics with no story connecting them. It also explains why a debater who contradicts themselves loses credibility fast: an incoherent story fails Fisher's first test before anyone checks the evidence. You do not have to choose between the two models. Toulmin tells you how to build each argument. Fisher tells you how to connect your arguments into a case a judge believes.

Debaters have built their own structures out of these ideas, designed to make arguments easy for a judge to follow and easy to check. You will spend most of this course using two of them. This section introduces both; later chapters teach you to build them. Figure 2.2 Two structures debaters use The Contention Model and the Uniqueness Model side by side, so students see that one stacks support under a single claim while the other walks from the world now to the world after a plan. The Contention Model is the structure for fact and value debates. A contention is one major argument for your side, and it has three parts. The claim states, in one sentence, what the contention proves. The warrant is the reasoning and evidence that prove it: Toulmin's grounds, warrant and backing gathered in one place. The implication explains why the claim matters for the resolution, so the judge knows what to do with it. In a value debate, a contention adds a fourth step, a tie-back to the criterion, which shows how the argument meets the standard your side asked the judge to use. If that sounds familiar, it should. The Contention Model is the four qualities of a good argument from Section 2.1, put in order. Chapter 6 teaches it for fact debates, and Chapter 13 adds the criterion for value debates. The Uniqueness Model is the structure for policy debates. A policy argument compares two worlds, the world as it is now and the world after a plan, so this model has four parts that walk from one to the other. Uniqueness describes the world now. The link says what the plan does. The internal link explains what changes because of it. The impact says why that change matters to people. The affirmative uses the model to build advantages, reasons the plan makes things better, and the negative uses the same four parts to build disadvantages, reasons it makes things worse. The Uniqueness Model is a story in Fisher's sense, about how one world turns into another, told one step at a time so the judge can check each step. Chapter 14 teaches it. Why two structures instead of one? Because the questions are different. A fact or value resolution asks whether something is true or what matters more, and a single well-supported claim can answer that on its own. A policy resolution asks whether a change makes the world better, and no single claim can answer that. A contention can prove a problem exists. It cannot prove the plan fixes the problem without causing a worse one. The Uniqueness Model forces every argument to describe both worlds. At a glance Structure Parts Used for Taught in Contention Model Claim, warrant, implication, and in value debates a tie-back to the criterion Fact and value debates Chapters 6 and 13 Uniqueness Model Uniqueness, link, internal link, impact Policy debates Chapter 14

When you deliver an argument, name its parts so the judge can follow: "My claim is ___." "The reason is ___." Or, with evidence: "According to ___, ___." "That matters because ___." When you answer an argument, aim at the warrant: "Their claim depends on the assumption that ___. That assumption is wrong because ___." Spoken, a complete argument sounds like this: "My claim is that zoos are bad for animals. The reason is that captivity shortens their lives. A 2008 study in Science found that female African elephants born in European zoos had a median life span of 16.9 years, compared with 56 years for elephants dying of natural causes in Kenya's Amboseli National Park. That matters because the purpose of keeping animals in zoos is supposed to be their welfare, and a shorter life is the clearest sign that welfare is not being served."

Argument: "You should start at a community college. It costs a fraction of what the university does, and you'd transfer with the same degree." Part In this argument Claim You should start at a community college. Grounds It costs a fraction of the university's tuition. Warrant (unstated) When two paths lead to the same degree, the cheaper one is better. Backing The bachelor's degree is what employers see, not where you spent your first two years. Qualifier Usually. Rebuttal Unless your credits do not transfer, or you would not finish after transferring. The rebuttal row is where the other side will attack. Someone who argues against this choice does not need to dispute the cost. They need to show the paths do not lead to the same degree as reliably as the warrant assumes.

Argument: "A universal basic income would reduce poverty, because giving people money directly lets them buy what they need." The claim is that UBI reduces poverty; the grounds are that it gives people money. The warrant, that people use the money on necessities, carries the whole argument, and it is exactly what critics dispute. A careful debater supplies backing, such as research on how people spent money in guaranteed income programs, and a qualifier: "for most recipients." Told as a story, the argument also has to pass Fisher's tests: does it hang together, and does it match what the judge believes about how people behave?

Judges look for complete arguments. A claim with no warrant is an assertion, and most judges will give it little or no weight even if the other side never answers it. A claim with a warrant but no implication leaves the judge asking why they should care. When two arguments clash, judges usually prefer the one whose warrant was explained and defended over the one whose warrant was assumed.

Asserting instead of arguing. "Our plan is better" with no reason is not an argument. Forgetting the implication. Every argument needs a "that matters because." Overclaiming. "Always" and "never" invite a single counterexample. Use qualifiers honestly. Attacking grounds when the warrant is weaker. Accept the statistic and question what it proves. Contradicting your own story. If your first argument says the policy will barely change anything and your second says it will transform the economy, the judge stops trusting both.

Drill: find the warrant (10 minutes, pairs). Each partner writes five short arguments from advertisements, social media posts or overheard conversations. Swap lists. For each argument, write the unstated warrant in one sentence and rate it believable or not. Discuss the ones you rated differently. Writing exercise. In groups, write one argument using the Contention Model on the resolution "Being talented is preferable to being disciplined." Then, individually, rewrite it in all six parts of Toulmin's model, 200 to 300 words.

s: 3.1 The resolution decides the debate you are having
x: Every debate starts with a resolution: a single sentence that the affirmative argues for and the negative argues against. Resolutions come in three kinds, and the most important thing to know about them is this: the kind of resolution determines the kind of debate. A fact resolution produces a debate about what is true. A value resolution produces a debate about what matters most. A policy resolution produces a debate about what should be done. Each kind is judged by a different standard and built from different structures. So the first thing you do with any resolution is identify which kind it is. Resolutions are identified by their wording.

A fact resolution asks whether a statement is true. You should be able to settle it, at least in principle, by looking at the world, without deciding what you value. Two markers identify a fact resolution: A verb of being or prediction: is, are, does, has, have or will. A call to evaluate whether something is empirically true. Examples: "Climate change is irreversible." "Free bus fares increase ridership." "Students who start at a community college are as likely to earn a bachelor's degree as those who start at a university." Fact debates are decided by preponderance of evidence: the side with the better quantity and quality of evidence and reasoning wins.

A value resolution asks for a judgment about what is good, better or more important. Listing evidence is not enough to win one, because the resolution asks you to decide what matters most, and evidence alone cannot settle that. A value resolution may have any of three markers: The word ought. Language of prioritization or preference: "more than," "over," "preferable to," "does more good than harm." An evaluative judgment that cannot be proven true or false by evidence alone: "good," "just," "harmful." Examples: "Learning ought to be valued over grades." "Affordability ought to matter more than prestige in choosing a college." "Lowering the voting age does more good than harm." Value debates are unusual: part of the debate is about how to decide the debate. Each side proposes a value, the principle that matters most, and a value criterion, the way to measure whether that value is achieved. For example, a side might take justice as its value and minimizing wrongful convictions as its criterion. Two sides can agree on the value and disagree on how to measure it, or disagree on both. Chapter 13 covers this in full.

A policy resolution asks whether an action should be taken. Policy resolutions are the easiest to identify, because almost all of them follow one formula: who should do what? Who: an actor, the agent that would take the action. "The United States federal government," "California," "this college." Should: the call to action. Do what: the action itself. "Establish a universal basic income," "make its public buses free to ride." Examples: "This city should make its public buses free to ride." "The United States should substantially increase its foreign aid for global public health." The affirmative in a policy debate defends a specific plan, one example of the resolution in action. If the resolution says the federal government should raise the minimum wage, the affirmative might defend raising it to \$20 an hour. The plan has to be an example of the resolution: a plan to create a universal basic income does not prove the minimum wage should be raised, even if it addresses the same problem. Chapter 15 covers what makes a plan legitimate. Policy debates are decided by net benefits: the judge adds up the advantages and disadvantages of the plan and votes for whichever world, with the plan or without it, is better. An actor + should + an action Net benefits Figure 3.1 Identifying a resolution A two-question test for sorting any resolution into fact, value or policy, and the standard each kind is decided by. Sometimes a resolution could be read as more than one kind. "The United States ought to prioritize renewable energy" has ought, which suggests value, but also names an actor taking an action, which suggests policy. When that happens, the affirmative's job is to argue for its reading using the markers above, and the negative may argue for a different reading.

Any subject can be debated all three ways, and seeing that is the best way to understand the difference between them. Kind Resolution on choosing a college Resolution on universal basic income Fact Students who start at a community college are as likely to earn a bachelor's degree as those who start at a university. A universal basic income would reduce poverty in the United States. Value Affordability ought to matter more than prestige in choosing a college. Economic security ought to be valued over economic growth. Policy A high school graduate should start at a community college instead of a university. The United States federal government should establish a universal basic income. The three are connected. Settling the fact question tells you what each path leads to. Settling the value question tells you which of those outcomes matters more. Only then can you decide the policy question with confidence. This book follows the same order: fact debate in Part II, value debate in Part IV and policy debate in Part V, each building on the last. This idea is ancient. Classical rhetoricians called the point a dispute turns on its stasis, and they listed the questions in order: does the thing exist (conjecture), what is it (definition), is it good or bad (quality), and what should be done about it (procedure). Two thousand years later, debaters still find that most disagreements are really about one of those four questions. When you are stuck in an argument, ask which one you are actually disagreeing about.

Every debate has rules about who has to prove what. Three ideas, all borrowed from law and from the nineteenth-century rhetorician Richard Whately, govern the whole book. The burden of proof belongs to the affirmative. The affirmative is asking the judge to accept something new, so it has to give reasons. If the affirmative gives no reasons, the negative does not need to say anything. The burden of rejoinder belongs to whoever speaks next. Once a side has made an argument, the other side has to answer it or accept it. An argument nobody answers is treated as true for the rest of the debate. Presumption is the default outcome if nobody proves anything. It usually favors the negative, because the negative is defending the status quo, the world as it is now. If the affirmative's case and the negative's answers come out even, the judge votes negative, because the affirmative did not meet its burden. As Whately put it, presumption favors what already exists. These ideas explain how the Scale from Chapter 4 works. If the judge ends the debate with nothing on either side, or with both sides exactly balanced, presumption breaks the tie.

The affirmative is expected to define any term in the resolution that a reasonable judge might not understand, or that could be understood more than one way. You do not need to define every word, and often you need to define none. But when a term matters to the debate, define it, and cite where your definition comes from. Use a real source: a dictionary, a statute, an agency or a scholar in the field. "According to the Merriam-Webster dictionary, ..." is fine, as long as the definition you read is actually in that dictionary. A made-up definition with a dictionary's name attached is fabricated evidence, and in competition it can lose you the round. Chapter 9 covers evidence ethics in detail. Definitions also shape the debate. If the resolution says "public transit" and you define it to include only buses, you have narrowed what the negative can argue about. Doing that fairly is part of the affirmative's job; doing it unfairly invites a topicality argument, which you will meet in Chapter 16.

The first part of an affirmative case, sometimes called the top of case, uses these frames: "The resolution today is ___." "This is a ___ resolution, because it ___." For example: "This is a policy resolution, because it names an actor, uses the word should, and calls for a specific action." "I define ___ as ___, according to ___." "The judge should decide this debate by ___." Spoken, a top of case for a value resolution sounds like this: "The resolution today is that affordability ought to matter more than prestige in choosing a college. This is a value resolution: it uses the word ought and asks you to rank two considerations against each other. I define prestige as a school's reputation and selectivity, the factors measured in national rankings. I will argue that you should decide this debate by asking which factor does more to improve a student's life after graduation."

Subject: grading in general education courses. Fact: "Pass/no pass grading reduces student stress." The verb reduces makes a claim that evidence can test. Preponderance of evidence decides it. Value: "Learning ought to be valued over grades." The word ought and the comparison make it a value resolution. The sides will need values and criteria. Policy: "This college should replace letter grades with pass/no pass in general education courses." Actor (this college), should, action (replace letter grades). Net benefits decides it. The affirmative in the policy debate carries the burden of proof. If it shows only that some students prefer pass/no pass, without showing any benefit to adopting it, presumption favors keeping letter grades.

Subject: foreign aid for global health. Fact: "Foreign health aid saves more lives per dollar than domestic health spending." Testable by evidence. Value: "A nation's obligations to its own citizens ought to outweigh its obligations abroad." A ranking of two obligations; a value debate. Policy: "The United States should substantially increase its foreign aid for global public health." The affirmative's plan would need to say by how much and for what programs, and to define "substantially" in a way it can defend.

A judge decides the debate by the criterion that fits the resolution: preponderance of evidence for fact, the winning value and criterion for value, and net benefits for policy. If the affirmative misidentifies the resolution, for example by arguing a policy resolution as if it were a value question, the judge may hold it to the wrong standard, or accept the negative's argument that it never addressed the resolution at all. And if neither side clearly wins, the judge votes on presumption, which usually means negative.

Ignoring the resolution's wording. The kind of resolution comes from the words on the page, not from the subject. Choosing a value that repeats the resolution. If the resolution says learning ought to be valued over grades, "learning" as your value just restates your side. Chapter 13 explains this trap. Defending a plan that is not an example of the resolution. A plan that addresses the same problem by a different action does not prove the resolution. Inventing definitions. Cite real sources, word for word. Forgetting the burden of proof. The affirmative cannot win just because the negative was weak. It has to prove something.

Drill: resolution sort (10 minutes, individually, then pairs). Classify each of these as fact, value or policy, and underline the words that tell you: (1) Social media does more harm than good for teenagers. (2) Remote work will become the norm for office jobs. (3) The state should require financial literacy courses for high school graduation. (4) Privacy ought to be valued over convenience. (5) Hamsters make good pets. (6) The college library has enough study space. Compare answers with a partner and argue out any you disagree on. Writing exercise. Choose a subject you care about. Write a fact, a value and a policy resolution on it. For each, write one sentence naming the criterion the judge would use and one sentence explaining how settling the earlier resolutions would help decide the later ones.

t: Intro to Refutation (Arguments of Fact and Value)
s: 4.1 Clash is what makes it a debate
x: Two speeches that never respond to each other are not a debate; they are two speeches. Debate happens when the sides engage the same points, which debaters call clash. The skill that creates clash is refutation: responding to your opponent's arguments. New debaters often find refutation harder than building their own case, because their own case can be written in advance and refutation has to happen in the moment. This chapter gives you a frame for delivering any answer, a way to choose which answer to give, a way to keep track of the debate as it happens, and a picture of how the judge puts it all together at the end.

t: Intro to Refutation (Arguments of Fact and Value)
x: Every answer you give should have four parts. They tell the judge which argument you are answering, what your answer is, why they should believe it, and what it means for the debate. Signal: "They say..." Name the argument you are answering, briefly, so the judge knows where to write your answer. State: "We say..." Give your counter-claim. Support: "Based on..." Give the evidence or reasoning behind your counter-claim. Summarize: "That means..." Explain how your answer resolves the clash in your favor. Here is the frame in use on nuclear energy: "They say nuclear energy is unsafe. We say that even if it is not perfectly safe, it is the safest form of large-scale energy we have. Based on research summarized by Our World in Data, coal causes about 25 deaths for every terawatt-hour of electricity it produces and gas about 3, while nuclear power causes a small fraction of one. That means safety is a reason to prefer nuclear energy to the sources it would replace, not a reason to reject it." The summary step is the one beginners skip, and it is the one that wins debates. Without it, the judge has two competing claims and no instruction on which to prefer. With it, you have told the judge how to resolve the disagreement. The four-step frame is training wheels. Experienced debaters drop the literal phrases "they say" and "we say" and tag each answer with its claim instead. But the four functions never go away. Every good answer still signals, states, supports and summarizes.

s: 4.3 Choosing an answer: significance, relevance and accuracy
x: The four-step frame tells you how to deliver an answer. It does not tell you what to say. Sasan Kasravi, a former Diablo Valley College competitor and coach, developed a simple way to find an answer together with this book's author: every argument can be challenged on three grounds. Significance: does the argument matter? Even if it is true, is the impact large enough to affect the decision? "They say nuclear power risks meltdowns, but there have been only a handful of major meltdowns in the history of nuclear power. That risk is far smaller than the deaths from the fossil fuels nuclear power would replace." Relevance: is the argument connected to the resolution or to what the other side is defending? "They say removing patents on antibiotics would have helped stop COVID, but COVID is caused by a virus, and antibiotics do not work on viruses." Accuracy: is the argument true? Is their evidence wrong, outdated or misread? "They say the city's buses are empty, but the transit agency's own ridership report from last month shows the opposite." These three questions match how philosophers who study everyday reasoning test arguments. Ralph Johnson and J. Anthony Blair proposed that a good argument's premises must be relevant, sufficient and acceptable. Kasravi's version is built for speed. In a debate, you do not have time to evaluate every argument from scratch; you have time to ask three questions and pick the answer that does the most damage. The most effective answers often combine them: "Even if they are right about this, it does not matter, because..." concedes accuracy and attacks significance. Chapter 19 builds a larger set of answers on the same foundation.

x: Kasravi's questions tell you what kind of answer to give. Before you can ask them, you have to see exactly what your opponent is claiming, and arguments in a debate rarely arrive in a tidy form. A syllogism is a way to lay one out. A syllogism is an argument in three parts. The major premise is a general rule. The minor premise places a specific case under that rule. The conclusion is what follows if both premises are true. The classic example: all humans are mortal (major premise); Socrates is a human (minor premise); so Socrates is mortal (conclusion). The value of a syllogism for refutation is this: if both premises are true and the conclusion follows from them, the conclusion has to be true. You cannot beat the conclusion by simply denying it. You have to beat a premise. Laying an argument out as a syllogism shows you where the premises are, so you can find the weakest one. Chapter 2 showed that most real arguments are enthymemes: they leave a premise unstated. Writing the argument as a syllogism forces the missing premise into the open, and the unstated premise is often the weakest part, because the speaker never had to defend it. Use three steps: Lay it out. On your flow, write the opponent's argument as a major premise, a minor premise and a conclusion. If one premise was never said, write it in. Test each premise. Ask Kasravi's questions of each one. Is it accurate? Is it relevant to this case? Does it matter? Answer the weakest one. Deliver that answer in four steps. The judge never needs to hear the word "syllogism"; it is a tool for finding your answer, not a way to say it. Here is the method on the AI fact resolution. The affirmative argues: "AI will create more jobs than it destroys, because new technologies always have." As a syllogism: Major premise: New technologies create more jobs than they destroy. Minor premise: AI is a new technology. Conclusion: AI will create more jobs than it destroys. The minor premise is hard to deny. The major premise is where the argument lives, and laying it out shows that it is really a claim about the past standing in for a prediction about the future. The negative can attack it on relevance: "They say new technologies always create more jobs. We say AI is different from the technologies their history describes, because earlier machines replaced physical labor, while AI performs the thinking tasks that past workers moved into. That means their history does not tell us what AI will do, and their contention has no support left." The negative did not have to prove that AI will destroy more jobs than it creates. It only had to show that one premise does not hold, and the conclusion fell with it.

x: You cannot answer an argument you did not write down. Flowing is the note-taking system debaters and judges use to record a debate so that every argument and every answer can be tracked. It is called a flow because arguments flow across the page from speech to speech. The basic system: One column per speech. Turn your paper sideways and draw a column for each speech in order. The first speech goes in the left column, the answers to it in the next column, and so on. One row per argument. Write each argument on its own line. When someone answers it, write the answer in the next column on the same row, so the clash lines up across the page. Abbreviate everything. You will not have time to write full sentences. Drop vowels, use symbols (an up arrow for "increases," a down arrow for "decreases," a delta for "change") and develop shorthand you and your partner can both read. Use separate sheets for separate positions. In a policy debate, each advantage and each disadvantage gets its own sheet of paper, or its own tab in a spreadsheet. Figure 4.1 A sample flow How a flow is laid out: one column per speech, answers written on the same row as the argument they answer, and an unanswered argument marked as dropped. Two words come straight out of flowing. An argument is dropped when the other side never answers it; on the flow, its row has an empty space in the next column. Under the burden of rejoinder from Chapter 3, a dropped argument is treated as true. An extension is carrying an argument forward into a later speech, reminding the judge it still stands and explaining why it matters. Arguments that are not extended into the final speeches usually drop out of the judge's decision. Flowing is the reason debaters signpost: they announce where they are on the flow before making an argument. "On their first contention, two answers." A judge who knows where to write will flow everything you say. A judge who has to guess will miss some of it.

t: Intro to Refutation (Arguments of Fact and Value)
s: 4.6 How the judge decides: the Scale
x: At the end of a debate, the judge has to turn a page of notes into a decision. The simplest way to picture that process is a balance scale. When I was in fifth grade, my teacher, Ms. Fatheringham, taught algebra with a balance and a pile of small white and blue cubes. If you put the same thing on both sides of the balance, you could take it off both sides and nothing changed. Whichever side was heavier after that was the answer. A judge decides a debate the same way: Place each standing impact on its side. Every reason to vote affirmative that survived the debate goes on the affirmative's side. Every reason to vote negative goes on the negative's side. An impact counts only if it was explained, extended and not defeated by an answer. Cancel what both sides share. If both sides win the same impact, it does not help either of them. Weigh what is left. The judge compares the remaining impacts using the debate's criterion and the weighing arguments the debaters made. Chapter 10 teaches you how to make those arguments. If the Scale is level or empty, vote on presumption. As Chapter 3 explained, that usually means negative. Figure 4.2 The Scale The judge's decision as a balance: impacts both sides share cancel out, and whatever is left tips the Scale. The Scale explains the difference between two kinds of answers. An answer that puts something on your side of the Scale is offense: a reason to vote for you. An answer that takes something off your opponent's side is defense: a reason not to vote for them. You need both. Defense alone can at best level the Scale, which leaves the decision to presumption. Offense is what tips it.

By the end of this chapter you should be able to: Name the six elements of effective delivery and adjust each one for a debate. Choose between manuscript, impromptu and extemporaneous delivery. s: 5.1 Delivery is part of the argument
x: Chapter 1 described noise: anything that keeps your message from reaching the judge. In a debate, the biggest source of noise you control is your own delivery. An argument mumbled too fast to flow does not exist for the decision. An argument delivered clearly, at a pace the judge can write down, gets weighed. That is the reason delivery matters in a debate class. You are not being graded on charisma. You are learning to remove the noise between your arguments and the person deciding.

Delivery can feel like one big skill you either have or do not. It is easier to improve once you break it into parts. This section uses six elements. Each one can be practiced on its own, and each one, done badly, adds a specific kind of noise. Volume is how loud or soft you speak. The test is simple: can the judge at the back of the room hear every word without leaning in? Nervous speakers tend to get quieter as a speech goes on, and quieter still at the moments that matter most, such as the last line of an argument. Do the opposite. Your most important sentences should be your loudest. Volume also signals confidence. A judge hears a debater who speaks up as someone who believes what they are saying. Pace is how fast or slow you speak. In a debate, the right pace is the fastest pace at which the judge can still flow, meaning write down your arguments as you make them. That pace depends on the judge, which is why the communication model puts the receiver at the center. The best gauge is the judge's pen. If it stops moving while you are still talking, you have lost them, and everything you say until they catch up is lost too. Vary your pace on purpose: slow down for your claims and your weighing, and move faster through material the judge has already heard. Tone is the variation in energy, emotion and formality in your voice. A debate calls for a tone that is confident and professional, but not flat. A speech delivered in one unchanging tone makes every argument sound equally important, which means none of them stands out. Let your tone rise when you reach the argument you most want the judge to remember, and stay calm and even when you answer an attack, which tells the judge the attack did not worry you. Clarity is how easy it is to understand each word you say. It mostly comes down to articulation: finishing your words, hitting final consonants, not letting sentences trail off. Clarity matters more the faster you go. A slow speaker can mumble a little and still be understood; a fast speaker who mumbles is just making sound. If you have to choose between speed and clarity, choose clarity every time. Fluidity is how naturally your speech flows. The biggest threat to fluidity is verbal filler: sounds and words like "um," "like" and "you know" that fill a gap while your brain catches up. A few are normal. A lot of them make you sound unsure and waste time you do not have. The fix is not to talk faster. It is to pause. A one-second silence sounds deliberate and confident to a listener, even when it feels endless to you. Eye contact is where you focus your attention while you speak. In a debate, look at the judge, not your opponent. Your opponent is not the one deciding, and arguing at them turns the round into a personal exchange the judge is watching from outside. You will be reading from notes, so you will not hold eye contact the whole time. Aim to look up at the judge at the end of each argument, which is also when you can check their pen. None of these needs to be perfect. A debater with average delivery and clear structure beats a polished speaker with no structure almost every time. But each element you improve removes noise. At a glance Element What it is In a debate Volume How loud or soft you speak Loud enough for the back of the room. Get louder for your most important lines, not quieter. Pace How fast or slow you speak Slow enough for the judge to flow. If their pen stops, you are going too fast. Tone Variation in energy, emotion and formality Confident and professional. Vary it so your key arguments stand out. Clarity How easy it is to understand each word Finish your words. Clarity matters more as you speed up. Fluidity How naturally your speech flows, including verbal filler Pause instead of saying "um." Eye contact Where you focus while you speak Look at the judge, not your opponent, at the end of each argument.

Manuscript delivery means reading from a prepared text. It is common in formats where debaters read evidence, and it is the right choice for your first constructive speech, when you have written the case in advance. The risk is reading to the page instead of the judge; look up at the end of each argument. Impromptu delivery means speaking with no preparation. You will do this in cross-examination and whenever you answer something unexpected. Extemporaneous delivery means speaking from an outline after limited preparation. Most rebuttal speeches are extemporaneous: you have notes on your flow and a plan, but you are composing sentences as you go. A useful rule for beginners: manuscript for the first speech, extemporaneous for everything after. As you get comfortable, you will rely less on the page even in the first speech.

Judges flow, and a judge who knows where you are going can write down everything you say. Two habits make that easy. A roadmap is a one-sentence preview of the order of your speech, given before the timer starts or in the first seconds. "I'll start on their disadvantage, then go back to our case." Many judges expect one, and it costs you nothing. Signposting means announcing where you are as you move through the speech. "Now on their first contention." "My second answer." "That takes me to the impact." Every time you move to a new argument, say so. Signposting is the spoken version of the structure you write. In Chapter 14 you will learn to deliver positions in subordinated notation, with numbered claims and lettered support. Saying the numbers and letters out loud is signposting.

Communication apprehension is anxiety connected to speaking. Almost everyone has some. It shows up as a racing heart, a shaky voice or a blank mind, and it is a form of psychological noise. The goal is not to eliminate it, which is rarely possible, but to keep it from getting in the way. Much of it comes from three thinking patterns: All-or-nothing thinking: believing that a speech that falls short of perfect is a failure. Overgeneralization: treating one bad experience as proof that it will always go badly. "I froze once, so I always freeze." Fortune telling: expecting things to go badly no matter how much you practice. Noticing which pattern you are in is often enough to loosen its grip. Four strategies help: Preparation: know your content. Most anxiety before a speech is uncertainty about what you will say. Practice: run the speech out loud, timed, more than once. Rehearsing in your head is not the same. Mindfulness: notice the anxiety without judging it. "My heart is racing" is information, not a verdict on your ability. Grounding: bring your attention back to the present moment. Feel your feet on the floor, take a slow breath, and look at one friendly face. Debate has one advantage over most public speaking: your judge is trained to listen for arguments, not to judge your nerves. A shaky voice delivering a good argument still wins the argument.

Every speech in a debate has a time limit, and most judges stop listening when it runs out. Running out of time before you reach your best argument is the same as never making it. In my classes, the three most common reasons students lose points on their debates are timing, refutation and verbal filler. Each has a simple fix: Timing: time your outline out loud, with a recording, at least three times before the debate. Refutation: write answers to the arguments you expect before the debate, using the four-step frame from Chapter 4. Verbal filler: deliver your first speech from a manuscript, so you never search for words. In rebuttals, budget your time before you stand up. Decide how many seconds each part of the flow gets, and move on when that time is spent, even if you have more to say.

Roadmap: "I'll start on their case and then go to our advantage." Signpost a new argument: "Now on their second contention." Signpost your answers: "Two answers. First, ___. Second, ___." Signpost a transition inside a position: "That takes me to the impact." Close: "For all these reasons, I urge an affirmative ballot." A rebuttal opening with a roadmap and signposts sounds like this: "Two places today: their disadvantage, then our case. On the disadvantage, three answers. First, there is no link: their evidence is about federal programs, and our plan is run by the state. Second..."

Resolution: This college should replace letter grades with pass/no pass in general education courses. A student gives the affirmative's first speech. She has written it as a manuscript and timed it three times: it runs four minutes and forty seconds against a five-minute limit, leaving room for a slower pace in the room. Before starting she gives a roadmap ("two advantages: student stress and course exploration"), and she signposts each part as she reaches it. She marks two places on her manuscript where she will look up at the judge and slow down: the end of each advantage's impact. When her voice shakes in the first ten seconds, she pauses, takes a breath and continues. The judge flows every argument.

Resolution: The United States federal government should establish a universal basic income. A negative debater has four minutes for a rebuttal and four things to cover: the affirmative's two advantages, his own disadvantage, and his final weighing. He budgets the time before standing: one minute for each advantage, one minute extending the disadvantage, one minute weighing. He gives a roadmap in one sentence. Halfway through the second advantage, he sees the minute is spent and moves on, saying "I'll group the rest of their answers here: none of them address our link." He reaches the weighing with a minute left, which is where the debate is decided.

Judges do not usually vote on delivery directly, but delivery decides what reaches the judge's flow, and the flow decides the debate. Clear signposting means your arguments are written in the right place. A pace the judge can follow means nothing is lost. Many judges also award speaker points, a separate score for speaking quality, where delivery, organization and professionalism count directly.

Speaking faster to fit more in. If the judge cannot flow it, it does not count. Cut arguments instead. Skipping the roadmap. It takes five seconds and helps the judge with every argument after it. Reading to the page. Look up at the end of each argument. Filling silence with filler. A pause is fine. "Um" is noise. Not timing practice runs. A speech that runs five minutes in your head often runs six out loud.

Drill: one-minute signposting (10 minutes, pairs). Each partner gives a one-minute speech answering three made-up arguments. Use a roadmap and signpost every answer. By the end of this chapter you should be able to: Explain what a fact resolution asks and why it is decided by a preponderance of evidence. Name the stock issues of a fact debate and the burden each side carries. Build a contention with a title, a claim, warrants and an implication. Write the top of a fact case: definitions and the criterion. Answer a fact case with refutation and counter-contentions. Explain what a settled fact hands to the value and policy debates that follow it.

A fact resolution asks whether something is, was or will be true. It does not ask whether that thing is good, and it does not ask anyone to do anything. Chapter 3 gave you the markers: words like is, are, has and will, and a question you could, at least in principle, check against the world. "Starting at a community college costs less than starting at a four-year university" is a fact resolution. So is "Climate change is irreversible." So is the resolution this book uses for its fact debate: "Artificial intelligence will cause more job creation than job displacement." That last one is a predictive fact. Nobody can check it yet, because the future has not happened. A predictive fact debate is not about who knows the future. It is about which prediction the evidence better supports: trends, expert forecasts, and what has happened when similar technologies arrived before. That makes predictive facts some of the most interesting fact debates, because the evidence is real but incomplete, and both sides have room to work. Fact debates can look like the easy warm-up before the "real" debates about values and policies. They are not. Almost every value or policy argument rests on a factual claim somewhere underneath it. An argument that AI does more harm than good, or that the government should restrict it, collapses if the facts about what AI does turn out to be wrong. Learning to debate facts is learning to test the ground every other argument stands on.

Every debate needs a criterion, the standard the judge uses to decide who won. Without one, a judge has to invent a standard, and two judges watching the same debate could invent different ones. Stating the criterion out loud tells the judge exactly what question to answer. The criterion for a fact debate is preponderance of evidence: the side whose evidence and reasoning, taken together, better support its answer to the resolution wins. The term comes from civil law, where it means that a claim is more likely true than not. That definition carries three lessons for debaters. First, the affirmative does not need certainty. "More likely than not" is a much lower bar than "beyond a reasonable doubt," the standard in criminal trials. An affirmative arguing that AI will create more jobs than it displaces does not have to prove the future. It has to show the evidence leans its way. Second, quality counts as much as quantity. One careful study of a thousand employers outweighs three blog posts repeating the same guess. When two pieces of evidence conflict, the judge asks which is better: more recent, more directly about the resolution, from a source in a position to know. Chapter 8 covers judging source quality in depth. Third, reasoning counts too. Preponderance of evidence sounds like a contest of citations, but a judge also weighs the logic connecting the evidence to the claim. A well-explained warrant with modest evidence can beat a big statistic that nobody explains.

Stock issues are the minimum elements an affirmative needs to win a resolution. If any one is missing, the affirmative has not done its job, however good the rest of its case is. A fact debate has three. Topicality means the affirmative's arguments must prove the resolution itself is true, not a claim that sounds close to it. An affirmative that proves AI will create thousands of jobs building data centers has proved something true, but not the resolution, which asks whether creation will outrun displacement. Topicality keeps the debate on the question the resolution asks. The criterion is the second stock issue. In a fact debate the criterion is almost always preponderance of evidence, so this stock issue is usually met with a single sentence. It still needs saying, because it tells the judge how to decide and gives you something to point back to in your last speech. Contentions are the third. A contention is a major argument, built in the Contention Model, that proves the resolution true. An affirmative needs at least one. Most fact cases run two or three, because a case with one contention can be beaten by beating one argument. Each side also carries a burden, a job it must do to have a chance of winning. The affirmative has the burden of proof: it must prove the resolution true. If the evidence ends up truly even, the affirmative has not met that burden, and the negative wins. (Chapter 3 called this presumption.) The negative has the burden of rejoinder: it must respond to the affirmative. (After that, as Chapter 3 explained, the burden passes to whoever speaks next.) A negative that ignores the affirmative's contentions and talks about something else leaves those contentions standing, and under preponderance of evidence, an unanswered argument with any support beats no argument at all. At a glance Term What it requires Who it belongs to Topicality Arguments that prove the resolution itself, not a nearby claim Affirmative Criterion A stated standard for deciding: preponderance of evidence Affirmative (both sides argue under it) Contentions At least one argument, in the Contention Model, proving the resolution true Affirmative Burden of proof Prove the resolution true; a tie goes to the negative Affirmative Burden of rejoinder Respond to the affirmative's arguments Negative

Chapter 2 introduced the Contention Model. Here we build one contention, piece by piece, for the affirmative on the AI resolution. The title is a short label for the contention, two to four words. Its job is practical: it gives the judge a heading to write on the flow and gives both sides a name to use for the rest of the debate. Make it efficient, not clever. "Net job growth" tells the judge what the contention is about. "The robots are hiring" makes the judge guess. Our title will be "Net job growth." The claim is the single sentence the contention proves, the contention's thesis. A strong claim states what is true and, ideally, why: "AI will create more jobs than it displaces, because the technology that automates old tasks also creates demand for new kinds of work." A judge who hears only the claim should already know what the contention argues. The warrants are the evidence and reasoning that prove the claim: Toulmin's grounds, warrant and backing from Chapter 2, gathered in one place. A contention usually has two or three, each introduced with a signpost. Our first warrant is evidence. In its Future of Jobs Report 2025, the World Economic Forum surveyed more than 1,000 large employers and estimated that, by 2030, AI and information-processing technology will create about 11 million jobs and displace about 9 million. Our second warrant is historical. A 2024 study led by MIT economist David Autor found that about 60 percent of U.S. workers are employed in occupations that did not exist in 1940. New technology has repeatedly created kinds of work nobody predicted. Each warrant gives the judge a separate reason to believe the claim, so losing one does not lose the contention. The implication explains why the claim matters for the resolution, and it is the part beginning debaters most often skip. Without it, the judge has a true statement and no instructions. Ours: "Because the employers closest to the technology expect it to create more jobs than it removes, and because past technologies have done the same, the preponderance of evidence says the resolution is true." Notice that the implication ties the contention back to the criterion. That is what turns a fact into a reason to vote. Delivered with signposting, the contention sounds like this: "My first contention is net job growth. My claim is that AI will create more jobs than it displaces. My first warrant is the World Economic Forum's 2025 survey of over a thousand employers, which expects AI to create about 11 million jobs and displace about 9 million by 2030. My second warrant is history..." At a glance Part What it does Example Title Labels the contention for the flow Net job growth Claim States what the contention proves AI will create more jobs than it displaces. Warrants Supply the evidence and reasoning World Economic Forum employer survey; 60 percent of U.S. jobs are in occupations that did not exist in 1940. Implication Explains why the claim proves the resolution under the criterion The preponderance of evidence says creation will outrun displacement.

A complete affirmative case has two layers. The top of case comes first and sets the terms of the debate: definitions and the criterion. The contentions come after it and do the proving. Figure 6.1 The parts of a fact case How a fact case is put together: the top of case (definitions and the criterion) sets the terms, and each contention underneath it runs title, claim, warrants, implication. A definition states what a key word in the resolution means for this debate. Define the terms that could reasonably be read more than one way, take each definition from a real source as Chapter 3 showed, and keep it short enough to say in one sentence. Definitions look like a formality, but in a fact debate they can decide the outcome, because they decide what counts as evidence. Take the AI resolution. The same World Economic Forum report that expects AI and information processing to add jobs on net expects robotics and autonomous systems to be the largest net job destroyer of any technology trend, with a net loss of about 5 million jobs. If "artificial intelligence" includes robots, the numbers shift against the affirmative. If it means software that performs tasks requiring human-like judgment, they do not. Both sides should notice that before the debate starts, because a judge will. The criterion follows the definitions, usually in one sentence: "The standard for this debate is preponderance of evidence: whichever side better supports its answer with evidence and reasoning should win." Then come the contentions, each signposted. Two well-built contentions usually beat four thin ones, because a thin contention gives the negative an easy target and costs you time you could spend extending what is working. The negative builds its own case the same way, with one difference. Its arguments are called counter-contentions, contentions that prove the resolution false. A negative does not have to run counter-contentions; refuting the affirmative can be enough. But counter-contentions give the judge a positive reason to vote negative rather than only reasons to doubt the affirmative, and under preponderance of evidence that matters. A judge comparing two sets of evidence needs something on the negative's side of the scale.

The negative's burden of rejoinder means answering each contention. Chapter 4's four steps (signal, state, support, summarize) work here, and Chapter 2's lesson about warrants points you to the best target. Look for the connection between the evidence and the claim, and test it. Against the net job growth contention, the negative has several answers. It can attack the warrant: the World Economic Forum figures are employer expectations, not measured outcomes, and a gap of 2 million jobs out of 20 million is small compared with how wrong forecasts can be. It can attack the historical warrant: the same MIT research found that automation's negative effects on employment were more than twice as large from 1980 to 2018 as from 1940 to 1980, so the past may not be a reassuring guide. It can raise the definition, as above, and argue that robots belong inside "artificial intelligence." And it can run a counter-contention of its own. That last option comes with a warning. Suppose the negative finds a Goldman Sachs Research estimate that widespread AI adoption could displace 6 to 7 percent of the U.S. workforce. That sounds like strong negative evidence. But the same report's authors wrote that they remained skeptical AI would lead to large employment reductions over the next decade, and they expected the displacement to be temporary as new jobs appear. An affirmative who has read the whole report will use the negative's own source against it. The lesson: before you read a piece of evidence, read the rest of the source, and make sure it does not argue the opposite of what you are using it to prove. After the answers, both sides compare. Under preponderance of evidence, the final speeches should not just repeat evidence. They should tell the judge why their evidence is better: more recent, more directly about the resolution, wider in scope, or harder to dispute. The judge's question is not "who had evidence?" Both sides will. It is "whose evidence, on balance, is more convincing?"
