x: This book's debates run in a sequence on one subject: fact, then value, then policy. The order is deliberate. Whatever a judge concludes in a fact debate becomes something the later debates can build on. Figure 6.2 One subject, three debates How a settled fact becomes a premise for the value debate, and both become premises for the policy debate, using the community college example. Take the individual-level example. If you establish as a fact that starting at a community college costs less, the value question becomes sharper: does saving money matter more than the experience of four years on one campus? And if saving money wins the value debate, the policy question nearly answers itself: you should start at a community college. Each debate inherits its premises from the one before it. The AI sequence works the same way. If the fact debate establishes that AI will create more jobs than it displaces, the value debate over whether AI does more harm than good starts with a point on one side of the scale. If the fact debate goes the other way, the point moves. Chapter 13 shows how to use a fact you have already won inside a value debate. For now, notice that winning a fact debate is never only about that day's ballot.

Open the top of case: "Before my contentions, two definitions and a standard." State the criterion: "The standard is preponderance of evidence: whoever better supports their answer should win." Signpost a contention: "My first contention is net job growth. My claim is..." Signpost warrants: "My first warrant is... My second warrant is..." Deliver the implication: "This matters because..." Compare evidence: "Prefer our evidence for two reasons: it is more recent, and it measures outcomes instead of guesses."

Resolution: Starting at a community college costs less than starting at a four-year university. The affirmative defines "costs" as tuition and fees and states the criterion. Its first contention, "Lower tuition," cites the College Board's Trends in College Pricing: in 2025–26, average published tuition and fees were \$4,150 for in-district students at public two-year colleges and \$11,950 for in-state students at public four-year universities. The implication: across two years, a student saves roughly \$15,600 in tuition and fees alone by starting at a community college. The negative attacks the definition first. Published tuition is a sticker price, it argues, and "costs" should mean what a student actually pays after grants, plus what it costs to finish a degree. Its counter-contention, "Lost credits," argues that a transfer student whose credits do not transfer pays for extra semesters, which can erase the savings. (In a real debate the negative would need evidence for how often that happens; here it is the shape of the argument that matters.) The judge's decision turns on the definition. If "costs" means tuition and fees, the affirmative's evidence is strong and directly on point. If it means the full cost of finishing a degree, the negative has raised a real question the affirmative must answer with evidence about transfer outcomes. A good affirmative sees this coming and defends its definition in its first speech.

Resolution: Artificial intelligence will cause more job creation than job displacement. The affirmative runs two contentions. "Net job growth" uses the World Economic Forum's employer survey. "New work" uses the MIT finding that about 60 percent of today's U.S. jobs are in occupations that did not exist in 1940. The negative defines AI to include robotics, attacks the forecasts as expectations rather than outcomes, and runs one counter-contention, "Faster disruption," arguing from the same MIT research that automation's damage to employment has grown in recent decades. In the last speeches, the affirmative argues its definition is the common one and that the negative's own historical evidence still shows new work being created. The negative argues that small forecast margins cannot carry a burden of proof. A judge applying preponderance of evidence might reasonably go either way, and that is the sign of a good fact resolution. What decides it is which side did the comparing.

A judge in a fact debate asks one question: on balance, is the resolution more likely true than not? To answer it, the judge looks at which contentions survived the refutation, then compares the evidence and reasoning behind them. Judges reward debaters who do that comparison out loud, saying why one study beats another, rather than leaving the judge to sort it out. If the comparison is truly even, the judge votes negative, because the affirmative carries the burden of proof.

Skipping the implication. A warrant without an implication leaves the judge with a fact and no reason to vote. Proving a nearby claim. Showing that AI creates jobs is not the same as showing it creates more than it destroys. Treating definitions as a formality. In a fact debate, the definition often decides what counts as evidence. Reading evidence without reading the source. If the rest of the article says the opposite, your opponent will find it. Ending with more evidence instead of comparison. The last speech should tell the judge why your evidence is better.

By the end of this chapter you should be able to: Identify five patterns of reasoning and the test question for each. Define a fallacy and explain why a fallacious argument is not automatically false. Recognize eleven common fallacies and explain what goes wrong in each. Call out a fallacy in a debate by naming it, explaining it and saying what it does to the argument. Check your own case for fallacies before your opponent does.

Chapter 2 showed that the weakest part of most arguments is the warrant, the connection between the evidence and the claim. Reasoning is the process of drawing that connection: moving from what you know to what you conclude. Every warrant uses some kind of reasoning, usually without saying which kind. That matters in a debate because each kind of reasoning has its own way of failing. If you know which kind an argument uses, you know which question to ask, and the question often finds the flaw. This chapter first names five common patterns of reasoning and their tests, then looks at fallacies, the common ways reasoning goes wrong.

To compare the patterns, we will use one claim throughout: a debater argues that a community college's new drop-in tutoring center is raising pass rates in its math courses. (The example is hypothetical.) There are at least five ways to support that claim, and each one can be tested differently. Reasoning by example draws a general conclusion from specific cases. The debater says: "Pass rates went up in Algebra, Statistics and Calculus this year, the first year the center was open." Three cases support a general claim about math courses. The test question is: are there enough examples, and are they typical? Three courses out of three is persuasive. Three hand-picked courses out of twelve, with the other nine unchanged, is not. Reasoning by example is the basis of most research, since a study is a large, carefully chosen set of examples, and it is also the pattern behind the most common fallacy in this chapter, the hasty generalization. Causal reasoning argues that one thing produces another. The debater says: "Students who used the center passed at higher rates, because tutoring helps them catch mistakes before exams." The test question is: is this the real cause, and the only one? Maybe the students who chose to use the center were already the most motivated, and would have passed anyway. Maybe the department changed textbooks the same year. Two things happening together does not prove that one caused the other. Causal reasoning is the backbone of policy debate, where every link and internal link is a causal claim, so learning to test it now pays off in Part V. Reasoning by analogy argues that because two cases are alike in important ways, what is true of one is true of the other. The debater says: "A nearby college opened a similar center three years ago, and its math pass rates rose. Ours will too." The test question is: are the two cases alike in the ways that matter for this conclusion? If the other college also hired more instructors that year, or serves a very different group of students, the analogy weakens. Analogies are persuasive because they make something unfamiliar feel familiar, which is also what makes a weak one dangerous. Sign reasoning argues that one thing is evidence that another exists, without claiming one causes the other. The debater says: "The center is packed every afternoon before midterms, which shows students find it useful." A full room is a sign of use, the way smoke is a sign of fire. The test question is: is the sign reliable, or could it point to something else? A packed center could mean it is useful, or that it is the only quiet room on campus with outlets. Reasoning from authority argues that a claim is true because a qualified source says so. The debater says: "The college's institutional research office concluded the center raised pass rates." Most debate evidence works this way: you read what an expert found because you cannot run the study yourself. The test question is: is this source an expert on this question, and in a position to know? An institutional research office studying its own campus qualifies. A celebrity's opinion about tutoring does not. Chapter 8 covers how to judge sources in detail. At a glance Pattern How it works Test question Reasoning by example Specific cases support a general conclusion Are there enough examples, and are they typical? Causal reasoning One thing produces another Is this the real cause, and the only one? Reasoning by analogy Two cases alike in key ways share an outcome Are the cases alike in the ways that matter? Sign reasoning One thing indicates another exists Is the sign reliable, or could it mean something else? Reasoning from authority A qualified source says it is so Is the source an expert on this question and in a position to know?

A fallacy is the use of invalid or otherwise faulty reasoning in the construction of an argument. Fallacies have two qualities worth remembering. First, they are deceptive. A fallacy usually looks like good reasoning at first glance, which is why it works on audiences and why it is worth learning to spot. Nobody is persuaded by reasoning that looks broken. Second, a fallacious argument is not necessarily false. It is bad reasoning, not a wrong conclusion. "Everyone I know thinks the earth orbits the sun, so it does" is a fallacy (an appeal to popularity) with a true conclusion. This matters in a debate. Showing that your opponent's reasoning is fallacious removes their support for a claim. It does not prove the opposite claim. Treating it as if it did is itself a mistake, sometimes called the fallacy fallacy.

The eleven fallacies below fall into three families. Some bring in something irrelevant to the claim. Some draw too large a conclusion from too little evidence. Some build a false picture of the choices or consequences. Fallacies of relevance An ad hominem (Latin for "to the person") attacks the person making an argument instead of the argument. "Don't listen to my opponent's plan to lower tuition. He failed college algebra twice." His grade has nothing to do with whether the plan would work. In a debate, ad hominem attacks also cost you with judges, who expect you to engage the argument and often penalize personal attacks in speaker points. A red herring is a distraction that pulls attention from the argument at hand, whether the distraction is intentional or not, true or false. A professor asks why an essay is three days late, and the student answers that the parking lot is full every day. The parking lot may well be full. It is not the answer to the question. In a debate, a red herring often appears as a long answer to an argument nobody made, and the fix is to bring the judge back to the question that was actually asked. A straw man replaces an opponent's actual position with a distorted or exaggerated version that is easier to beat. Your opponent argues that students need less homework, and you respond that they want to eliminate homework, exams and attendance. You have beaten an argument nobody made. Straw men are easy to catch in a debate because the judge has the real argument on the flow. When you answer, quote your opponent's actual words first. An appeal to popularity (sometimes called ad populum) claims something is true because many people believe it. "Millions of people believe in astrology, so it must work." How many people believe a claim tells you about public opinion, not about whether the claim is true. Polls can be good evidence for a claim about what people think; they are poor evidence for anything else. An appeal to tradition claims something is right because it has been done that way for a long time. "Bloodletting is one of the oldest medical treatments, so it is tried and true." Age shows that a practice has survived, not that it works. In policy debates, the negative often defends the status quo, and it should defend it by showing it works, not only that it is familiar. An appeal to authority claims something is true because an authority says so, when the authority is not an expert on the question or when the authority is the only support offered. This one needs care, because debate evidence depends on experts, and reasoning from authority is often good reasoning. The fallacy happens in two situations. The first is a source speaking outside its expertise: a famous physicist's opinion about the economy is not expert evidence about the economy. The second is treating "an expert said so" as the end of the discussion when the expert's own reasons are available and weak, or when other experts disagree. The fix is to ask what the expert found and why. Fallacies of weak evidence A hasty generalization draws a broad conclusion from evidence that is too small or too unrepresentative to support it. "My dad smoked two packs a day and lived to 90, so smoking can't be that bad for you." One case cannot outweigh studies of millions. This is reasoning by example that fails its test question, and it is probably the fallacy you will see most often in debates, usually as one vivid story offered as proof of a trend. The no true Scotsman fallacy protects a generalization from a counterexample by redefining the group. A: "No college student actually likes 8 a.m. classes." B: "I'm a college student, and I love my 8 a.m." A: "Well, no real college student would pick an 8 a.m." Instead of giving up the generalization, A quietly changes its meaning so no counterexample can count. In a debate it often shows up when a definition shifts mid-round to dodge an answer. Point back to the original definition on the flow. A false analogy claims that because two things are alike in one way, they must be alike in another way that does not follow. "A college is like a business, so it should cut any class that does not make a profit." Colleges and businesses share some features, like budgets, but a college's purpose is not profit, so the comparison breaks down at the exact point the conclusion depends on. This is reasoning by analogy that fails its test question. Fallacies of false choices and consequences A slippery slope claims that one step will lead through a chain of events to an extreme outcome, without showing why each step follows. "If we let students use calculators on one quiz, soon nobody will learn arithmetic, and engineering degrees will be worthless." Each link might be possible, but none is shown. Not every chain argument is a slippery slope. A policy disadvantage is also a chain, and it is legitimate when every link has evidence. The fallacy is in skipping the proof, not in having a chain. A false dilemma (or false dichotomy) presents two options as the only ones when more exist. "Either you transfer to a UC or you've wasted your life." Students transfer to many kinds of schools, enter careers directly, or go back later. In a debate, a false dilemma often hides in a framing like "either we pass this plan or the problem gets worse." The answer is to name the third option. At a glance Fallacy What goes wrong Example Ad hominem Attacks the person, not the argument "He failed algebra, so ignore his tuition plan." Red herring Distracts from the question Answering a late essay with the parking problem Straw man Answers a distorted version of the argument "Less homework" becomes "no homework, exams or class." Appeal to popularity Many believe it, so it is true "Millions believe in astrology." Appeal to tradition Long-standing, so it is right "Bloodletting is tried and true." Appeal to authority A source outside its expertise, or "an expert said so" as the only support A physicist's opinion offered as proof about the economy Hasty generalization Too little or unrepresentative evidence "My dad smoked and lived to 90." No true Scotsman Redefines a group to dodge a counterexample "No real college student likes 8 a.m. classes." False analogy Alike in one way, assumed alike in another "A college is a business, so cut unprofitable classes." Slippery slope An unproven chain to an extreme outcome Calculators on one quiz lead to worthless degrees. False dilemma Only two options offered when more exist "Transfer to a UC or you've wasted your life."

x: Spotting a fallacy is half the job. The other half is answering it in a way a judge will credit, and that takes three moves. Figure 7.1 Calling out a fallacy The three moves of a fallacy answer in a debate: name the flaw, explain why the reasoning fails, and say what that does to the argument. First, name it. "That's a hasty generalization." Naming the flaw tells the judge what kind of problem you are about to show and makes your answer easy to flow. Second, explain it. Show the judge where the reasoning breaks, in terms of this argument: "Their only evidence is one study at one school, and the resolution is about community colleges nationwide." This is the step beginning debaters skip, and it is the step that wins the argument. A judge who has never heard the term "hasty generalization" can still follow the explanation. A judge who only hears the label has been given a word, not a reason. Third, say so what. Tell the judge what the flaw does to the argument and the debate: "That means their first contention has no support left, so the only evidence on this question is ours." This is Chapter 4's "That means..." step, and it connects your answer to the decision. Two cautions. Do not overuse fallacy names. A debater who calls everything a fallacy sounds like they are reciting a list, and many weak arguments are better answered with counter-evidence than with a label. And remember section 7.3: proving that an argument is fallacious removes its support, but it does not prove the opposite. If you need the judge to believe the opposite, you still need your own evidence. Finally, use this chapter on yourself first. Before a debate, read each of your warrants and ask its test question from section 7.2. Any fallacy your opponent could find, you can find first, and fix.

Name and explain: "That's a hasty generalization. One student's story is not evidence about all students." Test a cause: "They've shown the two happened together, not that one caused the other." Answer a straw man: "That's not our argument. What we said was..." Break a false dilemma: "There's a third option they've ignored." Close the answer: "That means their contention has no support left."

Resolution: Starting at a community college costs less than starting at a four-year university. The negative's counter-contention says: "My older sister started at a community college, lost a whole semester of credits when she transferred, and ended up paying more. Starting at a community college costs more." That is a hasty generalization: one transfer story offered as proof about all students. The affirmative names it, explains that one case cannot show how often credits are lost, and points out that the negative has no evidence about transfer outcomes in general. The so-what: the counter-contention has no support, so the affirmative's tuition evidence is the only evidence about cost on the flow. Notice what the affirmative did not say. It did not claim credits are never lost. The sister's story may be true, and a negative with real data about lost credits could make the argument well. The fallacy is in the jump from one case to a general claim.

Resolution: Artificial intelligence will cause more job creation than job displacement. The negative argues: "Polls show most people are worried AI will take their jobs, so AI will destroy more jobs than it creates." That is an appeal to popularity. What people fear is evidence about public opinion, not about labor markets. The affirmative also hears a false dilemma in the negative's summary ("either AI replaces workers or it's useless to employers") and names the third option the affirmative's own evidence describes: AI that changes what workers do without replacing them. The negative has a fallacy to call out too. The affirmative's second contention says that because past technologies created more work than they destroyed, AI will as well. The negative argues this is a weak analogy: earlier technologies automated physical or routine tasks, while AI can perform some of the judgment-based tasks that new jobs were built around. That is an argument about whether the cases are alike in the ways that matter, which is exactly the test question for reasoning by analogy. Whether it wins depends on which side explains the comparison better.

Judges do not award points for naming fallacies. They credit what the explanation does to the argument. A clearly explained flaw in a warrant can remove a contention from the debate; an unexplained label usually changes nothing. Judges also notice when a debater uses a fallacy themselves, especially a straw man, because the real argument is on the judge's flow for comparison.

Naming without explaining. "That's a slippery slope" is a label, not an answer. Treating a fallacy as proof of the opposite. Bad reasoning for a claim does not make the claim false. Calling all expert evidence an appeal to authority. The fallacy is a source outside its expertise, or "an expert said so" with nothing behind it. Calling every chain a slippery slope. A chain with evidence for every link is a legitimate argument. Answering with a straw man. Quote your opponent's actual argument before you answer it.

Drill: fallacy flag (15 minutes, small groups). One student reads a short argument aloud, built around one of the eleven fallacies. The first student to name the fallacy must then explain where the reasoning breaks and say what it does to the argument. A name without the explanation and the so-what earns no point. Rotate readers. Writing exercise. Find an argument in a news article, opinion piece or social media post that commits one of the fallacies in this chapter. In 200 words, identify the fallacy, explain where the reasoning breaks, and rewrite the argument so it uses sound reasoning instead.
Move: Prove. Builds on: Chapters 2 and 6. Where you use it: the first hours you spend on any new resolution, and every time you prepare for a debate after that.

By the end of this chapter you should be able to: Explain how research for a debate differs from academic research, and why looking for the source that says you are right is a trap. Use three levels of research to move from a new topic to specific evidence. Search efficiently with keywords, operators and the right tool for the question. Get the full text of a source legally through your library and open-access tools. Judge a source's quality using source types, lateral reading and the four SIFT moves. Use AI tools in research without letting them supply your evidence.

In debate, research is the process of finding relevant information about the resolution in order to build arguments for your side and answers to your opponent's. That definition hides something important. Debate research is goal-oriented research: you know the conclusion you need before you start looking. You were assigned a side. Your job is to prove it. That is not how academic research usually works. A scientist or historian starts with a question and follows the evidence wherever it goes; the conclusion comes last. A debater starts with the conclusion and goes looking for support. Lawyers work this way too, and so does anyone writing an advocacy brief, so there is nothing dishonest about it. But it creates a specific temptation. Call it the search for IAmRight.com: the imaginary website that says, in one perfect sentence, exactly what you need it to say. Every debater has typed a search hoping to land there. The trouble is that the sources that come closest to IAmRight.com are often the weakest ones you could find. Careful researchers qualify their claims, describe their limits and report results that cut both ways. The sources that state your conclusion in the boldest possible terms, with no caveats, are usually opinion pieces, advocacy groups, blogs and social media posts. A search engine will happily find them, because you asked for them. The deeper problem is confirmation bias, the tendency to notice, favor and remember information that supports what you already believe. Goal-oriented research feeds it. When you are hunting for support, a sentence that agrees with you feels like a find, and the paragraph after it, the one where the author explains why the claim is more complicated, is easy to skip. That is how debaters end up reading evidence out of context, which Chapter 6 showed can hand your opponent a weapon and Chapter 9 treats as an ethics problem. None of this means you should stop doing goal-oriented research. Debate is advocacy, and advocacy needs evidence. It means you need habits that keep the goal from bending what you find. The rest of this chapter is those habits.

The most important habit is to be literature-informed: let your reading shape your arguments, instead of deciding your arguments first and then hunting for evidence to fit them. The "literature" is simply the body of serious writing on a topic: studies, reports, books and expert analysis. In practice, being literature-informed means that the first thing you do with a new resolution is read, not search for quotes. Spend your first stretch of preparation, even if it is only a few minutes before a debate with limited prep time, reading about the topic to learn what the experts actually argue about, which impacts the topic can reach and where the strongest evidence is. Then choose arguments that the literature supports. Your goal (your side) does not change. What changes is that you pick the route to it after looking at the map, instead of drawing the route first and hoping a road is there. This habit also solves the IAmRight.com problem. If the literature does not support an argument, a literature-informed debater drops the argument. A debater who started with the argument keeps searching until some source, any source, says it. One more piece of the habit: research both sides. You will often debate both sides of the same resolution, and even when you do not, the best way to prepare answers is to know your opponent's strongest evidence before they read it. Reading the other side also makes your own arguments better, because the sources that take the controversy seriously are usually the most credible ones on either side.

Research on a new resolution moves through three levels, from wide to narrow. Each level asks a different kind of question. (Librarians use the words primary, secondary and tertiary to describe kinds of sources, such as original data, analysis of that data, and encyclopedias. This book uses different names for the levels of research to avoid mixing the two up.) Figure 8.1 Three levels of research Research narrowing from wide to specific: exploratory research maps the topic, focused research follows the questions it raises, and targeted research looks for one specific answer. Exploratory research is research without a specific goal: you are learning the territory. On the AI fact resolution, an exploratory question is "How is artificial intelligence changing work?" Good sources at this level are overviews: news explainers, the executive summaries of major reports, and reference sites like encyclopedias. Reference sites are fine to read here, and their footnotes are a good map to better sources, but they are not sources you cite in a debate. By the end of exploratory research you should know the topic's vocabulary, its major studies and experts, and where the real disagreement is. Focused research has a general goal: you are following up on the questions exploration raised. "Which occupations are most exposed to AI?" "What does the World Economic Forum's jobs report actually measure?" "Who disagrees with it, and why?" At this level you start reading studies and reports in full, and you start to see which arguments the literature can support on each side. Targeted research has a highly specific goal: you are looking for a particular answer that you have reason to believe the literature will confirm. "How many jobs did employers attribute to AI in their 2025 layoff announcements?" This is the level where evidence for your case actually gets found, and it is also where the pull toward IAmRight.com is strongest. The rule at this level: if the literature does not confirm the answer you expected, change the argument, not the evidence. The levels are not a one-way trip. Targeted research often turns up something surprising that sends you back to focused research, and that is the literature leading, which is exactly what you want. At a glance Level Goal Example question (AI resolution) Typical sources Exploratory None yet: learn the territory How is AI changing work? Explainers, report summaries, reference sites (to read, not cite) Focused General: follow the questions exploration raised Which occupations are most exposed to AI? Full reports, studies, expert analysis Targeted Specific: find an answer you expect the literature to confirm How many jobs did employers attribute to AI in 2025? The specific study, dataset or report that answers it

Most students search the way they talk, typing a full question into a search engine. Good researchers search the way authors write. A few habits make a large difference. Use as few words as possible, and use the words an expert would use. "Will AI take people's jobs?" finds opinion and worry. "AI job displacement estimate" finds the reports those opinions are about. When a good source uses a technical term, such as "occupational exposure" or "labor displacement," add it to your searches. Learn a few search operators, symbols and commands that tell a search engine exactly what you want. These work in Google and many other search tools: Quotation marks search for an exact phrase: "job displacement". A minus sign excludes a word: AI jobs -crypto. site: limits results to one website or type of website: site:bls.gov for the Bureau of Labor Statistics, or site:.gov for U.S. government sites. filetype:pdf limits results to PDFs, which is where many full reports live. OR (in capitals) finds either term: "artificial intelligence" OR "machine learning" employment. Use the right tool for the question. A general search engine is good for exploratory research and for finding reports from organizations. A news search (such as Google News) is best for current events. Google Scholar searches academic writing; its "Cited by" link shows newer work that responds to a study, which is one of the fastest ways to find both support and criticism. Your college library's library databases, collections of journals, magazines and newspapers your college pays for, give you sources a search engine cannot. For U.S. policy topics, government sources such as the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the Census Bureau, the Congressional Budget Office and the Congressional Research Service publish data and nonpartisan analysis for free. Keep a research log as you go: for every source you might use, record the author, the author's qualifications, the title, the publication, the date and the link. Recording it later means finding it again later, usually the night before a debate.

Many of the best sources sit behind paywalls. You will often find a perfect-looking abstract and then a request for payment. Do not pay, and do not settle for the abstract: you cannot responsibly use a source you have not read. There are legal, free ways to get most of what you need. Start with your college library. As a student, you already have access to its databases, usually through your student login from anywhere. You can also link Google Scholar to your library: in Scholar's settings, the Library Links option lets you add your college, and results your library can provide will show a full-text link. Reference librarians are the most underused research tool on any campus. They are experts at finding sources, and helping students is their job. Next, look for an open access copy, a version of the article that is legally free to read. Many authors post copies of their work in university repositories. In Google Scholar, the "All versions" link under a result often finds one. Unpaywall, a free browser extension from a nonprofit, checks an index of legal open-access copies whenever you land on a paywalled article and links you to a free version if one exists. If those fail, ask your library about interlibrary loan, which borrows articles and books from other libraries, or email the author. Researchers usually want people to read their work and are often happy to send a copy. For newspapers and magazines, your college or public library may offer free access as well. Everything in this section is legal and free for students. Stick to these routes. Evidence you cannot show was obtained honestly is not evidence you want to defend in front of a judge.

Once you have a source, you need to decide how much a judge should trust it. Start with the type of source, then check the specific source in front of you. Some types of sources are generally strong. Peer review is the process in which other experts check a study before a journal publishes it, so peer-reviewed academic journals are among the most credible sources you can use. Government reports from agencies like the Bureau of Labor Statistics or the Congressional Budget Office are usually strong, especially for data. A think tank is an organization that researches and advocates on public policy. Reputable think tanks and research groups publish serious analysis, but most have a known perspective, and some are funded by groups with a stake in the issue. Use their work, and know where they stand. Major news outlets and professional publications are generally good, especially for recent events. They are best used for what happened and what experts said, and less for causal claims, which a reporter is usually summarizing from someone else. When a news story reports a study, find the study. Some types of sources do not belong in a debate case. Blogs and social media posts are usually one person's opinion with no checking. Reference sites, such as online encyclopedias and pro-and-con summary sites, are useful for exploratory research but are summaries of other sources; cite the sources they summarize instead. Source types are a starting point, not a verdict. A peer-reviewed study can be weak, and a blog post by a leading economist can be excellent. The question is always about the specific source. Here, the habits of professional fact checkers help. In a well-known Stanford study, Sam Wineburg and Sarah McGrew watched historians, professional fact checkers and Stanford undergraduates evaluate websites on social and political issues. The historians and students mostly read vertically, staying on a site to judge it by how it looked and what it said about itself. The fact checkers practiced lateral reading: they quickly left the site and opened new tabs to see what other sources said about it. The fact checkers were faster and more accurate. Mike Caulfield, a researcher at the University of Washington, condensed fact checkers' habits into four moves called SIFT. They fit debate research well. Figure 8.2 Four moves for checking a source (SIFT) Mike Caulfield's four SIFT moves, each with the question a debater asks at that step. Stop. When you find a source that seems perfect, especially one that gives you a strong emotional reaction or exactly the sentence you wanted, pause before you use it. Ask whether you know who wrote it and whether you trust them. IAmRight.com should set off this alarm. Investigate the source. Spend a minute finding out who is behind it, using lateral reading. Who is the author, and what are their qualifications? Who publishes the site, and do they have a stake in the issue? In debate, this step also gives you something you will need anyway: the author's qualifications, which you will read aloud with the evidence (Chapter 9). Find better coverage. If a source is weak or you cannot tell, look for a better source making the same claim. If a blog says AI will destroy 40 percent of jobs, look for the report the number came from, or for experts who have assessed that claim. Often the better source is easy to find once you know the claim. Trace claims to the original context. Much of what you find online is a summary of a summary. Follow the claim back to its original source and read what that source actually says, including the paragraphs around the sentence you want. Chapter 6's Goldman Sachs example is what happens when a debater skips this move. After SIFT, ask the questions that matter for a debate in particular. Is the author qualified on this specific question? Is the source recent enough for the topic? On a fast-moving topic like AI, a three-year-old prediction may already be out of date. Does it speak directly to the resolution, or to something nearby? And for studies, how was it done: how large was the sample, and who was in it? At a glance Question What to check Who wrote it? The author's qualifications on this specific question Who published it? The publisher's reputation, perspective and funding What kind of source is it? Peer-reviewed study, government report, think tank, news, or opinion Is it recent enough? The date, measured against how fast the topic changes Is it on point? Whether it addresses the resolution or only something nearby What does the original say? The full context of the claim, traced back to its source

AI tools can make you a faster researcher, and they can also end your credibility in one debate. The difference is whether you treat them as a research assistant or as a source. Used as an assistant, AI is genuinely helpful. It can summarize a topic during exploratory research, brainstorm arguments for both sides, suggest counterarguments you had not considered, propose search terms an expert would use, check whether your explanation of an argument is clear, and help you adapt an argument for a particular audience. In each of those uses, you check the result against real sources before it goes anywhere near a debate. Used as a source, AI is dangerous. AI chatbots can produce a hallucination: a confident, fluent, specific answer that is simply false, including statistics, quotations and citations to studies that do not exist. In Mata v. Avianca (2023), lawyers in New York filed a brief citing court decisions that ChatGPT had invented. When the court could not find the cases, the lawyers stood by them at first. Judge P. Kevin Castel fined the lawyers and their firm \$5,000 and required them to send his opinion to the real judges the fake decisions had been attributed to. Professionals with law degrees made this mistake. A student in a debate round can make it too. The rule is simple: never use a quotation, statistic or citation you have not read in its original source. If an AI tool points you to a source, go read the source. Some tools now link the sources they summarize, which is useful, but summaries can still misstate what a source says, so the rule still applies. And follow your course's policy on AI use, including any requirement to disclose it. A coach's view, from this book's author: you are responsible for every word you put in an outline, every piece of evidence you read in a debate and every word you say in a round. AI makes mistakes. Catching them is your job, not the tool's.

Read qualifications with evidence: "Professor of economics at MIT, in a 2024 study..." Compare sources: "Prefer our evidence: it's a peer-reviewed study, and theirs is a blog post." Trace a claim: "Their card is a news summary. The original study says something narrower." Question a source in cross-examination: "Who is your author, and what are their qualifications?" Point out a stake: "Their source is funded by the industry the resolution would regulate."

Resolution: Starting at a community college costs less than starting at a four-year university. Exploratory: what does "cost" include? Reading overviews turns up the difference between published price (tuition and fees) and net price (what students pay after grants), and the fact that living costs, books and time to degree all count. Focused: how do net prices compare, and what happens to transfer students? Targeted: what is the published tuition at each type of school? The College Board's annual Trends in College Pricing answers that directly, and the federal College Navigator site shows the net price for specific schools. The IAmRight.com moment comes early. A community college's own web page promises students will "save thousands." It says exactly what the affirmative wants. SIFT stops the debater: the source has an obvious stake in the claim. Finding better coverage leads to the College Board data, which supports the same conclusion and is far harder to attack.

Resolution: The United States federal government should substantially restrict the development of artificial intelligence. Exploratory research starts with what the law currently says, and the Congressional Research Service is a strong place to start, because it writes nonpartisan explanations of current policy for members of Congress. Focused research looks for the main arguments on both sides: think tanks across the political spectrum, academic research on AI risks and benefits, and statements from AI companies, which are informative but come from parties with an obvious stake. Targeted research then finds specific evidence for the arguments the literature supports. Partway through, the debater finds a headline (this part of the example is hypothetical) claiming that experts say AI will probably end humanity. It is a perfect IAmRight.com sentence for the affirmative. Tracing the claim to its original context turns up a survey whose actual question and results are far more qualified than the headline. The literature-informed move is to read the survey, report what it actually found, and build the argument on that, even if it sounds less dramatic. A judge who hears the opponent read the full survey will trust the qualified version more.

Most judges do not evaluate source quality on their own initiative. They compare evidence when the debaters give them a reason to. That means source quality is an argument you have to make out loud, using the questions in section 8.6. Judges also notice credibility: a debater who cannot answer "who is your author?" loses some of the judge's trust in every piece of evidence they read afterward. Evidence that turns out to be fabricated or badly out of context can lose a debate on its own. Chapter 9 covers evidence ethics in detail.

Debaters who start with targeted searches find quotes without understanding the topic. Citing a summary of a summary. Trace the claim to the original and read what it actually says. Using only the abstract. If you cannot get the full text through the library or an open-access copy, do not use the source. Treating an AI answer as evidence. Never use a statistic, quotation or citation you have not read in its original source. Losing the citation. Record the author, qualifications, date and link when you find a source, not later.

Drill: research race (20 minutes, small groups). Your instructor gives each group a list of specific questions, such as the title of a particular study, a statistic from a government report, or the qualifications of a named expert. Groups race to find each answer and must show the original source, not a summary. Afterward, each group explains which searches and tools worked and which wasted time. Drill: sixty-second SIFT (10 minutes, pairs). Each partner finds an article or website making a claim about AI and jobs. Swap. You have sixty seconds to investigate the other's source using lateral reading, then report who is behind it and whether you would use it in a debate. Writing exercise. Keep a research log for the AI fact resolution: five sources, at least two of them peer-reviewed or government sources, each with full citation information, the author's qualifications, and a two-sentence note on what the source shows and how you got the full text.

By the end of this chapter you should be able to: Name the three parts of a card and explain what each one does. Cut a card from a source: copy the text, write a tag, highlight what you will read, and cite it. Read evidence aloud and explain it so a judge knows what it proves. Explain the main rules of evidence ethics and why breaking them can lose a debate. Compare competing pieces of evidence and tell a judge which to prefer.

In debate, a card is a single piece of evidence formatted according to the standards of debate. The name is old. Debaters once copied quotations onto index cards and filed them in boxes; today the cards live in documents, but the name and the format stuck. Every card has three parts, and each one has a different job. The tag is a one-sentence summary of what the card proves, written by you, in your words. It is the claim. When you read a card in a speech, the tag is what the judge writes on the flow, so a tag should be short, specific and certain: "AI raised productivity at the firms that adopted it" tells the judge exactly what to write. A tag is also a promise. Whatever the tag claims, the text you read aloud has to support. The citation is the record of who wrote the evidence, when, and where it was published. A full citation includes the author's name, the author's qualifications (what makes them an expert), the date, the title, the publication and a link or other way to find it. In a speech you read a short version, usually the author's last name, the year and the qualifications ("Rivera '25, labor economist at the state university"), while the full citation stays in your document so anyone who asks can find the source. In the document, emphasize only the author's name and year, the part you read aloud, so it is easy to spot. The card text is the evidence itself, copied exactly from the source. It is the warrant: the part that actually proves the tag. A card's text should include at least the full paragraph the evidence comes from, with the original paragraph breaks kept intact, because the sentences around a claim are often what show whether you have represented it fairly. You will not read the whole paragraph aloud. Highlighting marks the parts you will read. At a glance Part What it is What it does Tag One sentence, in your words States the claim the card proves; it is what the judge flows Citation Author, qualifications, date, title, publication, link Shows the source is credible and lets anyone find it Card text The source's exact words, at least a full paragraph, with read portions highlighted Supplies the warrant that proves the tag

Cutting a card means turning a source into a card. It takes five steps, and doing them in order prevents most mistakes. Figure 9.1 Anatomy of a card The three parts of a card as they appear on the page: the tag on top, the citation below it with the author and year emphasized, and the full paragraph of text with the read portion highlighted. First, find and read the source, all of it, using the habits from Chapter 8. Second, copy the text: the full paragraph that contains the evidence, exactly as written, with nothing added or changed. If a key claim is spread over two paragraphs, copy both. Third, write the tag, after you have read the text, not before. A tag written first tends to claim what you wanted the source to say; a tag written after reading claims what it actually says. Fourth, highlight. Highlighting marks the words you will read aloud in a speech. It exists because time is short: a judge does not need every word of a paragraph, only the words that prove the tag. Good highlighting follows three rules. It must prove the tag on its own: if a judge heard only the highlighted words, would they believe the tag? It must still make sense: highlighted words that skip the subject of a sentence ("will pass" without saying what will pass) leave the judge guessing. And it should be efficient: long unbroken runs of highlighted text usually include words the judge does not need. Most debaters use a highlighter color for the read words and underlining or bold for the important context around them; your class may set a standard. Fifth, cite it, with every part of the citation. Browser tools can fill in much of a citation automatically, but check the result, especially the author's qualifications, which tools often miss and which you will read aloud. A finished card might look like this (the source here is invented for illustration): AI tools raised worker productivity, especially for less experienced workers. Rivera '25, Dana Rivera, labor economist, State University, "What Happened When the Help Desk Got AI," Journal of Workplace Studies, March 2025, [link] The card text would follow: the full paragraph from the article, with the sentences reporting the productivity gain and who gained most highlighted, and the rest left unhighlighted but still on the page.

In a speech, you read a card in order: tag, short citation, highlighted text. "AI tools raised productivity, especially for less experienced workers. Rivera '25, labor economist at State University: [highlighted text]." Read the tag a little more slowly than the text, because it is what the judge writes down. Then do the part beginning debaters skip: explaining evidence, saying in your own words what the card proves and why it matters for the debate. Evidence does not speak for itself. A judge hears a card once, at speed, and may not catch the key sentence. A short explanation after the card ("This matters because the resolution is about whether new jobs replace lost ones, and these workers kept their jobs and got better at them") turns a quotation into an argument. The same rule applies later in the debate. When you extend a card in a rebuttal, extend its warrant, not just its name. "Extend Rivera" tells the judge nothing they can weigh. "Extend Rivera: the firms that adopted AI kept their workers and made them more productive, which answers their displacement argument" gives the judge a reason. In formats without prepared evidence, such as parliamentary debate, the same principle applies with no card at all: name your source if you can, but always make and explain the argument the evidence would contain, because there is no card for the judge or your opponent to check.

Evidence ethics are the rules that keep evidence honest. Debate depends on trust: a judge cannot check every card during a round, so the activity only works if debaters represent their sources accurately. Breaking these rules is not a strategic risk. It is cheating, and tournaments and classrooms treat it that way, often with a loss and sometimes with more. The most common violation is reading evidence out of context: presenting a source as supporting a claim it does not support, usually by leaving out the sentences that qualify or contradict it. A card that says "AI will eliminate millions of jobs" is out of context if the next sentence says "but our model predicts it will create even more." This is why the card text includes the full paragraph and why Chapter 8 insists you read the whole source. If the rest of the article undermines your card, do not use the card. Highlighting can create the same problem. Highlighting that skips words so the read version says something the full sentence does not (reading "AI will destroy jobs" out of "AI will not destroy jobs") misrepresents the source as surely as a fabricated quote. The test: would the author agree that your highlighted words fairly state what they wrote? Clipping is claiming to read more of a card than you actually read, for example by marking text as highlighted and then skipping parts of it in the speech. Your opponent and judge rely on your document to know what evidence was read, so clipping misrepresents the debate itself. If you decide mid-speech to read less of a card, say so: "I'll stop the card there." The most serious violations are fabrication (inventing evidence or citations) and distortion (changing a source's words). Chapter 8's warning about AI hallucinations belongs here too: a fabricated citation is fabricated whether you or a chatbot invented it, and you are responsible for it. A practical test covers all of these. Ask whether your evidence would survive your opponent reading the whole source. If they could rehighlight your card, reading different words from the same paragraph to make it say the opposite, the card is not just weak. It is a weapon for the other side.

Debates often come down to two cards that disagree. A judge cannot simply count cards; under any criterion, the judge has to decide which evidence is more convincing. Evidence comparison means giving the judge reasons to prefer your evidence, out loud, in your speech. Chapter 8 introduced the questions; here is how to use them as arguments. Qualifications. Is one author an expert on this specific question and the other not? A labor economist outranks a technology journalist on employment data. Recency. On fast-moving topics, newer evidence can account for events older evidence could not. Recency matters most when something has changed between the two dates; a newer card is not better just because it is newer. Specificity. Evidence that speaks directly to the resolution, the place or the situation in the debate beats evidence about something nearby. A study of AI at community colleges beats a general claim about technology in schools if the debate is about community colleges. Method. For studies: how big was the sample, how was it chosen, and what was actually measured? A survey of a thousand employers beats one company's experience. Certainty. Evidence that takes a clear position beats evidence that hedges. A card that says something "could potentially" happen proves much less than one that says it "will." Before comparing, check whether the cards actually conflict. Two cards that seem to disagree often measure different things: one counts jobs lost in a single industry, the other counts jobs gained across the economy. Pointing out that your opponent's card does not answer yours can be stronger than arguing yours is better. At a glance Comparison The question Say it Qualifications Who is the expert on this question? "Our author studies labor markets; theirs writes about gadgets." Recency Has something changed since the older card? "Their card predates the policy change; ours accounts for it." Specificity Which speaks directly to this debate? "Ours is about community colleges; theirs is about schools in general." Method Which study is better designed? "A thousand employers beats one company's experience." Certainty Which takes a clear position? "Their author says it could happen; ours says it will."

Read a card: "[Tag]. Rivera '25, labor economist at State University: [highlighted text]." Explain it: "This matters because..." Extend a warrant: "Extend Rivera: the firms that adopted AI kept their workers. That answers their displacement argument." Compare: "Prefer our evidence for two reasons: it's more recent, and it measures outcomes instead of predictions." Challenge context: "Read the next sentence of their card. The author says the opposite." Stop a card honestly: "I'll stop the card there."

Resolution: Starting at a community college costs less than starting at a four-year university. The affirmative cuts a card from the College Board's annual pricing report. Tag: "Community college tuition is roughly a third of public four-year tuition." The citation names the College Board, the report title and the year. The text includes the full paragraph comparing published prices, with the two figures and the sentence identifying them as average published tuition and fees highlighted. The affirmative leaves unhighlighted, but on the page, the paragraph's note that published prices differ from what students pay after grants. That unhighlighted sentence is exactly what the negative points to: the card measures sticker price, not net price. The affirmative cannot be accused of hiding anything, because the sentence was on the page, and it has its answer ready, because it read the whole source. Honest cutting protects you as well as your opponent.

Resolution: Artificial intelligence will cause more job creation than job displacement. Both sides read cards about the same 2025 employer survey. The affirmative's card is tagged "Employers expect AI to create more jobs than it displaces." The negative's card, from a technology news site, is tagged "Experts warn AI will displace millions of workers." In the rebuttals, the affirmative compares: its card comes directly from the survey report while the negative's is a summary of it; and the negative's card, read in full, reports the same survey's displacement figure without its creation figure. That last point is a context argument, and a strong one, because it uses the negative's own evidence to show the comparison favors the affirmative.

Judges weigh evidence by the reasons the debaters give them. Without comparison, many judges treat conflicting cards as a wash, and the debate turns on something else. With comparison, the better card wins that part of the debate. Judges also notice ethics: a debater caught reading evidence out of context loses credibility on every other card, and in many settings a clear violation is grounds to lose the round.

Writing the tag first. Read the text, then write a tag that claims what the text actually proves. Tags that overclaim. If the highlighted text says "could," the tag cannot say "will." Cutting only one sentence. Keep at least the full paragraph, with its breaks, so the context is on the page. Highlighting that does not make sense. If the highlighted words leave out what the sentence is about, the judge cannot follow it. Reading without explaining. A card read with no explanation is a quotation, not an argument. Extending names instead of warrants. "Extend Rivera" gives the judge nothing to weigh.

Drill: cut and swap (20 minutes, pairs). Each partner cuts one card on the AI fact resolution from a source found in Chapter 8's research log: full paragraph, tag, highlighting and full citation. Swap cards. Your partner reads only the highlighted words aloud and says whether they prove the tag, then tries to rehighlight the paragraph to support the opposite claim. Fix anything that fails. Writing exercise. Find two cards on the same question that disagree. In 250 words, compare them on at least three of the five comparison questions, and end with a one-sentence instruction to a judge about which to prefer and why.
Move: Weigh. Builds on: Chapters 1 and 4. Where you use it: before every debate, when you size up your judge, and at the end of every debate, when you tell that judge why your impacts matter more.

By the end of this chapter you should be able to: Analyze an audience using four elements: interests, understanding, attitudes and beliefs. Adapt a speech's content, wording and delivery to a particular judge. Describe the differences between lay and technical judges and adjust for each. Compare impacts using five weighing terms: magnitude, probability, timeframe, reversibility and sequencing. Deliver weighing a judge can use to decide.

Chapter 1 ended with the point that the receiver matters most: you do not win by being right in the abstract, you win by convincing a specific judge. This chapter turns that idea into a method. Audience analysis is the process of identifying an audience and adapting a speech to their interests, level of understanding, attitudes and beliefs. Each of those four elements is a question you can ask about any judge. Interests are how much your audience wants to know about a topic. A judge who follows technology news is already interested in an AI debate; a judge who does not may need a reason to care in your first thirty seconds. You adapt to interest mostly through content: lead with the example most likely to matter to this person, and connect abstract stakes to concrete people. Understanding is how well your audience grasps the meaning you intend. It depends on what the judge already knows about the topic and about debate. A judge who has never heard the term "internal link" will not follow an argument built on it. You adapt to understanding through word choice and explanation: define terms the first time you use them, swap jargon for plain words, and slow down for the steps that carry the most weight. Attitudes are the positive or negative feelings your audience already has toward your content or your delivery. One judge loves fast, dense debate; another is annoyed by it. One finds jokes welcome; another finds them unprofessional. You adapt to attitudes through delivery and tone, and through timing: how you spend your speech time signals what you think matters. Beliefs are the statements your audience holds to be true before you say a word. A judge who believes technology always creates more jobs than it destroys is a different audience for the AI fact debate than one who believes the opposite. You do not need to share a judge's beliefs, and you should never pretend to. You adapt to beliefs through content: acknowledge the belief, show you have taken it seriously, and give the judge a reason to set it aside for this debate. A judge asked to reverse a belief needs more evidence and better explanation than a judge asked to confirm one. At a glance Element The question How you adapt Interests How much does this judge want to know about the topic? Content: lead with what will matter to them Understanding What does this judge already know about the topic and about debate? Word choice, definitions, explanation, pace Attitudes How does this judge feel about my content and style? Delivery, tone and how I spend my time Beliefs What does this judge already hold to be true? Content: acknowledge the belief and give reasons to set it aside

Judges vary on a range from lay to technical. A lay judge has little or no debate experience: a community member, a parent, a teacher from another field, or a classmate. A lay judge decides the way most audiences do, by asking which side made more sense and seemed more credible. They are less likely to flow carefully, less likely to know debate vocabulary, and more likely to be influenced by clear structure, confident delivery and good examples. A technical judge has debate experience, often as a former competitor or coach. Technical judges flow closely, know the vocabulary, and tend to decide on the arguments as they stand on the flow at the end of the debate: which were answered, which were dropped, and how the debaters told them to weigh what was left. They are more willing to vote on an argument a lay judge would find strange, as long as it was won. The difference is easy to overstate. Both kinds of judges reward clear structure, explained warrants and explicit weighing; the difference is mostly in how much explanation they need and how much debate shorthand they accept. The safe adjustment for a lay judge is to slow down, cut the jargon, use fewer arguments explained more fully, and spell out why each one matters. The adjustment for a technical judge is to make sure every important argument is on the flow and extended, and to answer every argument your opponent could win on. If you are not sure which kind of judge you have, debate for a smart person who is new to debate. Both kinds of judges can follow that. Many tournaments ask judges to write a judge philosophy, a short statement of how they decide debates, what they like and what they dislike. In a class, your instructor is often your judge, and the rubric and comments are their philosophy. Read it, and adapt to it. Adapting is not pandering; it is communicating with the person in front of you.

Most debates end with both sides winning something. The affirmative has an impact left on the Scale, and so does the negative. The judge then has to decide which matters more, and if the debaters do not tell them how, the judge will decide on their own, which is the outcome you least want. Impact calculus is the direct comparison of impacts, and of the scenarios that lead to them, in a debate. It is the closest thing debate has to a key that opens every lock: in most close debates, the side that does the better weighing wins. Figure 10.1 Five ways to weigh impacts The five weighing terms as five questions a judge can ask when two impacts are on the Scale. Five terms give you the comparisons. The first three apply in almost every debate. Magnitude is how severe an impact is, whether measured in numbers ("ten million jobs") or described in quality ("the loss of the right to vote"). Magnitude asks: how big? An impact that affects more people, or affects them more deeply, has greater magnitude. Students often reach for magnitude first, and it is powerful, but it is rarely enough on its own. A huge impact that is very unlikely may not outweigh a smaller one that is nearly certain. Probability is the comparative likelihood that an impact happens. Probability asks: how likely? It depends on the strength of every link in the chain that leads to the impact. Chapter 14 will show that each step in a chain adds a chance to fail, which is why a short, well-evidenced chain to a moderate impact can outweigh a long, speculative chain to a catastrophe. Timeframe is how soon an impact happens and how long it lasts. Timeframe asks: how soon, and for how long? An impact that happens tomorrow can come before one decades away, since the near-term impact cannot wait while the long-term one may still be prevented. But timeframe cuts both ways: an impact that lasts for generations may outweigh a sharp but brief one. Two more terms apply in fewer debates, and win them when they do. Reversibility is the degree to which an impact can be undone once it happens. Reversibility asks: can it be fixed? A recession is terrible but economies recover; a species, once extinct, is gone. When one side's impact is permanent and the other's is not, reversibility gives the judge a strong reason to prevent the permanent one first. Sequencing is how one impact affects whether another will happen. Sequencing asks: does one cause the other? If your opponent's impact is mass starvation and your impact is a war that would itself cause mass starvation, then preventing your impact prevents theirs too. Sequencing is often the strongest weighing argument available, because it does not ask the judge to choose between impacts at all. It shows that one impact contains the other. At a glance Term The question Example argument Magnitude How big? "Our impact affects millions; theirs affects one industry." Probability How likely? "Our impact needs two steps, both with evidence; theirs needs five." Timeframe How soon, and how long? "Our harm is happening now; theirs is decades away." Reversibility Can it be undone? "A recession ends; a lost species does not come back." Sequencing Does one cause the other? "The war causes the starvation, so preventing the war prevents both."

Knowing the terms is not the same as weighing well. Three habits make the difference. First, compare, do not just describe. "Our impact is very large" is description. "Our impact is larger than theirs because it affects every worker, not just one industry" is weighing. Every weighing argument should mention both impacts. Second, weigh on more than one term, and answer your opponent's weighing. If your opponent says their impact is bigger and you say yours is more likely, the judge now has to weigh the weighing. Help them: explain why probability matters more than magnitude in this debate, for example because the opponent's chain is so speculative that its size does not matter. Third, start early. Weighing saved for the last thirty seconds of the last speech is rushed and easy to miss. Strong debaters set up their weighing in their first speech ("this impact is irreversible, and that will matter at the end of the debate") and build it through every speech after.

Magnitude: "Even if they win their impact, ours is bigger, because..." Probability: "Their impact depends on five things all going wrong. Ours is already happening." Timeframe: "Our impact comes first. Theirs is decades away and can still be prevented." Reversibility: "Their harm can be undone. Ours cannot." Sequencing: "Our impact causes theirs, so voting for us solves both." For a lay judge: "Here's what this means for real people..."

Resolution: Students should start at a community college rather than a four-year university. The judge is a parent volunteer, a lay judge who believes, from their own experience, that the four-year campus experience matters. The affirmative's audience analysis says: interested (they care about students), limited debate understanding, positive attitude toward clear explanation, and a belief against the resolution. So the affirmative acknowledges the belief up front ("the campus experience is real, and we're not dismissing it"), uses plain words, and weighs explicitly: its impact (lower debt) is more probable, since it happens to every student who saves on tuition, and less reversible, since debt follows students for years, while the campus experience is partly available to transfer students later. Every weighing claim names both impacts.

Resolution: Artificial intelligence does more harm than good. The affirmative's impact is long-term job displacement; the negative's is faster medical research that saves lives. The negative weighs on magnitude and timeframe: lives saved now, against economic harm that may be temporary. The affirmative answers with probability and sequencing: the medical benefits depend on several uncertain steps, while displacement is already measurable, and widespread job loss would reduce access to the very healthcare the negative's impact depends on. The judge, a technical judge, now has two competing frames. Whoever explains why their frame should come first in this debate wins the ballot.

Judges look for the debater who tells them how to decide. Without weighing, a judge has to compare impacts on their own and may use standards neither side argued. With weighing from only one side, that side's frame usually wins. With weighing from both sides, the judge looks for who compared more directly, answered the other side's weighing, and connected the weighing to the evidence on the flow.

Describing instead of comparing. Weighing has to mention both impacts. Only arguing magnitude. A huge, unlikely impact can lose to a smaller, certain one. Weighing too late. Set up your weighing early and build it through the debate. Ignoring the opponent's weighing. If both sides weigh, explain why your frame should come first. Debating the same way for every judge. Adjust explanation, pace and vocabulary to the person deciding.

Drill: weigh it (15 minutes, pairs). Your instructor gives pairs of impacts, such as an economic collapse tomorrow against climate change over decades, or a nuclear war against mass starvation. One partner weighs for the first impact in thirty seconds using at least two terms; the other answers, using at least one different term, and explains why their frame should come first. Switch. Drill: same speech, two judges (15 minutes, small groups). Give a one-minute version of a contention to a "technical judge," then to a "lay judge." The group names three things that changed between the versions. Writing exercise. Pick a judge you might face in this class, such as a classmate, your instructor or a guest judge, and write a 200-word audience analysis covering all four elements. Then write the two weighing sentences you would deliver to that judge at the end of the AI value debate.
