By the end of this chapter you should be able to: Explain what cross-examination is for and what it is not for. Use cross-examination to build credibility, secure links and clarify, in that order of priority. Build a line of questions using the question ladder. Answer questions in a way that protects your case without dodging. Use what you learned in cross-examination in your next speech.

Cross-examination (often shortened to "cross-x" or "CX") is the period in a debate when one debater asks questions of the debater who just spoke. In most classroom formats, the questioner is the person who will speak next. It is the only part of a debate where the two sides talk to each other directly instead of to the judge, which makes it the most unpredictable part of the round and, for many students, the most nerve-racking. The purpose of cross-examination is to look like the debater who best understands the round. That may sound like a strange goal. It means cross-examination is not mainly about getting information, and it is definitely not about winning arguments in the moment. Arguments are won in speeches, where the judge is listening for them and writing them down. Cross-examination sets up those speeches, and it shapes how the judge sees both debaters for the rest of the round.

Cross-examination has three effective uses. They are listed here in order of value, and a strong questioner spends most of the time on the first two. The first use is ethos, the speaker credibility Chapter 1 introduced. Cross-examination is the only time the judge sees the two debaters engage directly, so it is where credibility shifts fastest. Good questions show that you understand your opponent's case, sometimes better than they do. Questions that reveal your opponent cannot explain their own evidence, or cannot say how their contention connects to the resolution, lower their credibility without a single insult. That last part matters: attacking the person instead of the argument is an ad hominem (Chapter 7), and judges punish it. The second use is securing a link: asking a question whose answer gives you something to use in your next speech. If you plan to argue that the affirmative's plan costs money, a question that gets them to admit the plan needs new funding has secured your link. Once your opponent has said it, they cannot easily deny it later, and you can quote their answer in your speech. The third use is clarification: asking about something you genuinely did not understand. Sometimes you have to; you cannot answer an argument you do not understand. But clarification questions work against the main goal, because every one tells the judge you were confused. Keep them short, ask them first, and move on. At a glance Use Goal Example question Ethos Show you understand the round better than your opponent "Can you explain how your second card supports your tag?" Securing a link Get an answer you can use in your next speech "Your plan needs new federal funding, right?" Clarification Understand something you missed (use sparingly) "What was your criterion?"

The biggest mistake new questioners make is asking for the conclusion directly. "Isn't your plan going to cost too much?" invites an easy "No," and now you have helped your opponent deny your argument on the record. A better approach climbs toward the conclusion one small step at a time. Call it the question ladder. Start at the bottom rung with closed questions, questions with short, factual answers, usually yes or no, that your opponent cannot reasonably deny. "Your plan creates a new federal agency?" "That agency needs staff?" "Staff need salaries?" Each answer is obvious, so your opponent will give it. Each one also commits them to a step in your argument. Climb one rung at a time, and stop before the top. The last step, "So your plan costs money you haven't accounted for," is the conclusion, and you do not need your opponent to say it. You will say it yourself, in your speech, where the judge is listening for arguments and your opponent cannot interrupt. Asking the final question gives your opponent a chance to deny it or to explain it away. Leaving it unasked lets you draw the conclusion from answers they already gave. Open questions, questions that invite long answers ("Can you explain your solvency?"), have a place but are risky. They give your opponent time to repeat their case. Use them when you expect the answer to be weak: an open question to a debater who does not understand their own evidence is one of the strongest ethos moves available. A variation is the fork: a question where either answer helps you. "Does your plan take effect immediately, or does it phase in?" If immediately, the negative argues it is too disruptive; if it phases in, the negative argues the harms continue in the meantime. The fork works only if you have prepared an argument for each answer. The pit of doom is different. It is a question where one answer clearly gives you access to an argument you are likely to make. Suppose the resolution calls for increasing subsidies for green power, and you have a strong disadvantage about the harms of solar panels, but the affirmative's plan text does not say whether solar is included. Ask: "Do you defend increasing subsidies for solar panels?" A yes hands you the link to your disadvantage. A no tells you something too: that disadvantage will not link, and you can spend your preparation on something else. Unlike the fork, the pit of doom does not need both answers to help you. It needs one answer that does, asked before your opponent works out what is at stake. Experienced debaters also use the reverse pit of doom. Here the questioner makes the opponent think that answering yes is the link, when the answer that actually gives the link is no. Imagine the negative's real argument is that subsidizing other green power while leaving solar out pulls investment away from solar companies. If the negative asks the solar question in a way that sounds like it is setting up a "solar is harmful" argument, the affirmative may try to dodge by answering no, and that no is exactly the link the negative wanted. This can go on indefinitely. Debaters who know each other, and know each other's teams, learn each other's habits, and each side tries to work out whether a question is a pit of doom or a reverse one. It works much like poker, where a player has to decide whether an opponent is bluffing, or is strong and only pretending to bluff. For a classroom debate, the lesson is simpler: before you answer a question about what your plan includes, think about which answer the questioner actually wants.

Three habits waste cross-examination time and cost credibility. The first, and the most common, is making arguments instead of asking questions: "Don't you think your evidence is outdated and your plan is a bad idea?" is a speech in disguise, and it hurts you in two ways. It gives your opponent extra speech time. Cross-examination is your time. If you make an argument instead of asking a question, your opponent can simply answer it, and they answer it on your clock instead of spending their own speech time on it. You have used your resource to do their work. It probably never reaches the flow. Most judges do not flow cross-examination, even though they usually treat the answers given in it as binding. The danger is in your memory. When you stand up for your speech, you remember making the argument, so you may not make it again. But you made it in cross-examination, so it is unlikely to be on the judge's flow, and it is missing from the part of the debate where it would have counted. Ask the questions in cross-examination, and make the argument in your speech. The second habit is obscuring the point: long, confusing questions make you look less clear, not your opponent. The third is pressing on parts of your opponent's case that you understood perfectly well but that seem weak. If you understood it, save the attack for your speech, where it counts. Two more rules keep cross-examination civil. Let your opponent answer; if an answer runs long, you can politely move on ("Thank you, that's helpful; next question"). And speak to the judge as much as to your opponent. You are performing for the person with the ballot.

Being questioned is half of cross-examination, and it has its own skills. The goal is to look confident and knowledgeable while giving away as little as possible. Answer honestly and briefly. Short answers give the questioner less to work with. Dodging looks worse than a direct answer; a judge who sees you refusing to answer a simple question assumes the honest answer hurts you. Watch the ladder. When a series of easy questions seems to be climbing somewhere, you can answer the rung while refusing the destination: "Yes, the agency needs staff, but the plan's funding covers that, as our second card explains." That kind of answer gives the questioner the fact without the conclusion. Do not make a concession, an admission that gives up part of your case, unless you mean to. If you do not know an answer, say what you do know: "Our evidence doesn't give that number; it says the cost is covered by the existing budget." And when a question is genuinely confusing, ask for it to be repeated. That is not weakness; it is precision.

Cross-examination only matters if you use it. A concession your opponent made in cross-examination and you never mention in a speech does not exist on the flow. In your next speech, bring it back explicitly: "In cross-examination, they admitted their plan needs new funding. That's the link to our first argument." Quoting your opponent's own words is one of the most persuasive moves in debate, because the judge heard them say it. Flow cross-examination the same way you flow speeches. Write down the important answers, especially concessions, in the margin next to the argument they affect. Then they are there when you need them.

Bottom rung: "Your plan creates a new agency, correct?" Next rung: "And that agency needs staff?" Moving on politely: "Thank you, that's helpful. Next question." Answering a rung, not the destination: "Yes, but as our second card explains..." Using it later: "In cross-examination, they admitted... That means..."

Resolution: Starting at a community college costs less than starting at a four-year university. The negative questions the affirmative. "Your evidence compares published tuition?" "Yes." "Published tuition is the price before grants?" "Yes." "Students at four-year schools often get grants?" "Some do." The negative stops there. In its speech, it climbs the last rung on its own: the affirmative's evidence measures sticker price, by its own admission, and the resolution is about what students actually pay. The affirmative answered honestly, which was right, but it missed the chance to answer the destination: "Yes, and our evidence shows the gap stays large even after grants." That answer would have taken the rung without giving up the argument.

Resolution: The United States federal government should substantially restrict the development of artificial intelligence. The affirmative questions the negative, whose disadvantage claims restrictions will push AI development to other countries. The affirmative uses the fork: "Does your evidence say other countries would develop AI faster, or that they'd develop it with fewer safety rules?" Either answer helps. If faster, the affirmative argues its plan includes international cooperation; if fewer safety rules, it argues that is exactly why U.S. leadership on safety matters. The negative, recognizing the fork, answers precisely: "Our evidence says faster, and it says cooperation agreements have failed before." Precise answers are the best defense against a fork.

Most judges do not decide debates on cross-examination alone, and many do not flow it at all. What judges take from it is an impression of which debater understands the round, and that impression colors how they hear every speech afterward. Concessions count only when a debater brings them into a speech. A judge will not do that work for you.

Asking the final question. Climb the ladder, then draw the conclusion in your speech. Making arguments instead of asking questions. Save arguments for speeches, where the judge flows them and your opponent has to answer them on their own time. Spending the period on clarification. Every confused question costs credibility. Dodging as the answerer. A direct, brief answer looks stronger than an evasive one. Forgetting to use the answers. A concession never mentioned in a speech does nothing.

Drill: build the ladder (15 minutes, pairs). Pick one argument you want to make against your partner's case. Write a ladder of four closed questions that climbs toward it without asking the conclusion. Run it on your partner, then deliver the conclusion in a thirty-second speech that quotes their answers. Drill: hot seat (15 minutes, small groups). One student presents a one-minute contention. Each group member asks one question. The presenter practices brief, honest answers that take the rung without giving up the destination. The group names the best answer and why. Writing exercise. Watch or read a cross-examination from a recorded debate, press conference or hearing. In 200 words, identify one question that worked, one that did not, and explain why using the ideas in this chapter.
Move: Weigh. Builds on: Chapters 4 and 10. Where you use it: every rebuttal speech, and especially the last speech you give in any debate.

By the end of this chapter you should be able to: Explain how rebuttals differ from constructive speeches. Extend an argument by its warrant, not just its name. Collapse to the arguments you are most likely to win. Compare your arguments with your opponent's on the flow. Write the ballot for the judge: tell them exactly why you win.

Most debate formats have two kinds of speeches. Constructives come first and build: they present the case, the contentions, the advantages and disadvantages, and the first answers to the other side. Rebuttals come last and decide: they take everything on the flow and turn it into a reason to vote. Rebuttals are usually shorter than constructives, and that is the point. You cannot say everything again, so you have to choose. Rebuttals have one firm rule: no new arguments. A new argument is an argument that was not made in a constructive and could have been. Bringing one up in a rebuttal is unfair, because your opponent may have no speech left to answer it, and most judges will ignore it. New evidence extending an argument that is already on the flow is usually fine, and so are new answers to arguments your opponent made in their last speech. New positions are not. That leaves four jobs, and this chapter takes them in order: extend, collapse, compare, and write the ballot.

An extension carries an argument from an earlier speech into the current one, so the judge knows it is still alive. An argument that is not extended is dropped, by you, and judges treat it as gone. A good extension has three parts: the claim, the warrant and the reason it still stands. "Extend our first contention, net job growth. The World Economic Forum survey shows employers expect AI to create more jobs than it displaces. Their only answer was that forecasts can be wrong, but they read no forecast showing the opposite, so our evidence is the only evidence on this question." Chapter 9 made the same point about evidence: extend the warrant, not just the name. "Extend contention one" tells the judge where to look but gives them nothing to weigh. Extending also means answering what your opponent said about the argument. An extension that ignores the answers sounds like you did not hear them.

To collapse is to choose the few arguments you are most likely to win and spend your rebuttal on them, letting the rest go. It is the hardest skill in this chapter, because it feels like giving up ground. It is the opposite. A rebuttal that tries to extend everything spends ten seconds on each argument and wins none of them convincingly. A rebuttal that collapses to one or two arguments has time to extend them fully, answer every attack on them, and weigh them. To decide what to collapse to, look at your flow and ask three questions about each of your arguments. Where am I winning? Arguments your opponent dropped or answered weakly are strong candidates. Which arguments matter most? An argument you are winning that has a small impact may not decide the debate. Which arguments outweigh what my opponent is winning? Your collapse should give you something on the Scale that is heavier than whatever they have left. You do not need to win every argument to win the debate. You need to win enough, and to show that what you won matters more than what you lost.

Comparison puts your arguments and your opponent's side by side and explains why yours should win. It uses everything from earlier chapters: comparing evidence (Chapter 9), weighing impacts (Chapter 10), and showing where your opponent's arguments do not answer yours (Chapter 4). The most useful comparison tool in a rebuttal is the even-if statement: "Even if they win their argument, we still win, because..." Even-if statements let you concede what you might lose and show it does not matter. "Even if AI displaces some jobs in the short term, our evidence shows the new jobs outnumber them by 2030, and they never answered the long-term trend." An even-if statement protects you against the arguments you are least sure about, because it gives the judge a path to vote for you whichever way those arguments go.

The last job of a final rebuttal is writing the ballot: telling the judge, in words they could copy onto their ballot, exactly why you win. Judges have to explain their decisions. A debater who gives them the explanation makes it easy to vote for them. A written ballot names one or two voting issues, the arguments that decide the debate, and explains why they outweigh everything else. It sounds like this: "Vote affirmative for one reason: AI's job creation outweighs its displacement. Our employer survey was never answered with contrary evidence, and their only offense, short-term disruption, is temporary while the new jobs last. Under preponderance of evidence, that means the resolution is true." Notice what that does: it names the issue, extends the warrant, compares with the opponent's best argument, and connects it to the criterion. Give the ballot at the end of your speech, or at the start as an overview and again at the end. Either way, the judge should never have to work out on their own why you think you won. At a glance Job What it means Sounds like Extend Carry an argument forward with its warrant and answer the attacks on it "Extend net job growth: the survey shows... Their answer fails because..." Collapse Choose the few arguments you are winning that matter most "I'm going for one argument in this speech." Compare Explain why your arguments beat theirs, including even-if statements "Even if they win short-term disruption, we still win, because..." Write the ballot Tell the judge exactly why you win "Vote affirmative for one reason..."

Rebuttals are given with little preparation time, so plan them on the flow before the speech. A quick plan has three steps. First, circle the arguments you are winning, using the three collapse questions. Second, draw a line through the arguments you are letting go. Third, write your ballot in one sentence at the top of your flow, and build the speech toward it. Start with your roadmap (Chapter 5), go argument by argument down your collapse, and end by reading the ballot you wrote. Watch the clock (Chapter 5): a rebuttal that runs out of time before the ballot has skipped the most important part.

Roadmap a collapse: "Two things in this speech: their disadvantage, then why our advantage outweighs." Extend: "Extend [claim]. [Warrant]. Their answer was [answer], but that fails because..." Collapse: "I'm going for one argument in this speech." Even-if: "Even if they win [their argument], we still win, because..." Flag a new argument: "That's a new argument in the last rebuttal. Please don't evaluate it." Write the ballot: "Vote [side] for one reason..."

Resolution: Starting at a community college costs less than starting at a four-year university. By the last rebuttal, the affirmative is winning its tuition contention: the negative's only answer was that published price is not net price, and the affirmative read evidence that the gap holds after grants. The affirmative is losing a smaller argument about living costs, where the negative showed many community college students still pay rent. The affirmative collapses to tuition, lets living costs go, and uses an even-if: "Even if living costs are similar, tuition alone saves thousands, and that's the cost the resolution is most about." Then it writes the ballot: "Vote affirmative for one reason: tuition savings survive their net-price argument, and they never showed any cost that outweighs them."

Resolution: Artificial intelligence does more harm than good. The negative goes into its last rebuttal with three arguments on the flow: medical research, productivity and education. It is winning medical research cleanly, losing productivity, and education is unclear. A weak rebuttal would extend all three for a minute each. This negative collapses to medical research, extends its warrant fully, weighs it against the affirmative's displacement impact on magnitude and reversibility (deaths prevented cannot be undone; job markets recover), and writes the ballot under the agreed framework of quality of life. The judge has one clear reason to vote negative and an explanation ready to copy onto the ballot.

Judges decide from the last rebuttals. They look for the arguments both sides extended, check which were answered, and weigh what is left the way the debaters told them to. Most close debates are won by the side whose final rebuttal made the decision easiest: a clear collapse, real comparison, and a ballot the judge can almost copy. New arguments in the last rebuttals are usually ignored, and debaters who point them out ("that's new, please don't evaluate it") help the judge do that.

Extending everything. Ten seconds per argument wins none of them. Collapse. Extending names without warrants. "Extend contention one" gives the judge nothing to weigh. Making new arguments. If it could have been made in a constructive, it is too late. Describing instead of comparing. Every rebuttal argument should mention what the other side said. Running out of time before the ballot. Plan the speech so the ballot is never what gets cut.

By the end of this chapter you should be able to: Explain what a value resolution asks and why it needs a framework instead of a fixed criterion. Choose a value and write a value criterion that measures it. Tie each contention back to the criterion. Recognize and avoid the tautology trap. Debate the framework itself, and win under your opponent's framework when you have to. Use facts established earlier, and explain what a value debate hands to policy.

A value resolution asks for a judgment: whether something is good or bad, or whether one thing matters more than another. Chapter 3 gave the markers: words like ought, better, more important, harmful or justified. "A college education is more valuable than work experience" is a value resolution. So is this book's: "Artificial intelligence does more harm than good." A value debate is different from a fact debate in one important way. In a fact debate, the criterion is settled before the debate starts: preponderance of evidence. In a value debate, the standard for deciding is part of what the debaters argue about. "More harm than good" according to what? Harm to jobs? To privacy? To human life? Different standards produce different answers, so each side has to propose a standard and defend it. That standard is called the framework.

A framework is the standard each side asks the judge to use to decide a value debate. It has two parts. Figure 13.1 How a value framework works The value names what matters most, the criterion measures it, and each contention ties back to the criterion to show it meets that measure. The value is the principle that should matter most in this debate: the thing the judge should try to protect or promote. Common values include quality of life, justice, liberty, human dignity, security and sustainability. A value is abstract on purpose. It names an ideal, not a measurement, which is why a value alone cannot decide a debate. Two debaters can both claim to promote "quality of life" and mean completely different things. The value criterion is how we know whether the value has been achieved: the measurement that turns an abstract value into something a judge can check. If the value is quality of life, the criterion might be reducing poverty, or minimizing suffering, or preserving access to healthcare. Each of those points the judge toward different evidence. A strong criterion is almost always a transitive verb plus a measurable outcome: minimizing suffering, maximizing economic security, preserving biodiversity. The verb says what to do; the outcome says what to count. A criterion like "fairness" fails this test, because it is just another value. A criterion like "reducing the number of people who lose their income" passes it, because a judge can compare sides on it. Here is a simple illustration. Imagine a debate about what makes the best athlete. Both sides might agree the value is athleticism but disagree on the criterion: one says whoever jumps highest, the other says whoever runs farthest. Or the sides might disagree on both: one side values strength, measured by the heaviest bench press, and the other values intelligence, measured by memorizing the most digits of pi. In the first case the debate is about measurement. In the second, it is about what matters at all. Real value debates can take either shape.

Chapter 2 said that in a value debate, a contention adds a fourth step after the claim, warrant and implication: the tie-back, which shows how the contention meets the criterion. The tie-back is what makes a contention count under the framework. Without it, the judge has a true argument but no instruction for how it fits the standard they were asked to use. Take the AI value resolution with the value of quality of life and the criterion of reducing poverty. An affirmative contention argues that AI displaces workers faster than they can retrain. The claim, warrant and implication prove the displacement. The tie-back finishes the job: "Displaced workers without new jobs fall into poverty, so this contention shows that AI increases poverty, which means it fails our criterion and does more harm than good." Every contention in a value case should end this way, pointing straight at the criterion. The tie-back is also a test. If you cannot write a clear tie-back for a contention, either the contention does not belong in the case or the criterion is wrong for your side.

Some resolutions tempt debaters into a circular framework. Take a resolution like "Economic growth ought to be valued over environmental protection." The affirmative is tempted to choose economic growth as its value, and the negative to choose environmental protection. But then the affirmative is arguing that economic growth matters more because economic growth is what matters most. That is a tautology: a justification that just repeats its conclusion. It gives the judge no independent reason to prefer either side, and it makes the debate impossible to resolve. The fix is to choose a value and criterion that sit above the resolution, a standard both sides could argue under. For that resolution, the affirmative might choose quality of life measured by reducing global poverty; the negative might choose the same value measured by reducing disease, or a different value such as sustainability, measured by ensuring humanity's long-term survival. Now the debate has real questions in it. Does economic growth or environmental protection do more to reduce poverty? To reduce disease? Each side can even argue that it wins under the other side's framework, which is a sign the framework is doing its job.

The framework debate is the part of a value debate where the sides argue about which value and criterion the judge should use. It often comes first in a speech, because the framework decides how everything else is weighed. Three moves cover most of it. First, defend your framework on its merits. Why is your value the most important one for this resolution? Why is your criterion the best way to measure it? Good reasons are about the resolution: "The resolution asks about harm, and poverty is the harm that touches the most people and shapes every other part of their lives." Second, attack your opponent's framework when it is weak. A criterion that cannot be measured, that is unrelated to the resolution, or that is just the resolution restated in other words is a real problem, and saying so is a legitimate argument. Third, and most important, be ready to win under their framework. This is called turning the framework: showing that even by your opponent's standard, your side wins. If the negative says the criterion should be reducing disease, the affirmative can argue that AI-driven job loss reduces access to healthcare and so increases disease. A debater who wins under both frameworks has made the framework debate irrelevant, and has won. A common mistake is to spend most of the debate on the framework. Frameworks are important, but they are a tool for weighing contentions, not a substitute for them. The judge still needs a reason, under whichever framework wins, to vote for you. At a glance Term What it is Example (AI value resolution) Value The principle that matters most Quality of life Value criterion How we measure the value: a transitive verb plus a measurable outcome Reducing poverty Tie-back The step that shows a contention meets the criterion "Displaced workers fall into poverty, so AI fails our criterion." Tautology A framework that just repeats one side of the resolution Valuing "economic growth" on a resolution about economic growth Turning the framework Winning under the opponent's framework too "Even under reducing disease, job loss cuts healthcare access."

s: 13.6 Using facts you have already established
x: This book's sequence puts the value debate on the same subject as the fact debate before it. That means you are not starting over. The research, evidence and arguments from the fact debate are now material for the value debate. If the fact debate examined whether AI will create more jobs than it displaces, both sides of the value debate already know the strongest evidence on that question, and both know how it was answered. An affirmative arguing that AI does more harm than good can use the displacement evidence directly in a contention, now with a tie-back to its criterion. A negative can use the job-creation evidence the same way. What changes is the question the evidence is answering. In the fact debate, the question was "is this true?" In the value debate, it is "how much does this matter, measured by our criterion, compared with everything else AI does?" Job numbers are now one impact among many, weighed against impacts on health, privacy, education and more.

s: 13.7 What a value debate hands to policy
x: A value debate settles what matters most. That is exactly what a policy debate needs to weigh its impacts. When the policy debate asks whether the federal government should restrict AI development, the advantages and disadvantages will compare very different impacts: jobs, safety, competitiveness, rights. The weighing arguments from the value debate (why poverty matters more than convenience, or why preventing irreversible harm comes first) carry straight into the policy debate's impact calculus. Chapter 15 shows how the affirmative uses them.

Present the framework: "My value is quality of life. My criterion is reducing poverty, because..." Tie back: "This means AI increases poverty, so it fails my criterion." Attack a criterion: "Their criterion can't be measured, so it can't help the judge decide." Name a tautology: "Their value is just their side of the resolution. That's circular." Turn the framework: "Even under their criterion, we win, because..."

Resolution: For most students, saving money is more important than the four-year campus experience. The affirmative avoids the tautology of valuing "saving money." It chooses the value of long-term well-being, with the criterion of minimizing financial insecurity after graduation. Its contentions argue that student debt shapes career choices and delays milestones like buying a home, each tied back to financial insecurity. The negative accepts long-term well-being as the value but proposes a different criterion: maximizing career opportunities. It argues that campus networks and on-campus jobs open doors. The affirmative turns the framework: transfer students reach the same campus in their third year, and graduating with less debt gives them more freedom to take the opportunities they find. The debate comes down to which criterion better measures long-term well-being, and whether the affirmative's turn holds.

Resolution: Artificial intelligence does more harm than good. The affirmative's framework is human dignity, measured by preserving people's control over decisions that affect their lives. Its contentions cover automated decisions in hiring and lending, and displacement from work, each tied back to loss of control. The negative's framework is quality of life, measured by minimizing preventable death, with contentions on faster drug discovery and earlier disease detection. In the rebuttals, the negative argues its criterion is more measurable and its impact more severe. The affirmative turns the framework partly, arguing that displacement worsens health outcomes, and argues its own criterion matters more because the loss of control is spreading and hard to reverse. The judge decides the framework first, then weighs the surviving contentions under it.

A judge in a value debate usually decides in two steps. First: which framework should I use? The judge looks at which value and criterion were better defended and which side answered the other's framework arguments. Second: under that framework, who wins? The judge looks for contentions with clear tie-backs to the winning criterion. A debater who loses the framework but wins under it still wins. A debater who wins the framework but has no contentions tied to it usually does not.

A criterion that is just another value. "Fairness" does not measure anything. Use a verb and a measurable outcome. The tautology trap. Do not make your value your side of the resolution. Skipping the tie-back. A contention without one does not count under any framework. All framework, no contentions. The framework is a tool for weighing arguments, not a replacement for them. Ignoring the opponent's framework. Answer it, and show you win under it too.

The other has two minutes to prepare and one minute to argue that their side wins under that framework. Writing exercise. Write a complete affirmative framework for "Artificial intelligence does more harm than good": value, criterion, a two-sentence justification, and one contention with a full tie-back. By the end of this chapter you should be able to: Name and define the four parts of the Uniqueness Model: uniqueness, link, internal link and impact. Write uniqueness that points in the right direction for your side. Carry an impact through to a terminal consequence: people suffering or people dying. s: 14.1 Why policy debate needs a different structure
x: In the fact and value debates you built contentions: a claim, the warrants that support it, and an implication that explains why it matters. That structure works when the question is whether something is true or what matters most. A policy resolution asks a different question: who should do what? The affirmative proposes a change, called the plan, and the judge has to decide whether the world is better with that change or without it. That means every policy argument is a comparison between two worlds. The first is the status quo, the world as it is now, where nobody adopts the plan. The second is the world of the plan. An argument that only describes one of those worlds is half an argument. The Uniqueness Model is built to describe both worlds and the path from one to the other. The affirmative's arguments in this structure are called advantages: reasons the world of the plan is better. The negative's are called disadvantages: reasons the world of the plan is worse. Both use the same four parts, in the same order. The rest of this chapter takes the four parts one at a time. Section 14.5 ends with a table that puts them side by side.

s: 14.2 Uniqueness: the world before the plan
x: Uniqueness describes the status quo on the specific subject of your position. An advantage about student debt describes student debt as it is today, not the economy in general. Uniqueness is also directional. You are not just describing the world; you are making a judgment about whether it is going well or badly. The affirmative is arguing for a change, so its uniqueness says things are currently bad. The negative is defending the world without the plan, so its uniqueness says things are currently good, or at least good enough that the plan would make them worse. Getting the direction wrong is one of the most common mistakes new debaters make. A negative that says "the economy is already collapsing" has just argued that the plan cannot be blamed for collapsing it. Sometimes uniqueness describes where the world is heading rather than where it is today. This is predictive uniqueness: "Without the plan, tuition will keep rising for the next five years." Predictive uniqueness is still a description of the status quo. It describes the future that happens if nobody acts.

s: 14.3 The link: what the plan does
x: The link is the simplest part of the model. It states what the plan does, matter of fact, with no judgment attached. If the plan raises the minimum wage to \$20, the link is "The plan passes and raises the minimum wage to \$20." Whether that is good or bad comes later. For the affirmative, the link is the plan itself. For the negative, the link is the part of the plan that sets the disadvantage in motion. Chapter 18 adds two other kinds of link: a perception link, where someone reacts to the plan (voters, a foreign government, investors), and a spillover link, where the plan leads to similar action elsewhere. Both still start from what the plan does.

s: 14.4 The internal link: the story of what changes
x: The internal link explains how the link changes the uniqueness. It is the story of what happens after the plan. If uniqueness says people are poor and the link says the plan raises the minimum wage, the internal link says that higher wages give people more money for food and rent. A useful way to write an internal link is the formula X is key to Y, where X is what the plan does and Y is the impact. "Lower tuition is key to graduating without debt." Each internal link is a claim that needs its own warrant, and that is where the strongest evidence in a position usually goes. Internal links can take more than one step. A tax cut for small businesses might keep those businesses open, which keeps their employees working, which keeps those families out of poverty. Every step is a place your opponent can attack, so write only the steps you need and support each one.

s: 14.5 The impact: getting to the end of the story
x: The impact is the consequence of the changes the internal link describes. It is the reason anyone should care. The rule for impacts is that they must be terminal. A terminal impact follows the chain of consequences all the way to its end, and in policy debate that end is almost always one of two things: people suffer, or people die. "People lose money" is not a terminal impact; it is another internal link. Follow it further. People who lose money skip meals and medical care, lose housing, and live shorter, sicker lives. Now you have an impact. Impacts can be quantified or qualified. A quantified impact gives a number: "This prevents 10,000 evictions a year." A qualified impact describes a harm that matters even if it is hard to count: "This prevents the dehumanization of people forced to choose between food and shelter." Both count. Quantified impacts are easier for a judge to compare, which matters when you reach weighing. A warning about terminalizing. Students who learn this rule sometimes stretch every argument to nuclear war. The longer the chain, the less likely each step becomes, and a judge who has read Chapter 10 will ask about probability. Get to suffering or death by the shortest chain your evidence supports. At a glance Part Question it answers Advantage (affirmative) Disadvantage (negative) Uniqueness What is the world like now? Things are bad now. Things are good now. Link What does the plan do? The plan does this. The plan does this. Internal link What changes because of it? That makes things better. That makes things worse. Impact Why does that change matter? Lives are saved and suffering is prevented. Lives are lost and suffering increases.

s: 14.6 Two worlds on the Scale: why uniqueness matters
x: In Chapter 4 you met the Scale: the judge puts each side's impacts on one pan or the other and votes for whichever side outweighs. The origin of that image is a fifth-grade algebra lesson. My teacher, Ms. Fatheringham, taught equations with a balance and white and blue cubes. Whatever you placed on both sides could be removed without changing which side was heavier. Policy debate works the same way. The judge compares the world of the plan to the status quo, and any impact that happens in both worlds cancels out. That is what the word "uniqueness" means: an impact is unique when it happens in only one world. A good advantage describes an impact that the status quo has and the plan removes. A good disadvantage describes an impact the status quo avoids and the plan causes. Debaters sum this up as uniqueness controls the direction of the link. Compare two positions about climate change. Strong advantage Weak (linear) disadvantage Uniqueness Climate change is getting worse now. Climate change is not a problem now. Link The plan cuts emissions. The plan cuts emissions. Internal link Lower emissions slow warming. Lower emissions keep warming low. Impact Fewer deaths from heat, drought and storms. Climate change stays limited. On the Scale The status quo has the harm and the plan removes it. The impact belongs to the affirmative. Both worlds have limited climate change. The impact cancels. The second position fails even if every sentence in it is true, because the plan does not change the outcome. An impact that already exists at the same level in both worlds is called linear, and it cannot tip the Scale. Figure 14.1 A linear impact cancels on the Scale Why uniqueness matters: if an impact happens in both worlds, it sits on both pans, cancels, and cannot decide the debate. This idea explains a pattern you will see on some topics. If the status quo is clearly bad on the topic's biggest issue, the affirmative can argue that doing something beats doing nothing. Debaters call this try or die. My view is that try or die is mostly a rhetorical move that lets the affirmative skip proving its plan works. In practice, though, judges often vote affirmative on a small risk of solving a large problem unless the negative gives them something on the other side of the Scale. Chapter 18 shows how to provide it.

Write and deliver positions in subordinated notation: each part of the model is a heading, and each claim under it is numbered, with its support lettered beneath. Your judge flows in the same structure, so speaking in it makes their job easy. The frames below work for any advantage: "Our first advantage is ___." "Uniqueness: right now, ___ is a problem." "The link is the plan: the plan ___." "Once the plan passes, ___ changes, and that leads to ___." "That means ___. That is our impact, and it only happens if you vote affirmative." A disadvantage uses the same frames with the direction reversed: "right now, ___ is going well," "that change causes ___," and "that is the impact, and it happens only in the world of the plan." Here is what a short advantage sounds like on the resolution Sam should get a dog. The example is hypothetical; in a real debate, each lettered point would carry evidence. "Our first advantage is home security. Uniqueness. One: there have been break-ins in Sam's neighborhood. A: three homes on Sam's street were burglarized this year. The link. One: the plan passes and Sam adopts a dog. The internal link. One: dogs deter burglars. A: burglars choose homes without dogs, and a dog wakes the household if someone does break in. The impact. One: Sam's family and home stay safe. That only happens if you vote affirmative." Notice what the speaker does: names each part before giving it, numbers each claim and letters each piece of support. A judge can flow that without guessing where anything goes.

Resolution: A high school graduate should start at a community college instead of a university. Imagine a graduate, Maya, who has been admitted to her state university and plans to borrow to pay for it. The affirmative writes an advantage about debt. Part Affirmative advantage: student debt Uniqueness Maya is about to start at a public university that costs much more per year than a community college. For 2025-26, average published tuition and fees are \$11,950 at public four-year colleges for in-state students and \$4,150 at public two-year colleges (College Board, 2025). Link The plan: Maya starts at a community college. Internal link Lower tuition for her first two years is key to borrowing less. Every year at the community college saves her the difference in tuition. Impact Less debt means smaller monthly payments after she graduates, more money for rent, food and medical care, and less financial stress in her early career. The negative answers with a disadvantage about finishing the degree, built from the same four parts with the direction reversed. Part Negative disadvantage: transfer risk Uniqueness Maya is on track for a bachelor's degree: she is admitted, enrolled and has a four-year plan. Link The plan: Maya starts at a community college instead. Internal link Transferring adds steps where students lose credits or stop out. The negative needs evidence for this claim, such as research on transfer students' completion rates. Impact A delayed or unfinished degree means lower lifetime earnings and the same financial stress the affirmative claims to prevent. Look at the two impacts. Both are about Maya's financial security, so the debate will come down to which world gives her more of it. That is the Scale at work.

Resolution: The United States federal government should establish a universal basic income. Part Affirmative advantage: poverty Uniqueness Poverty remains widespread in the United States. The official poverty rate was 10.6% in 2024, which is 35.9 million people (U.S. Census Bureau, 2025). Link The plan: the federal government pays every adult \$1,000 a month. Internal link A guaranteed income is key to covering basic needs, so fewer people have to choose between food and housing. This step needs evidence, such as studies of guaranteed income programs. Impact Poverty causes poor health and shorter lives. Reducing it means fewer people suffer and fewer die early. The uniqueness evidence here does real work. A judge who hears that 35.9 million people are in poverty understands what the status quo looks like before the affirmative has proposed anything.

When a position reaches the end of the debate, a judge asks three questions about it. Does each part still stand, or did the other side take one out? Does the impact belong to only one world? And is it bigger, more likely, faster or harder to reverse than what is on the other side of the Scale? The model also tells you where a position can break. Answer the uniqueness and the impact may already be happening without the plan. Answer the link and the plan does not cause it. Answer the internal link and the story falls apart in the middle. Answer the impact and it may not matter. Chapter 19 builds a full set of answers around those four points. If you are judging, put an impact on the Scale only if the debater explained it, and remove it if the other side won an answer to any of its parts. A position missing a part is incomplete; a disadvantage with no uniqueness, for example, has not shown that the plan changes anything.

Uniqueness pointing the wrong way. A negative that says things are already bad has conceded the plan is not to blame. Check the direction before you write anything else. Stopping at an internal link. "The economy gets worse" is not an impact. Ask "and then what happens to people?" until you reach suffering or death. Judging the plan in the link. "The plan passes and wrecks the economy" puts the internal link and impact into the link. Keep the link a plain description. Skipping steps in the story. If the internal link jumps from the plan straight to a huge impact, your opponent will ask how, and you will have nothing to point to. Reading a linear impact. If the impact happens at the same level without the plan, it cancels. Make sure your position changes the outcome.

By the end of this chapter you should be able to: Name the six stock issues of policy debate and explain what each requires. Write a clear plan text that answers "who should do what?" Distinguish structural, attitudinal and existential inherency, and explain why only two of them are worth arguing. Use the fact and value debates to supply the harms and the impact weighing for a policy case. Explain why a plan has to fall within the resolution, and what happens when the negative argues it does not.

Every policy resolution asks one question: who should do what? "The United States federal government should substantially restrict the development of artificial intelligence" names an actor (the federal government), a direction (restrict) and a subject (AI development). The affirmative's job is to answer the question with a specific proposal and prove that the world is better with it than without it. Chapter 6 introduced stock issues as the minimum elements an affirmative needs to win. Policy debate has six. Debaters often remember them as SHIPSAT: Significant Harms, Inherency, Plan, Solvency, Advantages and Topicality. An affirmative that fails any one of them has not proved the resolution should be adopted.

Significant harms are the problems that exist in the status quo because the plan has not been adopted. They are the reason anyone should care about the resolution. Harms must be significant, meaning large enough to justify changing policy; a minor inconvenience does not justify a new federal law. In the Uniqueness Model from Chapter 14, the harms live in the uniqueness of each advantage: the description of what is going wrong right now. Inherency is the barrier that keeps the status quo from solving the harms on its own. It answers the question every judge silently asks: if this is such a good idea, why hasn't it happened already? There are three kinds. Structural inherency is a law, rule or institution that blocks the solution or causes the harm. "Current federal law includes no licensing requirement for training the largest AI systems" is structural inherency: the gap is built into the system. Attitudinal inherency is a belief or attitude among decision-makers that prevents the solution: "Congress has been unwilling to regulate AI because members fear slowing American innovation." Attitudes can change, so attitudinal inherency is weaker than structural inherency, but it is legitimate when you have evidence that the attitude exists and is the reason for inaction. Existential inherency argues that because the harm exists, the status quo must be unable to solve it. That is circular: it uses the harm as proof of the barrier. It is the weakest kind of inherency and not one you should rely on. If you cannot name the structure or attitude blocking a solution, you probably have not researched the topic enough yet.

The plan is the specific action the affirmative proposes. It is written as a plan text, one or two sentences that state exactly who does what. A good plan text names the actor from the resolution, describes the action precisely enough to debate, and stays within the resolution. For the AI resolution: "The United States federal government should require a federal license before any company trains an artificial intelligence model above a set computing threshold." (This plan is an example for this book, not a description of current law.) Plan texts are short on purpose. They do not explain why the plan is good; the rest of the case does that. They say what the affirmative will defend, so the negative knows what it is arguing against. Vague plans make debates worse, because the affirmative can shift what it means in every speech. A clear plan text is a commitment. Solvency is the argument that the plan actually fixes the harms. It is the link and internal link of each advantage from Chapter 14: the plan does this, and that changes things in this way. Solvency needs evidence. A judge who believes the harms are real and the plan is legal still will not vote for a plan that would not work. Strong solvency evidence is specific to the plan's mechanism: evidence that licensing systems have reduced risk in other industries is better than evidence that "regulation helps." Solvency does not have to be total. A plan that solves most of a harm can still be worth adopting, as long as what it solves outweighs any disadvantages.

An advantage is an independent reason the world of the plan is better than the status quo. Each advantage is a full Uniqueness Model: uniqueness (the harm now), link (the plan), internal link (how the plan changes things) and impact (why it matters to people). "Independent" means each advantage can win the debate on its own. A case with two advantages makes the negative answer both; if the negative beats one, the other can still carry the round. Chapter 17 covers how to write advantages.

s: 15.5 What the fact and value debates supply
x: This book's sequence puts the policy debate last for a reason. By the time students debate whether the federal government should restrict AI development, they have already debated whether AI will cause more job creation than displacement, and whether AI does more harm than good. Those debates hand the policy debate two things. The fact debate supplies harms. The evidence about job displacement, privacy or safety risks that students tested in the fact debate becomes the uniqueness of an affirmative advantage: this is what is happening now. Students already know which of that evidence held up under attack and which did not. The value debate supplies weighing. The arguments about which impacts matter most (poverty against innovation, irreversible harm against temporary disruption) become the impact calculus of the policy debate. An affirmative that won the argument that irreversible harms come first can use it to weigh its advantages against the negative's disadvantages. That is why the sequence matters even outside this book's examples. Every policy decision rests on factual claims about what is happening and value claims about what matters. The policy debate is where they meet. At a glance Stock issue What it requires AI example Significant harms A real, sizable problem in the status quo Rapidly growing AI systems with no safety review Inherency A barrier keeping the status quo from solving it No federal licensing law exists (structural) Plan A specific action: who does what Federal license required above a computing threshold Solvency Evidence the plan fixes the harm Licensing has reduced risk in other high-risk industries Advantages Independent reasons the plan makes the world better Fewer catastrophic AI failures; protection for workers Topicality The plan falls within the resolution Licensing is a substantial restriction on development

Topicality is the requirement that the plan fall within the resolution. It is the affirmative's burden, but it usually only becomes an issue when the negative argues the plan is not topical. A plan to restrict AI development is topical on a resolution about restricting AI development; a plan to fund AI research is not, because it does the opposite. When you build a case, the best protection against a topicality argument is a plan text squarely inside the resolution's words. Chapter 16 covers how topicality arguments are built and answered.
Plan text: "The United States federal government should..." Inherency: "The status quo hasn't solved this because..." Solvency: "The plan fixes this because..."

Resolution: Students who are undecided about a major should start at a community college. Chapter 15 listed topicality as the sixth stock issue: the requirement that the plan fall within the resolution. It is the affirmative's burden, but it usually only becomes an issue when the negative argues the plan is not topical. A plan to restrict AI development is topical on a resolution about restricting AI development; a plan to fund AI research is not, because it does the opposite. Most topicality debates are closer than that, and they are decided by a four-part argument the negative presents and the affirmative answers. The interpretation is the negative's definition of a word or phrase in the resolution, usually from a source. "'Restrict' means to place a legal limit on an activity." The best interpretations come from sources that define the term in exactly the context of the resolution. A definition that explicitly excludes what the affirmative does is stronger than a general dictionary entry, and a definition from the field (a legal source for a legal term) is stronger than one from a general source. The violation explains how the affirmative's plan fails to meet the interpretation. "The plan requires a license but sets no limit; companies that apply will receive one, so nothing is restricted." The violation should be short and specific. The standards are the reasons the negative's interpretation is better than the affirmative's. Common standards include predictability (could the negative have expected this plan from the resolution's wording?), limits (does the interpretation keep the number of possible plans manageable?) and field context (does the definition come from experts in the topic?). The voters are the reasons topicality should decide the debate. Topicality is usually argued to come first, because a judge cannot decide whether a plan is a good idea under the resolution until they decide whether it is under the resolution at all. The common voters are fairness, because the negative could not prepare for plans outside the resolution, and education, because debates focused on the resolution teach more about its subject. The affirmative answers topicality in the same structure: it argues that it meets the negative's interpretation anyway (often the shortest and best answer), offers its own interpretation that it does meet, and explains why its interpretation is better, or at least reasonable. Many judges give the affirmative the benefit of the doubt if its interpretation is reasonable, even if the negative's is slightly better. Two special cases have their own names. A plan is extra-topical when it does what the resolution asks and then adds something the resolution does not include. On the AI resolution, a plan that licenses AI training and also pays for worker retraining is extra-topical: retraining is not a restriction on development. The problem is that the affirmative chose the extra piece, so it will always be one that helps the affirmative, and the negative could not have prepared for it. A plan is effects topical when its action is not what the resolution describes, but its results might be. A plan to raise electricity prices for data centers does not restrict AI development; it only makes development more expensive and hopes a restriction follows. The more steps there are between the plan and the resolution, the fewer of the negative's prepared links apply.

Topicality is usually described as a limit on the affirmative, but it is better understood as a division of ground: the arguments each side is entitled to make. The affirmative gets its plan, and the negative gets everything else. There is no negative resolution, so the negative can answer with disadvantages, counterplans or any other argument that clashes. The resolution is what tells the negative which plans to prepare for. When the affirmative steps outside it, the affirmative either takes ground that belonged to the negative or shrinks the negative's ground by making its prepared arguments irrelevant. Negatives call this abuse, and there are two kinds. Proven abuse is ground the negative actually lost in this debate: a disadvantage it read no longer links, or a counterplan it prepared no longer makes sense. Potential abuse is ground the affirmative's interpretation would let affirmatives take, even if it did not happen here. Most judges want proven abuse, and some will not vote on topicality without it. The best case for potential abuse is about preparation: even if no argument failed to link, not knowing what the affirmative might defend limited which arguments the negative could prepare and choose to read. Expect to lose that argument more often than you win it. The usual reply is that voting on potential abuse is like voting on a disadvantage nobody read: the affirmative could have done something unfair, but it did not. Not everyone accepts that topicality is about ground. Todd Graham and Brandon Merrell, writing in the journal Parliamentary Debate in 2016, argued that the test of topicality should be accuracy: whether the plan fits what the resolution's words actually mean. They point out a problem with the ground view. If topicality is only about protecting the negative's ground, the best interpretation is always the narrowest one, ideally a resolution with exactly one topical plan, even if every expert in the field defines the term differently. On the accuracy view, neither team wrote the resolution, and an affirmative that defends the most accurate meaning of its words has done its job even if that meaning leaves the negative little ground. Most judges still treat topicality as a question of ground, so argue it that way by default. An affirmative that is losing the ground debate, though, can shift to accuracy. The only way to win accuracy is with field context: evidence that experts in the subject define the term the way the affirmative does, and an explanation of why that source is the best authority on the term.

Most topicality debates are decided at the level of standards, so choose ones you can defend. Think of each standard as an internal link: it explains how an interpretation leads to the voters, fairness and education. A standard has to pass one test before it counts: the benefit must come from your interpretation and not from the other side's. This is the same idea as uniqueness in Chapter 14. Suppose an affirmative says its interpretation is better because it lets students learn about AI safety. If plans about AI safety are also topical under the negative's interpretation, both interpretations produce that benefit, and it cancels. Before you answer a standard, ask whether your opponent's interpretation is really the only one that provides it. Before you read one, write your interpretation so that it is. For the negative, two standards do most of the work. Predictable limits is the argument that the negative can prepare only if the set of topical plans is both manageable and knowable before the debate. "Limits" alone is not enough, because an affirmative can always answer that its own interpretation is even more limiting: it allows only the affirmative's plan. What matters is whether the negative could have known the limit in advance. Field context is the argument that the definition comes from experts in the resolution's subject. It is usually the easiest standard to win, because it reaches both voters: expert definitions teach the subject, and they are the ones a prepared debater would expect. That leads to the distinction topicality debates most often miss. The predictability of an interpretation is different from the predictability an interpretation produces. Suppose a criminal justice resolution has two interpretations of one of its terms. One comes from the Supreme Court and allows fifteen kinds of plans. The other comes from a stranger's blog and allows two. Once you know the blog's definition, the debate is very predictable: only two plans, and you know the disadvantages to both. But no one preparing for the topic would have found that blog. Predictability that exists only after the debate starts does not help the negative prepare, so the interpretation the negative could have predicted, the Supreme Court's, is better. The same answer beats a common affirmative trick, the counter-interpretation that is "your interpretation plus our plan." Adding one plan sounds harmless, but the negative could not have known which plan would be added. For the affirmative, the strongest standards are affirmative flexibility and field context. Affirmative flexibility argues that the affirmative needs room to be creative, because the negative is almost never constrained: it can read disadvantages, counterplans and other arguments against any plan, while the affirmative is bound by the resolution. As long as a plan stays within the resolution, unexpected plans are good for debate. Flexibility is a better version of a "creativity" standard. Creativity claims only education; flexibility also claims fairness, because it balances the negative's freedom. The negative's best answer to flexibility is that limits produce creativity. A designer told to build "anything" has less to work with than one told to build a phone that fits in a pocket and costs under a set price. An affirmative that has to find its best plan inside the resolution is doing harder and more creative work than one that leaves it. At one national college tournament, the resolution called for increasing the U.S. naval presence in the Persian Gulf. Most teams expected plans that sent warships, and prepared disadvantages about provoking Iran. One team's plan sent the Navy's two hospital ships, the USNS Comfort and USNS Mercy, which each hold about 1,000 hospital beds, carry no weapons and are painted with large red crosses. The plan plainly increased naval presence in the Gulf, so it was topical, and it made the expected disadvantages very hard to win. That is affirmative flexibility at work: unexpected, but inside the resolution.

A we meet is a no-link: if the plan meets the negative's interpretation, the topicality argument is over, which is why it comes first and is often the best answer. A counter-interpretation is a counterplan: it offers another way to define the term, and like a counterplan it is worth reading only if it wins standards the negative cannot reach or takes the negative's standards for itself. A counter-interpretation that is not more predictable, better limited or better grounded in the field gives the judge no reason to prefer it. A complete affirmative answer usually has six parts: we meet; a counter-interpretation; reasons the counter-interpretation is good; reasons the negative's interpretation is bad; no voting on potential abuse; and reasonability. Reasonability asks the judge to vote affirmative as long as the plan is a reasonable reading of the resolution, even if the negative's interpretation is slightly better. Its opposite, competing interpretations, asks the judge to adopt whichever interpretation wins on the flow, however small the margin. Explain what "reasonable" means by giving the judge a test, for example: "If the plan sounded like an example of the resolution when you first heard it, the negative could have expected it too." Otherwise the negative will argue that reasonability is arbitrary and invites the judge to substitute their own opinion. The best way to win reasonability, though, is to be plainly topical. Teams that write plans squarely inside the resolution rarely lose on topicality. For the negative, whether to go for topicality depends on those six answers. If the affirmative misses three or more of them, topicality is usually the strongest argument in the debate, and the negative can decide as soon as the affirmative finishes answering it. If the affirmative answers all of them well, topicality is an uphill fight that makes sense only when the negative is behind everywhere else. To go for it, extend it like a disadvantage: the interpretation, one clear violation with reasons each we meet fails, one or two standards, and the voters, and win competing interpretations. Because the negative will almost always go for predictable limits or field context, those explanations can be written and practiced before the tournament, with a blank for the topic-specific details. Topicality is the most common example of a theory argument: an argument about the rules of the debate instead of the merits of the plan. Any theory argument uses the same four parts. An interpretation states the rule, a violation shows the other side broke it, standards explain why the rule makes debates better, and voters explain why breaking it should decide the round. A negative that thinks a plan text is too vague to debate (section 15.3 in Chapter 15) would argue it in exactly this structure.

Topicality, negative: "Interpretation... Violation... Standards... Voters..." Topicality, affirmative: "We meet their interpretation, because..." Predictability: "The question isn't whether their interpretation makes the debate predictable once we know it. It's whether we could have predicted their interpretation before the round." Reasonability: "If our plan sounded like the resolution when you first heard it, we're reasonably topical. Don't vote on a definition that is better by a hair." Resolution: Students who are undecided about a major should start at a community college. The affirmative's plan has an undecided student enroll at a community college for two years with a guaranteed transfer agreement (Chapter 15 builds the rest of this case). The negative runs topicality. Its interpretation: "undecided" means a student with no intended major at all. Its violation: the affirmative's evidence is about students with a tentative major, who are not undecided. Its standard is limits: if a tentative major counts as undecided, nearly every first-year student is covered, and the resolution stops narrowing anything. Its voter is fairness. The affirmative answers in order. We meet: its plan applies only to students with no declared major, so whatever its evidence also discusses, the plan itself meets the negative's interpretation. Counter-interpretation: "undecided" means no declared major, which is the reading a student filling out an enrollment form would expect. Reasonability: the plan sounds like the resolution the moment you hear it. The we meet does most of the work. If the judge agrees the plan meets the negative's own definition, the argument is over, and the debate moves on to the advantages.

Resolution: The United States federal government should substantially restrict the development of artificial intelligence. The affirmative's plan requires a federal license before any company trains an AI model above a set computing threshold. The negative argues topicality on "substantially." Its interpretation: a substantial restriction prevents a meaningful share of the restricted activity. Its violation: a license that any company can obtain prevents nothing. Its standard is predictable limits: if a paperwork requirement counts as a substantial restriction, every reporting rule for AI companies becomes topical, and no negative could prepare for all of them. The affirmative answers with a we meet first: its licenses carry safety requirements that some companies will not meet, so the plan does limit development. Then a counter-interpretation: "substantially" means of real importance, not a fixed share. Its standards are affirmative flexibility and limits: the negative's reading would allow almost no plans, because few restrictions on a growing industry could be proven to stop a set share of it. The judge's first question is the we meet. If the affirmative has evidence that real companies would fail the safety requirements, topicality is over. If not, the judge compares the two interpretations, using reasonability or competing interpretations, whichever the debaters won.

A judge treats topicality as a gate that comes before the merits of the plan, and takes it in order. First, the we meet: if the plan meets the negative's interpretation, the argument is over. If not, the judge compares the interpretations through the standards, under reasonability or competing interpretations, whichever framework the debaters won. Then the voters: why the winning interpretation should decide the round. Many judges also ask whether the abuse is proven. A negative that wins its standards but cannot point to any argument it lost may still lose a judge who will not vote on potential abuse. Past the gate, the debate is about the plan itself.

Skipping the we meet. If the plan meets their interpretation, say so first. It is the shortest and best answer. Ignoring topicality until the last speech. Answer it the first time it is read. Arguing limits without predictability. Any affirmative can claim its own interpretation is the most limiting. A counter-interpretation that wins nothing. It should claim standards the negative cannot reach, or take the negative's. Going for topicality against complete answers. If the affirmative answered every part well, look for a better argument. Calling a voter a standard. Fairness and education are the voters. A standard explains how your interpretation produces them.

Chapter 14 taught the four parts of the Uniqueness Model, and Chapter 15 placed advantages among the stock issues. This chapter is about writing one. Students who have the structure memorized often still stare at a blank page, because they start at the top: "Uniqueness: ..." and then nothing. The fix is to write in a different order than you read. A reliable process has three steps. Step 1: research first. Do exploratory research on the topic before you write a word (Chapter 8). Do not force an advantage you thought of before reading; let the literature tell you where the strong arguments are. A few minutes of reading will usually show you two or three impact areas the topic clearly reaches, and save you hours defending one it does not. Step 2: start from the bottom. Once you have read, decide what impact you can reach, and write it first. This is starting from the bottom: you begin with the end of the story. A topic about increasing federal education funding suggests poverty and education impacts. A topic about military action suggests war impacts. A topic about AI development suggests impacts on jobs, safety and rights. Each possible ending is an impact scenario: a specific harm to people that the topic's literature connects to the resolution. Chapter 14's rule applies: the impact should be terminal, ending in people suffering or dying, by the shortest chain your evidence supports. Step 3: top down. With the impact written, go back to the top and fill in the rest. Uniqueness comes next: describe the status quo in a way that sets up your impact. If the impact is poverty, the uniqueness describes people losing income now. The link is the easiest part, because it is always a description of the plan. Then write the internal link last: the explanation of how the plan changes the situation you described in uniqueness, so that the impact is prevented. Internal links are where research is hardest and where advantages are most often attacked, so this is where your best evidence should go.
