x: Return to the small example from Chapters 4 and 14: the policy resolution "Sam should get a dog." After a little research, the obvious impact is security. So the advantage starts from the bottom: Advantage 1: Burglars. Uniqueness: ??? Link: ??? Internal link: ??? Impact: stopping burglars from stealing Sam's DVD collection. Then it moves to the top. Uniqueness: there have been burglaries in Sam's neighborhood. The link fills itself in: Sam gets a dog. The internal link does the real work: dogs bark at strangers, and burglars avoid homes with barking dogs. Now the advantage is complete, and the hardest part, the internal link, is also clearly the part to research most carefully. The same process works for a federal policy. On the AI resolution, start from the impact the literature supports, such as workers falling into poverty when AI displaces them faster than they can retrain. Then write uniqueness (displacement is accelerating now and retraining programs are not keeping up), the link (the plan requires licenses before the largest AI systems are trained) and the internal link (licensing slows the deployment of the most disruptive systems, giving workers and retraining programs time to adjust).

Some impacts happen all at once when a situation crosses a line. A brink is that line: the point at which a situation tips from manageable to catastrophic. The word appears constantly in debate evidence ("on the brink of collapse"), and used well, it strengthens two parts of an advantage. A brink strengthens uniqueness by explaining why now matters. An advantage that says "unemployment is high" is weaker than one that says "unemployment is approaching the level at which state relief funds run out." The second describes a threshold, a specific point that, once crossed, triggers the impact. It tells the judge that the status quo is close to disaster, so the plan's action is urgent. A brink also strengthens the internal link by explaining why a small change matters. If the status quo is near a threshold, even a modest plan can be the difference between crossing it and not. Without a brink, the negative can argue that the plan's effect is too small to matter. Brinks carry a risk. If your evidence says the world is on the brink, the negative will ask why it has not tipped already, and whether something else in the status quo will push it over regardless of the plan. Use brinks only when your evidence actually describes a threshold, and be ready to explain why the plan, not something else, decides which side of it we end up on.

Debate is a game of strategy, and the best answer to an argument is often one you made before your opponent said it. Pre-emption means anticipating the arguments your opponent is likely to make and building your answers into your case. Take a resolution about one-time student debt forgiveness. Experienced debaters expect a disadvantage arguing that forgiven debt creates a sudden tax bill for borrowers. A well-prepared affirmative researches the issue, learns that forgiveness can be structured to be tax-exempt, and writes that into its plan or advantage from the start. When the negative reads the disadvantage, the answer is already on the flow. Pre-emption has a cost: every sentence spent answering an argument before it is made is a sentence not spent proving your own. Pre-empt the arguments you are confident are coming and that would hurt the most. Leave the rest for your rebuttals.

Normal means is the argument that the plan would be carried out the way actions like it usually are: funded through the normal budget process, enforced by the agency that normally handles the area, and so on. It lets the affirmative keep its plan text short without leaving every detail undefended. If the negative asks how the licensing plan will be enforced, the affirmative can answer that, through normal means, the relevant federal agency would enforce it the way it enforces other licenses. Normal means is a claim, not a magic word. Being the first to say "normal means" does not settle anything; your opponent can argue that the normal way of doing things is different from what you claim, or that it would cause the very problem they are arguing. Like any other claim, it is stronger with evidence about how similar policies have actually been carried out. By the end of this chapter you should be able to: Write a disadvantage in the Uniqueness Model. Explain why a disadvantage's uniqueness must say things are good now. Write a link that respects fiat. The affirmative proposes a change. The negative has two ways to show the change is a bad idea. It can argue that the plan does harm: that is a disadvantage, a reason the world of the plan is worse than the status quo. And it can argue that the affirmative's own case is wrong: the harms are not real, the status quo is already solving them, or the plan will not work. Debaters call arguments of the first kind off-case, because they are new positions separate from the affirmative's case, and arguments of the second kind on-case, because they answer the case directly. A strong negative usually does both.

A disadvantage uses the same four parts as an advantage (Chapter 14), pointed in the opposite direction. Uniqueness says things are good now, in the area the disadvantage is about. Link says what the plan does to change that. Internal link explains how that change makes things worse. Impact is the harm to people that results. In short: things are good now, the plan changes them, the change is bad, and here is how bad. Take the AI policy resolution and a licensing plan. A negative might write a disadvantage about American AI leadership. Uniqueness: the United States currently leads the world in AI development, and that lead is holding. Link: the plan's licensing requirement slows American AI development. Internal link: slower development lets companies in other countries take the lead, moving jobs and investment with them. Impact: lost economic growth means lost jobs, and job loss pushes families into poverty, with all the health and life consequences that follow. Each step needs evidence, and Chapter 17's process works the same way here: start from the impact the literature supports and fill in the rest from the top. s: 18.3 Why uniqueness must say things are good
x: Chapter 14 explained that a shared impact cancels on the Scale: if a harm happens in both worlds, it cannot be a reason to choose either one. That is why every disadvantage needs uniqueness, and why its uniqueness has to point the right way. The negative defends the status quo. For the plan to cause the impact, the impact must not be happening already. So disadvantage uniqueness must establish that the status quo is good, or at least stable, in the area of the disadvantage. If the negative's uniqueness evidence says American AI leadership is already slipping, the negative has told the judge the impact is coming anyway, and the affirmative will happily agree. This creates a trap worth naming. When you research uniqueness, you will find plenty of evidence showing a trend getting worse. That evidence feels relevant, because it is about the right topic. But evidence that the status quo is declining is evidence against your disadvantage. Uniqueness evidence should say the good thing is happening and will continue unless something disrupts it. If the best evidence available says things are getting worse, you may need a different disadvantage. A related idea is link uniqueness: the link must also be unique to the plan. If something already happening in the status quo would cause the same link, such as another law already slowing AI development, then the plan adds little, and the affirmative will argue the disadvantage is non-unique.

Policy debate uses an agreement called fiat: for the purpose of the debate, everyone assumes the plan is adopted. The debate is about whether it should be, not whether Congress would actually pass it. Fiat keeps the debate on the merits. Fiat has a consequence for disadvantage links. A link should be about what the plan does once it is in effect, not about the process of passing it. An argument like "the plan would never get through Congress" is not a disadvantage, because fiat assumes it does. And a link that depends on details the affirmative never committed to, like claiming the plan is attached to some other bill, describes a different plan; the affirmative will point out that its plan, as written, does nothing of the kind. Keep links tied to the plan text and to what the plan would actually do. Chapter 14 mentioned two other kinds of link. A perception link runs through how someone reacts to the plan once it is in effect: investors, voters or a foreign government. A spillover link argues that the plan leads to similar action elsewhere, such as other states or countries copying it. Both respect fiat, because both start from the plan as adopted, and both need evidence that the reaction or the copying would actually happen.

On-case arguments go straight at the affirmative's stock issues. Two of the most useful are presses on inherency and solvency. An inherency press argues that the status quo will solve the harm without the plan. If federal agencies are already writing AI safety rules, or if major AI companies have committed to the same safety testing the plan requires, the plan adds little. An inherency press does not need to prove the status quo solves everything; it shrinks the affirmative's advantage by showing that much of the benefit happens anyway. A solvency press argues that the plan will not fix the harm. Licensing may not work if companies can train systems overseas, if the computing threshold is easy to avoid, or if the agency enforcing it lacks the expertise. Like an inherency press, a solvency press can be partial: "the plan solves some of the harm, but far less than the affirmative claims" is still a valuable argument, because it shrinks what goes on the affirmative's side of the Scale. The most powerful on-case argument is a case turn: an argument that the plan makes the affirmative's own harm worse. If the affirmative claims licensing improves safety, a negative might argue that licensing drives development to less careful companies abroad, making AI less safe overall. A case turn gives the negative offense on the affirmative's own advantage. Chapter 19 covers turns in detail. At a glance Argument What it says Effect on the Scale Disadvantage The plan causes a new harm Adds weight to the negative's side Inherency press The status quo already solves much of the harm Removes weight from the affirmative's side Solvency press The plan does not fix the harm, or fixes less of it Removes weight from the affirmative's side Case turn The plan makes the affirmative's own harm worse Moves weight to the negative's side

A negative strategy combines off-case and on-case arguments so they work together. A good strategy usually includes at least one disadvantage, so the negative has its own impact on the Scale, and on-case arguments that shrink the affirmative's advantages, so the disadvantage does not have to outweigh much. The pieces should not contradict each other. A negative that argues the plan will not work at all (a total solvency press) and that the plan will slow American AI development dramatically (a disadvantage link) has a problem: if the plan does nothing, it cannot slow anything down. The affirmative will point that out. Choose arguments that fit together: a partial solvency press ("the plan solves very little safety risk") can sit beside a disadvantage ("but it still slows development") as long as you explain why both are true. In the rebuttals, the negative collapses (Chapter 12), usually to the disadvantage plus the strongest case argument, and weighs: the disadvantage's impact against whatever is left of the advantage.

Disadvantage: "Uniqueness: things are good now. Link: the plan changes that. Internal link: the change is bad. Impact: ..." Inherency press: "The status quo is already solving this, because..." Solvency press: "Even if the harm is real, the plan doesn't fix it, because..." Case turn: "The plan actually makes their harm worse..." Weigh: "The disadvantage outweighs what's left of their advantage, because..."

Resolution: Students who are undecided about a major should start at a community college. The negative writes a disadvantage from the bottom: the impact is a delayed degree, which means delayed full-time earnings. Uniqueness: undecided students at four-year schools currently finish in a typical time when they use campus advising early. Link: starting at a community college separates them from the four-year advising system. Internal link: transfer students who change majors after transferring may need extra terms. Impact: a later graduation costs a year of full-time salary. On-case, the negative presses solvency: the affirmative's transfer guarantee only protects credits for some majors. The negative's ballot argument is that the disadvantage outweighs because lost salary is larger than the tuition saved.

Resolution: The United States federal government should substantially restrict the development of artificial intelligence. The negative reads the AI leadership disadvantage from section 18.2, with uniqueness evidence that the American lead is holding. On-case, it reads an inherency press on the safety advantage (major developers already conduct safety testing) and a partial solvency press (licensing does not cover models trained abroad). It avoids a total solvency press, which would contradict the disadvantage's link. In the last rebuttal, it collapses to the disadvantage and the inherency press, and weighs: the affirmative's remaining safety benefit is small because most testing already happens, while the disadvantage costs jobs and growth now.

A judge compares the worlds: what is left of the affirmative's advantages after the on-case arguments, against what the negative has won on its disadvantages. On-case arguments rarely win a debate alone, because a small advantage still beats nothing; the negative usually needs its own impact on the Scale. Judges also notice when negative arguments contradict each other, and they hold the contradiction against the negative.

Uniqueness evidence that shows decline. Disadvantage uniqueness must say things are good now. Links that ignore fiat. Argue about what the plan does, not whether it would pass. Contradictory negative arguments. A plan that does nothing cannot also cause a disaster. Only arguing on-case. Shrinking the advantage is not enough if nothing is on your side of the Scale. Forgetting the impact. A disadvantage without a terminal impact gives the judge nothing to weigh.

t: Refutation Continued (Refuting Arguments in Policy Debate)
x: Refutation is the process of responding to arguments. Chapter 4 introduced it for fact and value debates: the four-step answer, the significance, relevance and accuracy tests, laying an argument out as a syllogism to find its weakest premise, and the difference between offense and defense on the Scale. Those tools still work in policy debate. What changes is the shape of the arguments. Almost every policy argument is a chain of cause and effect running from a plan to an impact, and every link in that chain is a place to answer it. This chapter gives you a complete set of responses built for that shape, starting with a closer look at offense and defense. Every response falls into one of two kinds. A defensive argument says your opponent does not win: their argument is wrong, weak or irrelevant. In soccer terms, defense is saving a goal. An offensive argument says you win: their argument actually supports your side, or your argument matters more. Offense is scoring a goal. The difference matters because of the Scale. Defense removes weight from your opponent's side; offense adds weight to yours. A debater with only defense can, at best, reduce an opponent's argument to zero, and judges often hesitate to say any argument has a zero chance of being true. A debater with offense has a reason for the judge to vote for them even if some of the opponent's argument survives. Strong answers usually combine both: a little defense to shrink the argument, and some offense to turn the leftover risk your way.

x: B.U.T.T.O.N. is a memory aid for six responses to any advantage or disadvantage. It may be the second-worst acronym in the world; it is also one of the most useful. Each response attacks a different part of the Uniqueness Model. Figure 19.1 B.U.T.T.O.N. as offense and defense The six B.U.T.T.O.N. responses sorted into defense (reasons the opponent does not win) and offense (reasons you win). No brink (defense) argues that the change is too small to trigger the impact, or the status quo is too far from the impact for the change to matter. "If we all recycle, we can solve climate change" invites a no-brink answer: recycling is real but far too small a change to stop climate change on its own. No brink attacks the internal link, and it is especially strong against advantages that claim a modest plan will prevent a huge catastrophe. Non-unique (defense) argues that the impact is already happening in the status quo. "If we pass your plan, it will increase inflation" invites a non-unique answer if inflation is already high: the plan cannot cause what is already here. Chapter 14 explained why this works: an impact that happens in both worlds cancels on the Scale. Non-unique attacks the uniqueness. Link turn (offense) argues that the link actually goes the other direction: the plan prevents the impact instead of causing it. "Dropping out of college will save me tens of thousands on tuition" can be link turned: dropping out costs far more over a lifetime in lost earnings. A link turn takes your opponent's impact and makes it your impact. Impact turn (offense) argues that the impact is actually the opposite of what your opponent says: their good thing is bad, or their bad thing is good. "Democracy is good because it promotes peace" can be impact turned by arguing that democracy is bad: it needs consensus to act, so it is often too slow to solve major problems. Impact turns are powerful and risky, because you are defending a claim that sounds wrong. Use them only with strong evidence, and never on impacts like human suffering, where the turn is indefensible. Outweighs (offense) concedes that your opponent's argument may be true and argues that your impact matters more. "The housing crisis is a big deal, but if we build low-income housing, my property value might go down a little" invites an outweighs answer: people having homes matters more than a small drop in property value. Outweighs uses the impact calculus from Chapter 10. No link (defense) argues that the plan does not cause what your opponent claims. "If you step on a crack, you'll break your mother's back" deserves a no-link answer: there is no evidence that stepping on cracks causes spinal injury. No link attacks the link itself, and it is usually the first response debaters learn, because it simply says "that's not what happens." At a glance Response Type What it says Attacks No brink Defense The change is too small, or the impact too far away Internal link Non-unique Defense The impact is already happening Uniqueness Link turn Offense The plan prevents the impact instead Link Impact turn Offense The impact is actually good, or actually bad Impact Outweighs Offense Our impact matters more Weighing No link Defense The plan does not cause the impact Link

x: There is one combination you must never make. A double turn happens when you link turn and impact turn the same argument. Each turn is a good answer on its own. Together they point the argument back at your own plan. The easiest way to see it is to map one disadvantage and turn it each way. Here is the AI leadership disadvantage from Chapter 18, read against the licensing plan: DA 1: AI Leadership Uniqueness: The United States leads the world in AI development, and that lead is holding. Link: The plan's licensing requirement slows American AI development. Internal link: Slower development lets companies in other countries take the lead, and jobs and investment go with them. Impact: Lost jobs push families into poverty, with all the health and life consequences that follow. Turn the link. The affirmative argues that the plan does the opposite of what the negative says: Uniqueness: The United States leads the world in AI development. (Unchanged.) Link (turned): The plan protects American AI leadership. Licensing makes American AI systems the most trusted in the world, and it prevents the kind of disaster that would bring a public backlash and shut development down. Internal link: A stronger lead keeps jobs and investment in the United States. Impact: Families keep the jobs that keep them out of poverty. Why this is good for the affirmative: the negative's own impact has moved to the affirmative's side of the Scale. Every reason the negative gave for why poverty matters is now a reason to vote for the plan. Turn the impact. The affirmative concedes the link and argues that what the negative calls a harm is actually good: Uniqueness: The United States leads the world in AI development. (Unchanged.) Link: The plan slows American AI development. (Conceded.) Internal link: Slower development means slower AI-driven growth. Impact (turned): Slower growth is better for workers. Rapid AI growth displaces workers faster than they can retrain, so the growth the negative wants to protect pushes families into poverty. Slowing it down gives workers time to adjust. Why this is good for the affirmative: the plan still does what the negative said it does, but now that is a benefit. The disadvantage has become another advantage. Turn both. Now suppose the affirmative makes both arguments in the same speech: Link (turned): The plan protects American AI leadership and speeds up AI-driven growth. Impact (turned): Rapid AI-driven growth pushes families into poverty. Put together: The plan speeds up the growth that pushes families into poverty. Why this is no longer good for the affirmative: each turn was a good answer alone, but together they say the plan causes the very harm the affirmative just argued is bad. The negative does not need to answer either turn. It only needs to agree with both: "Extend their link turn and their impact turn. By their own arguments, the plan causes poverty." The affirmative has written a new disadvantage against itself. Pick one turn per argument, and make sure your other answers do not contradict it. If you turn the link, do not also argue the impact is good. If you turn the impact, concede the link.

x: Three responses fall outside the acronym but come up constantly. Alternative causes (defense) argues that other things will cause the impact regardless of the plan. If the negative says the plan will push families into poverty, the affirmative can point to other forces already doing so. Alternative causes shrink the plan's importance: if many things cause the impact, the plan's contribution is small. Root cause, or sequencing (offense), argues that your impact comes first because it causes your opponent's. Chapter 10 introduced sequencing as a weighing tool; here it works as a response: "Their impact is a symptom. Ours is the cause, so solving ours solves theirs too." No uniqueness (defense) is different from non-unique. It argues that your opponent never established the direction of the status quo at all: they read no uniqueness evidence, so the judge cannot know whether the impact is coming anyway. It is a simple, effective answer to disadvantages read without uniqueness.

x: Acronyms have to be memorized, and students sometimes struggle to pick the right letter under pressure. This book's author teaches another approach, called algebraic analysis. It derives every response from one expression, with no jargon required. Almost every policy argument says: doing X will cause Y, where X is the plan (the link) and Y is the impact. Call any competing impact Z. Every response is a statement about X, Y or Z. At the beginner level, four statements cover the basics. "X will not cause Y." That is a no link. "X will make Y less likely, not more" (or more likely, not less). That is a link turn. "Y is already happening." That is non-unique. "Z matters more than Y." That is outweighs. At the intermediate level, four more statements add depth. "Y will happen whether or not X happens." That is an inevitability claim: the impact cannot be prevented, so it should not count for either side. "Other things will cause Y." That is alternative causes. "We are so far from Y that X is too small to cause it." That is no brink. "Y doesn't matter that much." That is impact defense: the impact is real but smaller, rarer or more recoverable than claimed. The advantage of the algebra is that it works even when you have forgotten every name. Faced with any argument, write it as "doing X will cause Y," and then ask questions about each letter. Does X really cause Y? Is Y already happening? Would Y happen anyway? What else causes Y? Does Y matter? Is there a Z that matters more? Every question is a possible answer. More advanced levels add responses such as arguing the link has already been tested (if X caused Y, it would have happened already) and sequencing (Y determines whether Z happens).

s: 20.1 When the status quo is hard to defend
x: Chapter 18 showed the negative defending the status quo with disadvantages and case answers. Sometimes that is a losing position. On some topics, the affirmative's harm is real, well documented and getting worse: the status quo is simply bad. A negative who argues that the harm does not exist will lose credibility, and a negative who argues the plan causes a small disadvantage will lose the weighing. Debaters call this kind of topic affirmative-sided. The negative's answer is to stop defending the status quo and propose something better. A counterplan is a formal alternative proposal from the negative, different from the affirmative's plan, that solves the affirmative's harm in another way. Take an energy example. If the affirmative's plan is to invest in nuclear power to fight climate change, the negative might counterplan to invest in solar power instead. Now both sides agree climate change is bad and both claim to solve it. The affirmative's biggest impact no longer favors either side; it cancels on the Scale, just as Chapter 14 showed shared impacts do. An indefensible status quo is the most common reason to read a counterplan, but negatives read them for three reasons. The first is the one above: a negative stuck defending a bad status quo will lose to the affirmative's harms. The second is to take the affirmative's offense. Picture the Scale with the affirmative's impacts stacked on its side. A counterplan that solves the same harm lets the negative put the same weight on its own side, so the affirmative's biggest impact no longer tips the Scale. The third is to make a small net benefit large. Once the counterplan has cancelled the affirmative's advantages, the negative needs only a little offense to win. That third reason is the logic of a plan-inclusive counterplan, which does almost all of the plan but leaves out one piece. If the plan gives a grant to all 50 states, a counterplan that gives it to 48 states solves nearly everything the plan solves, and the debate turns on whether those two states should be left out. A modest reason to exclude them can be enough to win, which is also why many judges and coaches consider plan-inclusive counterplans unfair to the affirmative.

s: 20.2 Opportunity cost and the net benefit
x: A counterplan works on the idea of opportunity cost: choosing one option means giving up another. If the country builds nuclear plants, it does not spend that money and time on solar. The counterplan's claim is that the plan's opportunity cost is too high, because the counterplan is the better use of the same effort. To win, the counterplan needs a net benefit: a reason the world of the counterplan is better than the world of the plan. A net benefit can be a disadvantage to the plan that the counterplan avoids (nuclear power requires uranium mining, which harms the environment and health), or an extra advantage only the counterplan has (solar can be deployed much faster than nuclear plants can be built, and speed matters for climate change). Without a net benefit, the counterplan and the plan are just two ways to solve the same problem, and the judge has no reason to prefer the counterplan. The affirmative's first answer is usually a solvency deficit: something the plan solves that the counterplan does not. If nuclear power provides steady electricity when the sun is not shining, and solar alone cannot, the counterplan solves less of the climate problem than the plan. The debate then becomes a comparison: does the counterplan's net benefit outweigh its solvency deficit?

The affirmative has a second, often stronger answer. Is there any reason the country cannot invest in nuclear and solar? A permutation is the affirmative's argument that it is possible to do both the plan and all or part of the counterplan, and that doing both is better than doing the counterplan alone. In effect, it is a no-link argument: it says the counterplan is not a true opportunity cost to the plan, because choosing the plan does not mean giving up the counterplan. A permutation is a test, not a new plan. It asks whether the counterplan really competes with the plan. If the best world is "both," then the counterplan is not a reason to reject the plan; it is just a good idea to add to it. Because it is a test, a permutation works like a no-link argument against a disadvantage, or a "we meet" argument against topicality (Chapter 16). The affirmative is not changing its plan to "do both"; it is still defending the plan. It is showing that the negative's alternative is not a cost of choosing the plan. Permutations are worth reading for two reasons. First, they take back what the counterplan took. If the counterplan was supposed to cancel the affirmative's advantages, a permutation that includes the counterplan lets the affirmative claim those advantages again, along with anything extra the counterplan solves. If the negative's net benefit does not link to the permutation, the counterplan stops being a reason to vote negative. Second, permutations are cheap and low-risk. A good one takes about fifteen seconds, an affirmative almost never loses a debate because it read one, and a negative that fails to answer one has usually lost the counterplan. Figure 20.1 Counterplan, permutation and competition Three worlds on the Scale: the plan, the counterplan and the permutation (both), showing that a net benefit linked to the plan makes the counterplan alone the best world.

Permutations would be too easy if the affirmative could change its plan however it liked, so two rules keep them fair. The first rule is against severance: a legitimate permutation includes all of the affirmative's plan. The affirmative cannot drop the parts of its plan that link to the negative's disadvantage. Doing so would let it abandon ground it chose in its first speech, after the negative has already built arguments against that ground. The second rule is against intrinsicness: a legitimate permutation cannot add anything that is in neither the plan nor the counterplan. If the negative's net benefit is that nuclear power requires new uranium mining, the affirmative cannot permute "nuclear and solar, using only uranium that has already been mined." That adds a new idea to escape an argument the negative has already made. Put simply, a fair permutation is all of the plan plus some or all of the counterplan, and nothing else. The same rules can be written as a short formula. Any permutation is some share of the plan plus some share of the counterplan (or whatever counter-advocacy the negative defends): Permutation \= a% of the Plan + c% of the Counterplan Here a is how much of the plan the permutation keeps, and c is how much of the counterplan it adds. Each rule is a limit on those numbers. Permutation Formula In plain words Legitimate 100% of the Plan + c% of the Counterplan, where c is more than 0% and no more than 100% All of the plan, plus some or all of the counterplan Severance a% of the Plan + c% of the Counterplan, where a is less than 100% Drops part of the plan Intrinsic 100% of the Plan + c% of the Counterplan + X, where X is in neither the plan nor the counterplan Adds something new The two rules work as a floor and a ceiling on every permutation: 100% of the Plan ≤ Permutation ≤ 100% of the Plan + 100% of the Counterplan The rule of severance sets the floor. A permutation can never fall below all of the plan, so a must always be 100%. A permutation that keeps less than that has severed. The rule of intrinsicness sets the ceiling. A permutation can never go beyond everything in the plan and the counterplan put together. Notice that the ceiling is not about doing more of the same thing; it is about adding something new. Doing all of the plan and all of the counterplan is still under the ceiling. What breaks it is the X in the table: anything that appears in neither advocacy. One more limit sits at the bottom: c has to be more than 0%. A "permutation" with none of the counterplan in it is just the plan again, and it tests nothing.

The rules are easier to see with a small example. You are at the pet shop, and your plan is to buy three pets: an alligator, a bird and a cat. Call the plan A, B, C. Before you reach the register, a friend proposes a counterplan: buy a dog and an eagle instead. Call the counterplan D, E. A legitimate permutation must keep all of A, B and C, and it can add only D, E or both. That leaves exactly three legitimate permutations: Permutation What it leaves out What the debate is now about Alligator, bird, cat and dog The eagle Whether the eagle is bad, or is what makes the counterplan better Alligator, bird, cat and eagle The dog Whether the dog is bad, or is what makes the counterplan better Alligator, bird, cat, dog and eagle Nothing Whether the plan itself makes things worse than the counterplan alone Each legitimate permutation is a choice. The affirmative leaves out whichever part of the counterplan it thinks it can beat, and the debate narrows to that part. The third permutation takes all of the counterplan, so the negative can win only with a net benefit to the plan itself: some reason that buying the alligator, bird and cat is worse than buying only the dog and eagle. Anything else breaks a rule. "Alligator, bird and dog" severs: it drops the cat, which the negative may already have attacked (cats wreck the furniture). "Alligator, bird, cat and fish" is intrinsic: the fish is in neither the plan nor the counterplan, so the affirmative has invented new ground in the middle of the debate. An affirmative that can add a fish can add whatever it needs to escape any net benefit, which is why intrinsic permutations are unfair. In the terms of the formula in 20.4, the first keeps only two of the plan's three pets, so a is less than 100%; the fish is the X.

s: 20.6 How a counterplan beats the permutation
x: A counterplan survives the permutation in one of two ways. The first is mutual exclusivity: it is impossible to do both. The clearest case is a counterplan that does most of the plan but leaves out one part. If the plan does A, B and C, and the counterplan does only A and B, the permutation cannot work: doing A, B and C is not the same as doing only A and B, and the severance rule means the affirmative cannot drop C. The debate then comes down to whether C is good or bad. The second is competition: doing both is worse than doing the counterplan alone. This is where the net benefit matters most. If the negative's net benefit is a disadvantage to the plan itself, such as harm from uranium mining, then any world that includes the plan, including the permutation, still causes that harm. The counterplan alone avoids it. That is why a counterplan's net benefit should link to the plan, not just describe why the counterplan is nice. A net benefit that says "solar is fast" does not beat the permutation, because the permutation includes solar. A net benefit that says "nuclear causes harm" does, because the permutation includes nuclear. Both of these are forms of functional competition: the plan and counterplan compete because of what they would do. Some negatives try textual competition instead, arguing that a counterplan competes because its wording differs from the plan's. A counterplan identical to the plan except that it calls Taiwan "the Republic of China" does exactly what the plan does, but the negative claims a net benefit from the word choice. Most judges and coaches reject textual competition. It is easy to find an author who criticizes almost any word and nearly impossible to find one who says a debate must use one particular word, so the negative can win without disagreeing about anything the plan does. At a glance Term What it means Energy example Counterplan The negative's alternative that solves the harm another way Invest in solar instead of nuclear Net benefit Why the counterplan's world is better than the plan's Nuclear requires harmful uranium mining Solvency deficit What the plan solves that the counterplan does not Solar alone cannot supply steady power at night Permutation Do the plan and the counterplan Invest in nuclear and solar Competition Doing both is worse than the counterplan alone Any world with nuclear still mines uranium

Counterplan: "Counterplan: [text]. It solves their harm, and it has a net benefit..." Solvency deficit: "The counterplan doesn't solve [part of the harm], and that outweighs their net benefit." Permutation: "Permutation: do both. There's no reason to choose." Severance: "That permutation drops part of their plan. They can't sever." Competition: "The permutation still includes the plan, so it still causes the net benefit." Permutation with a text: "Permutation: do the plan and the dog. That leaves out the eagle, and the eagle is bad because..." Textual competition: "The counterplan does exactly what the plan does. Arguing over a word isn't a reason to reject the plan."

Resolution: Sam should get a dog. The affirmative's advantage: a dog's barking deters burglars from the neighborhood's recent break-ins. The negative concedes burglaries are a real problem and counterplans: install a home security system. Its net benefit is that a dog costs money and time every day for years, while a security system is a one-time cost. The affirmative permutes: get a dog and install the system. The negative answers that the net benefit links to the plan, so the permutation still includes the dog's daily cost. The affirmative answers with a solvency deficit: a camera records a burglary, but a barking dog prevents it, because burglars avoid homes with dogs. The judge weighs prevention against cost.

Resolution: The United States federal government should substantially restrict the development of artificial intelligence. Against the licensing plan, the negative counterplans: the federal government should require safety testing of the largest AI systems before deployment, without a license to train them. The net benefit is the AI leadership disadvantage from Chapter 18: restricting training slows American development, while testing before deployment does not. The affirmative permutes: do both. The negative argues competition: any world with the licensing requirement still slows development, so the permutation still links to the disadvantage. The affirmative answers with a solvency deficit: testing after training is too late for the most dangerous systems, whose risks arise during development. The debate turns on which is larger: the deficit or the net benefit.

A judge evaluates a counterplan in order. First, does it compete: does the permutation fail, either because the two cannot coexist or because doing both is worse? If the permutation wins, the counterplan is no reason to reject the plan. Second, if it competes, does the net benefit outweigh the solvency deficit? A counterplan with a strong net benefit and a small deficit usually wins; one with no net benefit never does.

A counterplan with no net benefit. Without one, there is no reason to prefer it over the plan. A net benefit that does not link to the plan. "The counterplan is good" loses to the permutation. "The plan is bad" does not. Severing in the permutation. The permutation must include the whole plan. Adding new ideas in the permutation. Nothing beyond the plan and the counterplan. Forgetting the solvency deficit. The affirmative's best answer is often something the counterplan cannot do.

Drill: counter it (15 minutes, pairs). One partner states a policy plan. The other proposes a counterplan and a net benefit that links to the plan. The first partner answers with a permutation and a solvency deficit. Switch. Drill: pet shop permutations (10 minutes, pairs). One partner names a plan of three things (pets, pizza toppings, classes to take). The other names a counterplan of two different things. Together, list every legitimate permutation. Then write one permutation that severs and one that is intrinsic, and explain what each did wrong. Finally, pick the permutation the affirmative should read and say what the debate would now be about. Writing exercise. Write a counterplan to the AI licensing plan, with a net benefit. Then write the affirmative's permutation and explain, in 150 words, whether the counterplan competes and why.
Move: All four. Builds on: Chapters 1 through 20. Where you use it: after this course, in competitive debate if you choose it, and in work, civic life and your own decisions whether you do or not.

By the end of this chapter you should be able to: Describe how the classroom debates in this book relate to the major competitive debate formats. Identify which competitive format fits your interests. Apply the four moves to arguments at work. Apply them to civic decisions and public arguments. Apply them to your own decisions.

This book has been organized around four moves. To build is to construct an argument with a claim, a warrant and an implication, whether as a contention, an advantage or a disadvantage. To prove is to support each part with research and evidence that would survive your opponent reading the whole source. To answer is to respond to one part of an opponent's argument at a time, with four-step refutation, B.U.T.T.O.N. or the algebra. And to weigh is to tell a judge why what you won matters more than what you lost. You have practiced the four moves in three kinds of debate on one subject: a fact debate about what is true, a value debate about what matters, and a policy debate about what to do. Those three questions, in that order, sit underneath almost every serious decision people make. That is why the moves outlast the course.

Competitive debate is debate as an activity, with tournaments, teams and coaches. Many colleges, including many community colleges, have debate teams, usually as part of a forensics program that also includes individual speaking events. Debate formats differ in how many people are on a side, how much research is done in advance, and who judges, but every one of them uses the four moves. Policy debate is the format closest to Part V of this book. Teams of two debate one policy resolution for an entire season, which allows deep research and large evidence files. Judges are usually experienced, and the debates are often fast and highly technical. If you enjoyed researching and building advantages and disadvantages, this is the format that rewards it most. Lincoln-Douglas debate pits one debater against another. In high school, it is usually a value debate, close to Chapter 13. At the college level, the version run by the National Forensic Association is a one-person policy format with evidence, combining the research of Part V with a faster pace for a single debater. Parliamentary debate gives debaters a new resolution at each round and a short preparation time, usually without prepared evidence. It rewards broad knowledge, quick thinking and the ability to make and explain arguments without cards, which is why Chapter 9 stressed explaining the argument a card would contain. Parliamentary resolutions can be fact, value or policy, so all three parts of this book apply. Public debate formats are built around persuading a general audience. Rounds are often judged by people without debate experience, so the skills of Chapter 10 (audience analysis, clear explanation and plain language) matter most. If you liked debating for lay judges, look for these formats. Whichever format interests you, the path in is the same: ask your instructor whether your college has a team. Most teams welcome beginners, and the skills from this course are a strong foundation. Most workplace arguments are policy debates in disguise. A proposal to change a schedule, buy new software or hire another person is an affirmative case: there is a harm, a barrier, a plan and an advantage. A manager weighing the proposal is a judge, usually a lay one. The habits from this course transfer directly. Lead with the claim. Support it with evidence your audience trusts. Anticipate the objections and pre-empt the strongest ones (Chapter 17). Compare costs and benefits explicitly, using the weighing terms of Chapter 10. And when someone pushes back, answer the warrant of their objection rather than repeating yourself. The same skills help when you are the one deciding. Asking "what is the internal link here?" or "is this already happening without the change?" are two of the most useful questions in any meeting.

Every ballot measure, school board decision and city budget is a policy resolution, and every campaign is an argument aimed at lay judges: you. The skills that make you a better debater make you harder to fool. Trace a viral claim back to its source (Chapter 8). Ask whether an alarming statistic is unique to the policy being debated or would happen anyway (Chapter 14). Notice a false dilemma or a slippery slope in a political ad (Chapter 7). Ask what the strongest argument on the other side is, and whether the people you agree with have answered it. Debate also teaches something harder: arguing for a position you do not hold, and seeing why reasonable people hold it. That does not mean every position is equally good. It means you understand the disagreement well enough to judge it, which is what civic life asks of everyone.

The individual-level examples in this book, such as starting at a community college or choosing a major, were chosen because the same moves work on personal decisions. A big decision has a fact question (what is actually true about my options?), a value question (what matters most to me?) and a policy question (what should I do?). Answering them in that order, with evidence, and with the strongest case for the option you are leaning against, is about as good a decision method as there is. This book began with the idea that argument is how people decide things together. It ends with the same idea, applied to the hardest audience you will ever face: yourself.

At work: "The problem is... it hasn't been fixed because... here's what I propose... and here's why it's worth the cost." In a meeting: "Is that already happening without the change?" About a claim online: "Where does that number come from?" About a decision: "What's the strongest case for the option I'm leaning against?"

A student finishing this course is deciding whether to join the college debate team. Fact: the team practices twice a week and travels to several tournaments a year. Value: the student cares most about building skills for a career in law. Policy: join the team for one season. The student weighs the time cost against the benefit, uses the even-if from Chapter 12 ("even if it takes time from work, the skills matter more for my goal"), and asks the coach about the commitment before deciding. The four moves did not make the decision. They made it a clear one.

A city proposes a sales tax to fund road repairs. A resident applies the book. Harms: are the roads actually in poor condition, according to a source with no stake in the vote? Inherency: why hasn't the existing budget fixed them? Solvency: does the measure guarantee the money goes to roads? Disadvantages: who pays the tax, and does it fall hardest on people with less? Weighing: which matters more in this city, safer roads or the cost to the residents least able to pay? The resident still has to decide. But now they know what they are deciding.

Outside the classroom, the judges are managers, voters, juries, committees and you. They rarely announce their criteria, and they rarely write ballots. But they decide the way the judges in this book did: by asking who made the clearest case, who answered the other side, and why what they won matters more. Everything you have practiced is preparation for them.

Treating debate as only a classroom skill. The four moves work everywhere arguments are made. Debating a lay audience like a technical one. Most real-world judges are lay judges. Adapt. Only seeking out arguments you already agree with. The strongest case against your view is the most useful one to know. Waiting to be asked. If competitive debate interests you, ask about your college's team.

Drill: everyday resolution (15 minutes, small groups). Each student brings one decision from work, school or community life. The group turns it into a fact, a value and a policy resolution, then names the strongest argument on each side of the policy resolution. Writing exercise. Choose a current ballot measure, local decision or workplace proposal. In 300 words, analyze it using the stock issues from Chapter 15 and the weighing terms from Chapter 10, and end with the strongest argument on the side you do not support.

The communication model breaks any act of communication into eight elements. It was built to describe communication in general, from a phone call to a television ad, but it maps cleanly onto a debate.
The sender is the person or source trying to communicate.
Encoding is turning thoughts into a message: deciding what to say and how to say it.
The message is the information being communicated.
The channel is the medium the message travels through.
The receiver is the audience that takes in the message.
Decoding is how the receiver interprets the message.
Feedback is the receiver's response, which tells the sender how the message landed.
Noise is anything that interferes with the message getting through.
Each use of the model happens inside a communication situation, a single, bounded event where communication takes place.
Ethos is an appeal to credibility: the audience believes you because of who you are or who you cite.
Pathos is an appeal to emotion: the audience is moved by what the argument makes them feel.
Logos is an appeal to reason: the audience is persuaded by evidence and logic.
Debate is a structured contest in which two sides argue over the same question in front of someone who decides between them.
The proposition being debated, also called the topic.
The affirmative argues that the resolution should be accepted.
The side that argues the resolution should not be accepted. Other formats call the sides government and opposition, or pro and con.
The person or panel who decides who won, and who often enforces the rules, such as speech times.
In constructive speeches, debaters may make new arguments. In rebuttal speeches, they may not, except to answer something new from the speech just before.
A later speech in which debaters may not make new arguments, except to answer something new from the speech just before.
Argument: "You should start at a community college.
A claim: the statement you want the audience to accept.
A warrant: the reasoning or evidence that supports the claim.
An implication: why the claim matters, the "so what."
The grounds are the evidence or facts offered in support of the claim.
Backing is support for the warrant itself, for when the audience doubts the connection.
A qualifier is a word or phrase that marks how strong the claim is, such as "probably," "in most cases" or "almost certainly."
The rebuttal is the set of conditions under which the claim would not hold.
Aristotle called an argument with an unstated premise an enthymeme.
In 1984 he proposed the narrative paradigm: people understand the world through stories, and they judge arguments by how good a story they tell.
Narrative coherence: does the story hang together?
Narrative fidelity: does the story ring true with the audience's own experience and values?
The Contention Model is the structure for fact and value debates.
The Uniqueness Model is the structure for policy debates.
Every debate starts with a resolution: a single sentence that the affirmative argues for and the negative argues against.
A fact resolution asks whether a statement is true.
A value resolution asks for a judgment about what is good, better or more important.
A policy resolution asks whether an action should be taken.
Fact debates are decided by preponderance of evidence: the side with the better quantity and quality of evidence and reasoning wins.
Each side proposes a value, the principle that matters most, and a value criterion, the way to measure whether that value is achieved.
Each side proposes a value, the principle that matters most, and a value criterion, the way to measure whether that value is achieved.
Policy debates are decided by net benefits: the judge adds up the advantages and disadvantages of the plan and votes for whichever world, with the plan or without it, is better.

Classical rhetoricians called the point a dispute turns on its stasis, and they listed the questions in order: does the thing exist (conjecture), what is it (definition), is it good or bad (quality), and what should be done about it (procedure).
It usually favors the negative, because the negative is defending the status quo, the world as it is now.
The burden of proof belongs to the affirmative. The affirmative is asking the judge to accept something new, so it has to give reasons.
The burden of rejoinder belongs to whoever speaks next. Once a side has made an argument, the other side has to answer it or accept it.
Presumption is the default outcome if nobody proves anything.
The skill that creates clash is refutation: responding to your opponent's arguments.
Debate happens when the sides engage the same points, which debaters call clash.
Significance: does the argument matter? Even if it is true, is the impact large enough to affect the decision?
Relevance: is the argument connected to the resolution or to what the other side is defending?
Accuracy: is the argument true? Is their evidence wrong, outdated or misread?
A syllogism is an argument in three parts.
The major premise is a general rule.
The minor premise places a specific case under that rule. The conclusion is what follows if both premises are true.
The conclusion is what follows if both premises are true.
Flowing is the note-taking system debaters and judges use to record a debate so that every argument and every answer can be tracked.
An argument is dropped when the other side never answers it; on the flow, its row has an empty space in the next column.
An extension is carrying an argument forward into a later speech, reminding the judge it still stands and explaining why it matters.

The picture this book uses for how a judge decides: each argument a side wins goes on its side of a balance, arguments that cancel come off both sides, and the heavier side wins. If the Scale is level or empty, the judge votes on presumption.
An answer that puts something on your side of the Scale is offense: a reason to vote for you.
An answer that takes something off your opponent's side is defense: a reason not to vote for them.
How you present an argument out loud. In a debate, your own delivery is the biggest source of noise you control: an argument the judge cannot flow does not count.
Volume is how loud or soft you speak.
Pace is how fast or slow you speak.
Tone is the variation in energy, emotion and formality in your voice.
Clarity is how easy it is to understand each word you say.
Fluidity is how naturally your speech flows.
The biggest threat to fluidity is verbal filler: sounds and words like "um," "like" and "you know" that fill a gap while your brain catches up.
Eye contact is where you focus your attention while you speak.
Manuscript delivery means reading from a prepared text.
Impromptu delivery means speaking with no preparation.
Extemporaneous delivery means speaking from an outline after limited preparation.
A roadmap is a one-sentence preview of the order of your speech, given before the timer starts or in the first seconds.
Signposting means announcing where you are as you move through the speech.
Communication apprehension is anxiety connected to speaking.
A fact resolution asks whether something is, was or will be true.
Every debate needs a criterion, the standard the judge uses to decide who won.
The criterion for a fact debate is preponderance of evidence: the side whose evidence and reasoning, taken together, better support its answer to the resolution wins.
Stock issues are the minimum elements an affirmative needs to win a resolution.
Topicality means the affirmative's arguments must prove the resolution itself is true, not a claim that sounds close to it.
Contentions are the third. A contention is a major argument, built in the Contention Model, that proves the resolution true.
Its arguments are called counter-contentions, contentions that prove the resolution false.
The title is a short label for the contention, two to four words.
The claim is the single sentence the contention proves, the contention's thesis.
The warrants are the evidence and reasoning that prove the claim: Toulmin's grounds, warrant and backing from Chapter 2, gathered in one place.
The implication explains why the claim matters for the resolution, and it is the part beginning debaters most often skip.
The affirmative has the burden of proof: it must prove the resolution true.

If the evidence ends up truly even, the affirmative has not met that burden, and the negative wins. (Chapter 3 called this presumption.) The negative has the burden of rejoinder: it must respond to the affirmative. (After that, as Chapter 3 explained, the burden passes to whoever speaks next.) A negative that ignores the affirmative's contentions and talks about something else leaves those contentions standing, and under preponderance of evidence, an unanswered argument with any support beats no argument at all.
The top of case comes first and sets the terms of the debate: definitions and the criterion.
A definition states what a key word in the resolution means for this debate.
Reasoning is the process of drawing that connection: moving from what you know to what you conclude.
Reasoning by example draws a general conclusion from specific cases. The debater says: "Pass rates went up in Algebra, Statistics and Calculus this year, the first year the center was open."
Causal reasoning argues that one thing produces another.
Reasoning by analogy argues that because two cases are alike in important ways, what is true of one is true of the other.
Sign reasoning argues that one thing is evidence that another exists, without claiming one causes the other.
Reasoning from authority argues that a claim is true because a qualified source says so.
A fallacy is the use of invalid or otherwise faulty reasoning in the construction of an argument.
An appeal to authority claims something is true because an authority says so, when the authority is not an expert on the question or when the authority is the only support offered.
An appeal to popularity (sometimes called ad populum) claims something is true because many people believe it.
An appeal to tradition claims something is right because it has been done that way for a long time.
An ad hominem (Latin for "to the person") attacks the person making an argument instead of the argument. "Don't listen to my opponent's plan to lower tuition.
A red herring is a distraction that pulls attention from the argument at hand, whether the distraction is intentional or not, true or false.
A straw man replaces an opponent's actual position with a distorted or exaggerated version that is easier to beat.
A hasty generalization draws a broad conclusion from evidence that is too small or too unrepresentative to support it.
The no true Scotsman fallacy protects a generalization from a counterexample by redefining the group. A: "No college student actually likes 8 a.m. classes."
A false analogy claims that because two things are alike in one way, they must be alike in another way that does not follow.

A slippery slope claims that one step will lead through a chain of events to an extreme outcome, without showing why each step follows. "If we let students use calculators on one quiz, soon nobody will learn arithmetic, and engineering degrees will be worthless."
A false dilemma (or false dichotomy) presents two options as the only ones when more exist. "Either you transfer to a UC or you've wasted your life."
In debate, research is the process of finding relevant information about the resolution in order to build arguments for your side and answers to your opponent's.
Debate research is goal-oriented research: you know the conclusion you need before you start looking.
The deeper problem is confirmation bias, the tendency to notice, favor and remember information that supports what you already believe.
The most important habit is to be literature-informed: let your reading shape your arguments, instead of deciding your arguments first and then hunting for evidence to fit them.
Exploratory research is research without a specific goal: you are learning the territory.
Focused research has a general goal: you are following up on the questions exploration raised.
Targeted research has a highly specific goal: you are looking for a particular answer that you have reason to believe the literature will confirm.
Learn a few search operators, symbols and commands that tell a search engine exactly what you want. These work in Google and many other search tools:

Your college library's library databases, collections of journals, magazines and newspapers your college pays for, give you sources a search engine cannot. For U.S. policy topics, government sources such as the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the Census Bureau, the Congressional Budget Office and the Congressional Research Service publish data and nonpartisan analysis for free.
Next, look for an open access copy, a version of the article that is legally free to read.
Peer review is the process in which other experts check a study before a journal publishes it, so peer-reviewed academic journals are among the most credible sources you can use.
A think tank is an organization that researches and advocates on public policy.
The fact checkers practiced lateral reading: they quickly left the site and opened new tabs to see what other sources said about it.
Mike Caulfield, a researcher at the University of Washington, condensed fact checkers' habits into four moves called SIFT.
AI chatbots can produce a hallucination: a confident, fluent, specific answer that is simply false, including statistics, quotations and citations to studies that do not exist.
In debate, a card is a single piece of evidence formatted according to the standards of debate.
The tag is a one-sentence summary of what the card proves, written by you, in your words.
The citation is the record of who wrote the evidence, when, and where it was published.

A full citation includes the author's name, the author's qualifications (what makes them an expert), the date, the title, the publication and a link or other way to find it. In a speech you read a short version, usually the author's last name, the year and the qualifications ("Rivera '25, labor economist at the state university"), while the full citation stays in your document so anyone who asks can find the source.
The card text is the evidence itself, copied exactly from the source.
Cutting a card means turning a source into a card.
Highlighting marks the words you will read aloud in a speech. It exists because time is short: a judge does not need every word of a paragraph, only the words that prove the tag.
Then do the part beginning debaters skip: explaining evidence, saying in your own words what the card proves and why it matters for the debate.
Evidence ethics are the rules that keep evidence honest.
The most common violation is reading evidence out of context: presenting a source as supporting a claim it does not support, usually by leaving out the sentences that qualify or contradict it.
Clipping is claiming to read more of a card than you actually read, for example by marking text as highlighted and then skipping parts of it in the speech.
Evidence comparison means giving the judge reasons to prefer your evidence, out loud, in your speech.
Reading different words from an opponent's card to make the same paragraph say something else, often the opposite. A card that can be rehighlighted against you is worse than a weak card.
Audience analysis is the process of identifying an audience and adapting a speech to their interests, level of understanding, attitudes and beliefs.
Interests are how much your audience wants to know about a topic.
Understanding is how well your audience grasps the meaning you intend.
Attitudes are the positive or negative feelings your audience already has toward your content or your delivery.
Beliefs are the statements your audience holds to be true before you say a word.
A lay judge has little or no debate experience: a community member, a parent, a teacher from another field, or a classmate.
A technical judge has debate experience, often as a former competitor or coach.
Many tournaments ask judges to write a judge philosophy, a short statement of how they decide debates, what they like and what they dislike.
Impact calculus is the direct comparison of impacts, and of the scenarios that lead to them, in a debate.
Magnitude is how severe an impact is, whether measured in numbers ("ten million jobs") or described in quality ("the loss of the right to vote").
Probability is the comparative likelihood that an impact happens.
Timeframe is how soon an impact happens and how long it lasts.
Reversibility is the degree to which an impact can be undone once it happens.
Sequencing is how one impact affects whether another will happen.
Cross-examination (often shortened to "cross-x" or "CX") is the period in a debate when one debater asks questions of the debater who just spoke.
The first use is ethos, the speaker credibility Chapter 1 introduced.
The second use is securing a link: asking a question whose answer gives you something to use in your next speech.
The third use is clarification: asking about something you genuinely did not understand.
A better approach climbs toward the conclusion one small step at a time. Call it the question ladder.
Start at the bottom rung with closed questions, questions with short, factual answers, usually yes or no, that your opponent cannot reasonably deny. "Your plan creates a new federal agency?"
Open questions, questions that invite long answers ("Can you explain your solvency?"), have a place but are risky.
A variation is the fork: a question where either answer helps you.
A cross-examination question where one answer clearly gives you access to an argument you are likely to make. Unlike the fork, it needs only one answer to help you.
Experienced debaters also use the reverse pit of doom. Here the questioner makes the opponent think that answering yes is the link, when the answer that actually gives the link is no.
Do not make a concession, an admission that gives up part of your case, unless you mean to.
Constructives come first and build: they present the case, the contentions, the advantages and disadvantages, and the first answers to the other side.
Rebuttals come last and decide: they take everything on the flow and turn it into a reason to vote.
An extension carries an argument from an earlier speech into the current one, so the judge knows it is still alive.
A new argument is an argument that was not made in a constructive and could have been.
To collapse is to choose the few arguments you are most likely to win and spend your rebuttal on them, letting the rest go.
Comparison puts your arguments and your opponent's side by side and explains why yours should win.
The last job of a final rebuttal is writing the ballot: telling the judge, in words they could copy onto their ballot, exactly why you win.
A written ballot names one or two voting issues, the arguments that decide the debate, and explains why they outweigh everything else.
The most useful comparison tool in a rebuttal is the even-if statement: "Even if they win their argument, we still win, because..."
A value resolution asks for a judgment: whether something is good or bad, or whether one thing matters more than another.
A framework is the standard each side asks the judge to use to decide a value debate.
The value is the principle that should matter most in this debate: the thing the judge should try to protect or promote.
The value criterion is how we know whether the value has been achieved: the measurement that turns an abstract value into something a judge can check.
Chapter 2 said that in a value debate, a contention adds a fourth step after the claim, warrant and implication: the tie-back, which shows how the contention meets the criterion.
The framework debate is the part of a value debate where the sides argue about which value and criterion the judge should use.
That is a tautology: a justification that just repeats its conclusion.
This is called turning the framework: showing that even by your opponent's standard, your side wins.
The first is the status quo, the world as it is now, where nobody adopts the plan.
The affirmative's arguments in this structure are called advantages: reasons the world of the plan is better.
The negative's are called disadvantages: reasons the world of the plan is worse.
Uniqueness describes the status quo on the specific subject of your position.
Uniqueness is also directional. You are not just describing the world; you are making a judgment about whether it is going well or badly.
This is predictive uniqueness: "Without the plan, tuition will keep rising for the next five years."
The link is the simplest part of the model.
The internal link explains how the link changes the uniqueness.
The impact is the consequence of the changes the internal link describes.
An impact that ends in harm to people, such as lost lives, poverty or loss of rights, rather than a step along the way.
An impact that already exists at the same level in both worlds is called linear, and it cannot tip the Scale.
Write and deliver positions in subordinated notation: each part of the model is a heading, and each claim under it is numbered, with its support lettered beneath.
Significant harms are the problems that exist in the status quo because the plan has not been adopted.
Inherency is the barrier that keeps the status quo from solving the harms on its own.
Structural inherency is a law, rule or institution that blocks the solution or causes the harm.
Attitudinal inherency is a belief or attitude among decision-makers that prevents the solution: "Congress has been unwilling to regulate AI because members fear slowing American innovation."
Existential inherency argues that because the harm exists, the status quo must be unable to solve it.
The plan is the specific action the affirmative proposes.
It is written as a plan text, one or two sentences that state exactly who does what.
Solvency is the argument that the plan actually fixes the harms.
An advantage is an independent reason the world of the plan is better than the status quo.
Topicality is the requirement that the plan fall within the resolution.
Chapter 15 listed topicality as the sixth stock issue: the requirement that the plan fall within the resolution.
The interpretation is the negative's definition of a word or phrase in the resolution, usually from a source.
The violation explains how the affirmative's plan fails to meet the interpretation.
The standards are the reasons the negative's interpretation is better than the affirmative's.
The voters are the reasons topicality should decide the debate.
A plan is extra-topical when it does what the resolution asks and then adds something the resolution does not include.
A plan is effects topical when its action is not what the resolution describes, but its results might be.
Topicality is usually described as a limit on the affirmative, but it is better understood as a division of ground: the arguments each side is entitled to make.
Proven abuse is ground the negative actually lost in this debate: a disadvantage it read no longer links, or a counterplan it prepared no longer makes sense.
Potential abuse is ground the affirmative's interpretation would let affirmatives take, even if it did not happen here.

Todd Graham and Brandon Merrell, writing in the journal Parliamentary Debate in 2016, argued that the test of topicality should be accuracy: whether the plan fits what the resolution's words actually mean.
